Study guide

The Somali world, from prehistory to today

24 modules researched from scholarly and reference sources: archaeology, population genetics, linguistics, Egyptian and classical texts, medieval chronicles, colonial archives, UN records and current reporting. Every answer in the games names its source, and every module ends with its bibliography and the debates scholars still have.

Module 1 · Geography

Land, climate and environment

1. Five states, one ecological zone

Somali speakers live across five political units: the Federal Republic of Somalia; the self-declared Republic of Somaliland (north-west, not recognised by the United Nations); the Republic of Djibouti; the Somali Regional State of Ethiopia (capital Jigjiga), whose lowlands are often called the Ogaden; and north-eastern Kenya, the former North Eastern Province, now Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties Lewis 2002 Mukhtar 2003. The borders are colonial and post-colonial; the ecology is continuous. Herders cross them every year following rain and grass, a fact that explains much of the region's politics (see m14, m16, m22).

Somalia proper covers about 637,500 km² (637,540 in the Library of Congress study; 637,657 in other references). Its coastline is given as 3,025 km by the Library of Congress and as 3,333 km in many other references; sources differ because of how the coast is measured, but on either figure it is usually called the longest coastline of any mainland African state LoC 1993. Two seas meet at its tip: the Gulf of Aden to the north and the Indian Ocean to the east. They meet at Cape Guardafui (Ras Caseyr), while Ras Hafun, a little to the south, is the easternmost point of the African mainland.

2. The land from north to south

The Library of Congress study divides the north into belts LoC 1993:

  • Guban (literally "burnt [land]"; the LoC glosses it "scrub land"): a hot, scrub-covered coastal plain on the Gulf of Aden, about 12 km wide in the west and as little as 2 km in the east. Its sandy watercourses flow only after rain.
  • The northern ranges: a steep escarpment of ranges running east from the Ethiopian border towards Cape Guardafui, with crests of about 1,800–2,100 m. The LoC calls them the Karkaar; modern usage often calls the western part the Golis and the high eastern block in Sanaag Cal Madow.
  • Cal Madow holds the highest point, Shimbiris, near Erigavo. Its height is given as 2,407 m (LoC), about 2,410–2,416 m and 2,460 m in other references; sources differ. Mist and winter rain feed relict forests of Juniperus procera (African pencil cedar) and many endemic plants.
  • Ogo plateau: a broken upland south of the ranges with no perennial rivers. Its arid eastern part slopes to the Indian Ocean as the Mudug plain; its wetter western part slopes south into the Haud.
  • Haud: undulating grassland and bush that becomes some of the best wet-season grazing in the Horn. It extends more than 60 km into Ethiopia, which is why its transfer to Ethiopia in 1954 became a lasting grievance (m16).
  • Nugaal valley: a long, broad valley in the eastern Ogo with seasonal watercourses, running from the Laas Caanood area to the sea near Eyl, where its seasonal floods reach the Indian Ocean Britannica.

South of the plateau lie the lowlands of the two rivers, a belt of coastal dunes from Mereeg (about 150 km north-east of Mogadishu) to near Kismayo, and the inter-riverine plain between the Shabelle and the Jubba, which the LoC calls the most arable zone of the country and the home of its largest settled population LoC 1993. Granite inselbergs such as Buur Heybe break this plain (m02).

"Guban, ranges, Ogo, Haud"Walk south from Berbera: burnt coastal plain, then the escarpment ranges (Golis/Karkaar, Cal Madow), then the Ogo plateau, then the Haud grasslands that run into Ethiopia.

3. Two permanent rivers

Somalia's only perennial rivers, the Jubba (Webiga Jubba) and the Shabelle (Webiga Shabeelle, "river of leopards"), both rise in the Ethiopian highlands LoC 1993. The Jubba is formed near Doolow, on the Ethiopia–Somalia–Kenya border, by the Ganale (Genale) and Dawa, and enters the Indian Ocean at Goobweyn near Kismayo. The Shabelle runs south-east to within about 30 km of Mogadishu, turns south-west near Balcad and runs parallel to the coast for more than 85 km. It is perennial only to a point south-west of Mogadishu; beyond, it fades into swamps and sand east of Jilib and reaches the Jubba only in high floods. Published lengths for the Shabelle range from about 1,600 km to over 2,000 km (Britannica gives 1,820 km); sources differ according to the method used Britannica.

The rivers carry most of their water during the Ethiopian rains, so floods in Somalia can come even when local rain is poor. They support flood-recession and canal irrigation (the Ajuran works, m10), and in the 20th century the banana and sugar plantations of the lower Shabelle and Jubba (m23).

4. Climate and the four seasons

The Somali lands are arid to semi-arid. Most of Somalia receives under 500 mm of rain a year; the north-east and much of the north 50–150 mm; the south-west 330–500 mm; a few northern highland and coastal sites over 500 mm LoC 1993. Temperatures exceed 45 °C on the Gulf of Aden plain in July but can fall below freezing on the northern heights in December. The main reason for the aridity is geography: the Ethiopian and Kenyan highlands block moisture from the Atlantic and the Congo basin, so Somali rain comes from the Indian Ocean alone Reid et al. 2019.

Rain is bimodal. Herders organise the year into four seasons LoC 1993 Hadden 2007:

SeasonMonths (approx.)Character
JilaalDecember–MarchLong dry season; the hardest for herds; animals crowd at permanent wells.
GuApril–JuneMain rains; fresh pasture; herds disperse to wet-season grazing such as the Haud.
Xagaa (Hagaa)July–SeptemberSecond dry season; hot and windy in the north, with light coastal showers in the south.
Deyr (Dayr)October–NovemberShort rains; more variable than the Gu.

Year-to-year swings are large. The Deyr in particular follows sea-surface temperatures in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific: warm western Indian Ocean conditions tend to bring floods, cool ones (as with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole in 2020–22) failed rains Reid et al. 2019 WMO/IGAD alert 2022.

Trap: the Gu is the main rainy season (spring), not the dry one, and Jilaal is the winter dry season. Learners often swap Gu and Jilaal, or treat Xagaa ("summer") as wet everywhere; it brings showers only on parts of the southern coast.

5. Monsoon winds and the sea

The western Indian Ocean has the strongest seasonal wind reversal on earth. From about December to February or March the north-east monsoon blows down the Somali coast; from about May or June to September the south-west monsoon blows up it, focused by a low-level jet (the Findlater or Somali jet) Schott & McCreary 2001. The south-west monsoon drives the fast Somali Current northwards and causes cold upwelling off the coast. That upwelling feeds rich fisheries but chills the coastal air, one reason the coast is so dry.

For traders the winds were a timetable. Ships from Arabia and India reached the Somali ports on the north-east monsoon and returned on the south-west; Greek ships from Egypt left in about July to catch the season for the "far-side" ports described in the Periplus Casson 1989. The full story of monsoon trade is in m06; here the point is that climate set the rhythm of commerce as much as of herding.

"North-east in winter, south-west in summer"NE monsoon (Dec–Mar) brings ships from Arabia and India south-west to the Somali coast; SW monsoon (Jun–Sep) carries them back and whips up the Somali Current.

6. Drought, famine and their causes

Drought is a recurring hazard; famine is a political and economic outcome. Somali pastoralism is built for drought: mobile herds, mixed species, and kinship networks that share wells and grazing Lewis 1961. Famines happen when drought combines with war, blocked access, market shocks or weak relief.

EventKey facts
1974–75 Daba Dheer ("long-tailed") droughtHit the Nugaal and other northern and central pastoral areas; the government moved many nomads to farming and fishing settlements in the south (m18) LoC 1993.
1992 famineDrought plus civil war in the inter-riverine south (m19).
2010–12 famineUN declared famine in Bakool and Lower Shabelle on 20 July 2011; declared over in February 2012. Estimated 258,000 excess deaths (October 2010 to April 2012), about 52% of them children under five Checchi & Robinson 2013.
2020–23 droughtRepeated failed rainy seasons from late 2020; an estimated 43,000 excess deaths in 2022, about half children under five AP 2023.

The 2013 mortality study for FAO and FEWS NET states the logic directly: the 2010–11 drought produced the poorest harvests since 1992–93, but its effects were compounded by reduced humanitarian assistance and rising food prices Checchi & Robinson 2013. Access restrictions by al-Shabaab also mattered (m20).

"Drought is the trigger, not the cause"Hazard + conflict + prices + blocked aid = famine. 2011: 258,000 deaths, half of them under-fives.

7. Plants, animals and herds

The arid north-east is the home of the frankincense trees (Boswellia) and myrrh trees (Commiphora), long exported from Somalia LoC 1993 Thulin & Warfa 1987. Two frankincense species matter most. Boswellia sacra (which now includes the old name B. carteri) grows in Oman, Yemen and the Somali north; Boswellia frereana is endemic to northern Somalia and yields the resin called maydi, sold abroad as "Coptic frankincense". Myrrh comes chiefly from Commiphora myrrha. These resins link the Somali coast to Punt (m05) and the Periplus (m06).

Elsewhere, acacia–commiphora bush dominates; the Haud shows banded "tiger bush"; aloes and candelabra euphorbias grow in the northern ranges; mangroves line the coast south of Kismayo. Endemic animals include the silver dik-dik, the Somali golden mole, the Warsangli linnet of Cal Madow, Ash's lark and the Obbia lark. Larger species once widespread are now rare: the Somali wild ass, the beira, the dibatag and the hirola (on the Kenya–Somalia border) are all threatened IUCN Red List.

The domestic economy rests on the camel (geel), sheep and goats (ari) and, in wetter southern areas, cattle (lo') Lewis 1961. Somalia has one of the largest camel herds in the world. Camels supply milk through the dry season, carry water and goods, and serve as the main unit of bridewealth and blood-compensation (m12).

8. Administrative geography

Before 1991 Somalia had 18 regions (gobollo, singular gobol): Awdal, Woqooyi Galbeed, Togdheer, Sanaag, Sool, Bari, Nugaal, Mudug, Galguduud, Hiiraan, Middle Shabelle, Lower Shabelle, Banaadir (Mogadishu), Bay, Bakool, Gedo, Middle Jubba and Lower Jubba Mukhtar 2003. They remain the reference grid for statistics and humanitarian maps, but power now runs through Somaliland and the federal member states (m21). Somaliland claims the five north-western regions of the former British protectorate, though Sool and eastern Sanaag are contested.

Scholarly debates

How long is Somalia's coastline, and is it the longest in mainland Africa?

Published figures differ: 3,025 km (Library of Congress country study, older CIA data) and 3,333 km (many other references and Somali official use). The gap comes from different measurement scales and methods. Both figures exceed those usually given for other mainland African states, so the 'longest in mainland Africa' claim is widely repeated, but the exact length is a convention, not a fixed fact.

Was the 2011 famine mainly a natural disaster or a political one?

Climate scientists and the FAO/FEWS NET mortality study agree that two failed rainy seasons linked to La Niña caused the worst harvests since 1992–93. The same study, humanitarian analysts and later reviews stress the compounding factors: rising food prices, reduced humanitarian assistance, al-Shabaab's restrictions on aid agencies and Western counter-terrorism rules that slowed funding. Most specialists now treat it as a drought turned into famine by conflict and policy, not as a purely natural event.

Module 2 · Prehistory

Prehistory and archaeology

1. The Horn in deep time

The Horn of Africa holds some of the oldest evidence for human technology and for our own species. Oldowan stone tools at Gona in Ethiopia's Afar region date to about 2.6 million years ago Semaw et al. 1997, and the Omo I skull from Omo Kibish in southern Ethiopia is at least about 233,000 years old, among the earliest Homo sapiens fossils known Vidal et al. 2022. The Somali lands sit beside these sites and beside the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one proposed route out of Africa. Yet the Somali archaeological record is thin: Acheulean hand-axes and Middle Stone Age (MSA) tools were collected from surface and river-terrace contexts in the colonial period, but few deposits have been excavated and dated Clark 1954 Brandt 1986. Absence of evidence here mostly reflects absence of research.

2. Naming the Stone Age: Clark's industries

The first synthesis was J. Desmond Clark's The Prehistoric Cultures of the Horn of Africa (1954), based on wartime survey in British Somaliland and earlier Italian work in the south. Clark, building on Italian work, grouped finds into regional industries named after type-sites or areas. Several names are still used, though most have been re-examined Clark 1954 Brandt 1986:

IndustryNamed afterCharacterCurrent status
HargeisanHargeisaBlades and burins together with Levallois (MSA-style) flakingRevived by Gutherz et al. 2014 from Laas Geel Shelter 7 as a mixed MSA/LSA facies of the end of the Pleistocene
Somaliland WiltonWilton (South African type-site)Microlithic Later Stone Age (LSA) industry of the northRefined with new data from upper Shelter 7
EibianBur Eibe (Buur Heybe); term from GraziosiPressure-flaked tools, partly on exotic chert, with wild fauna onlyKept by Brandt for the terminal-Pleistocene LSA at Buur Heybe
Doiana name of uncertain derivation in Clark's scheme (not explained in the sources checked)Later Stone Age complex of the south, with a "Lower Doian" phase transitional from the MagosianDefined from small surface collections; a coarse label, rarely used now; needs re-study with dated sites
"Hargeisan north, Eibian south"Stone Age industries are named after places: Hargeisan after Hargeisa in the north-west, Eibian after the Bur Eibe (Buur Heybe) inselberg in the south. "Somaliland Wilton" borrows a South African type-name.

In 2014 Xavier Gutherz and colleagues published the lithics from Shelter 7 at Laas Geel. The upper deposits held microlithic LSA industries; the lower deposits combined LSA blade and bladelet production with Levallois technique. That combination, they argued, reopens the question of a real "Hargeisan" phase and gives new evidence on the MSA–LSA transition in the Horn Gutherz et al. 2014.

3. Buur Heybe: hunters, burials and climate

Buur Heybe (Bur Eibe) is a large granite inselberg about 180 km north-west of Mogadishu in Bay region, in the inter-riverine south. More than 100 rockshelters are known there Reid et al. 2019. Paolo Graziosi excavated at the shelter of Gogoshiis Qabe in the 1930s (1935 in the account derived from Brandt; Reid et al. say the late 1930s) and published in 1940; this is usually called the first professional excavation in Somalia. Between 1983 and 1989 Steven Brandt's Buur Ecological and Archaeological Project (BEAP) re-excavated the site. It found a Late Pleistocene–Holocene sequence at Guli Waabayo and an early-to-late Holocene sequence at Gogoshiis Qabe Reid et al. 2019 Brandt 1988.

  • Burials: Brandt (1988), still the only detailed report, describes fourteen individuals from the early Holocene: eleven articulated primary burials, one secondary burial and two people represented by teeth. They are among the earliest dated evidence of mortuary practice in the Horn. Some graves contained horn cores of lesser kudu Brandt 1988.
  • Industries: Brandt kept Graziosi's term Eibian for the terminal-Pleistocene LSA and named a new early-to-mid Holocene industry, the Bardaale, made mostly on local quartz and limestone.
  • Climate: tooth-enamel isotopes from dik-dik and warthog show the African Humid Period (about 14,000–5,000 years ago) was wetter and less seasonal here than today, though less pronounced than further west, and that aridity increased towards the present Reid et al. 2019.

Guli Waabayo's radiocarbon dates on ostrich eggshell suggest use over about 30,000 years; this figure appears in only one source consulted here. The Eyle, agro-pastoralist potters and part-time hunters who live around Buur Heybe, are often described as descendants of earlier hunter-gatherers of the south; this is an ethnographic interpretation, not a genetic finding (see m03).

4. Laas Geel and the rock art of the north

Laas Geel ("the camel's well") is a granite outcrop at about 950 m on the Hargeisa–Berbera road, at the confluence of two seasonal rivers. Local people had long known the paintings, but they were first documented scientifically in November–December 2002 by the French mission Premières sociétés de production dans la Corne de l'Afrique, led by Xavier Gutherz of Université Paul-Valéry Montpellier Gutherz et al. 2003 French Ministry of Culture. The preliminary 2003 note described about ten decorated shelters; later work counts about twenty Gutherz et al. 2014 British Museum.

The art is polychrome: red, white, black, violet, brown and yellow. Most images show humpless cattle with lyre-shaped horns and marked udders. Their necks are drawn as wide rectangles filled with stripes, read as ceremonial mats or "plastrons". Small human figures with arms outstretched, sometimes holding a bow, stick or shield, stand beside the cows. Dogs are common; antelopes, possible monkeys and two giraffes are rare British Museum.

Dating. Laas Geel is better dated than most rock art because the French team excavated a shelter and recovered fallen fragments of painted wall from dated layers. They proposed the mid-4th to mid-3rd millennium BCE, making it one of the oldest pieces of evidence for cattle-keeping in the Horn; the French ministry summary gives the 3rd millennium BCE British Museum French Ministry of Culture. One caution: the excavated bovine bones were too poorly preserved to show whether the cattle were domestic.

Trap: "discovered in 2002" means documented by archaeologists in 2002. The local community already knew the site. And despite the name "camel's well", the paintings show cattle, not camels: camels enter Somali rock art much later.

Style and other sites. Pavel Červíček coined the term "Ethiopian-Arabian style" in 1971 for the Horn–Arabian rock-art tradition. Laas Geel fits that tradition but has its own features, and similar images at Dhaga Koure, Dhambalin and Karinhegane now support a distinct "Laas Geel style" British Museum. About 70 rock-art sites are now known in Somaliland.

  • Dhambalin (Sahil region, about 60 km east of Berbera): a sandstone shelter reported to Sada Mire by residents of Beenyo Dhaadheer in 2007. It shows cattle, goats, giraffes, hunters with bows and dogs, fourteen sheep, the first sheep identified in Somali rock art, and a hunter on an animal that may be a horse; Mire dates it stylistically to roughly 5,000–3,000 years ago Mire 2008.
  • Karinhegane (eastern Sanaag, between Las Khorey and El Ayo): a large panel of animal paintings in the Laas Geel tradition. Inscriptions there have been estimated at about 2,500 years old, a figure from older guidebook and survey literature that needs confirmation Hodd 1994, via Wikipedia.

5. Herds arrive: a relative chronology

Because few sites are excavated, archaeologists build a relative sequence from style and superimposition British Museum:

  1. Mid-3rd to 2nd millennium BCE (older at Laas Geel): naturalistic humpless cattle, sheep, goats and some wild animals.
  2. Progressive schematism; from the 1st millennium BCE, armed men with spears, bows and shields, sometimes fighting.
  3. Dromedaries appear around the end of the 1st millennium BCE; humped zebu cattle between the 1st century BCE and 1st century CE.
  4. Geometric signs, often read in Somalia as clan marks, appear late.

The French team describes the same order at Laas Geel itself: flat-backed cattle first, then new cattle forms, fat-tailed sheep and wild animals, and finally engraved camel herds French Ministry of Culture. The camel, now the emblem of Somali pastoralism, is a late arrival compared with cattle.

"Cows first, camels last"Cattle are painted from the 4th–3rd millennium BCE; camels only from the late 1st millennium BCE; humped zebu around the turn of the era.

6. Cairns, stelae and settlements

Stone cairns (taallo), stelae and burial mounds are widespread across the north; near Laas Geel, tombs marked by stelae and mounds stand close to the shelters British Museum. Few have been excavated or dated, so most cannot yet be tied to particular periods or peoples. Sada Mire's surveys place many of them in a landscape of ritual sites, and in Divine Fertility (2020) she argues that an ideology of "sacred kinship" and divine fertility, visible in cattle imagery, persisted in transformed form into later Somali practice Mire 2020. That is an interpretive model, not a consensus.

Towns came later. Coastal trading places of the classical era (m06) and the walled medieval towns of Awdal, such as Amud and Abasa, first surveyed by A. T. Curle in the 1930s (m08), belong to the historical period Curle 1937.

7. Why the record is so thin

Research history explains much. Miles Burkitt and P. E. Glover made the first rock-art studies in British Somaliland in the 1940s; Clark published in 1954; Italian teams worked briefly in the north-east in the late 1950s British Museum. After that, conflict stopped most work. The BEAP fieldwork ended in 1989 as war spread, and its collections survived only because they had been taken to the United States; the National Museum in Mogadishu was destroyed in the civil war Reid et al. 2019. Relative stability in Somaliland allowed the Laas Geel work and Mire's surveys, while the French mission reports that Puntland is still closed to foreign researchers French Ministry of Culture. Somaliland, unrecognised, cannot nominate sites under the 1972 World Heritage Convention, which only states parties can use UNESCO 1972. Mire, who directed Somaliland's Department of Archaeology, argues for a "knowledge-centred" heritage practice that protects local knowledge and use of sites, not only objects Mire 2007.

Scholarly debates

How old is the Laas Geel art, and how secure is its date?

The French team under Gutherz proposed the mid-4th to mid-3rd millennium BCE from painted fragments in excavated layers; the French ministry summary gives the 3rd millennium BCE. The British Museum notes that older dates have also been proposed. The date applies firmly only to the excavated shelter; other panels are placed by style. Whether the cattle were domestic cannot be shown from the bones, so 'earliest cattle-keepers' rests on the imagery.

Was there a real 'Hargeisan' industry?

Clark (1954) defined the Hargeisan from surface and poorly stratified collections; later reviews (Brandt 1986) treated many of Clark's industries cautiously. Gutherz et al. (2014) found LSA blade production combined with Levallois in the lower deposits of Laas Geel Shelter 7 and argued this revives the Hargeisan as a terminal-Pleistocene facies with mixed MSA/LSA features. More dated sequences are needed before it is accepted as a regional stage.

Do the Laas Geel cattle paintings show continuity with later Somali culture?

Sada Mire (2020) argues that ideas of sacred kinship and divine fertility visible in the cattle imagery persisted in transformed form for about three millennia. Others treat the paintings as the work of early herders whose links to later populations are unknown. Without excavated, dated sequences across the intervening periods, continuity is an interpretation, not a demonstrated fact.

Module 3 · Origins

Genetics and population history

1. What genetics can and cannot tell us

Population genetics measures how often particular DNA variants occur in samples of living (or ancient) people, and models how those frequencies arose. It describes probabilistic patterns of shared ancestry. It does not define who is Somali, which clan a person belongs to, or anyone's worth. Somali identity rests on language, religion, culture and the genealogical system (abtirsiinyo), all social facts that genes neither confirm nor refute Lewis 1998. Every figure below belongs to a specific study, sample and method, and should be read as a range, not a fixed property of "the Somali people".

Trap: A haplogroup is a branch of one line of descent (father-to-son Y chromosome, or mother-to-child mitochondrial DNA). It is a tiny fraction of a person's ancestry. A man who carries E-V32 is not "more Somali" than one who carries T or J, and no haplogroup maps onto a clan.

2. The paternal line: E-M78 and E-V32

The most striking Somali result is a very high frequency of one Y-chromosome lineage. Sanchez et al. 2005 typed 45 Y markers in 201 Somali men: 14 haplogroups appeared, led by E3b1 (today called E-M78) at 77.6% and K2 (today T-M70) at 10.4%. A single E3b1 sub-cluster marked by the rare DYS19-11 allele, "cluster γ", reached 75.1%. This cluster was later defined by the SNP V32, so it is now written E-V32. The authors estimated that the lineage entered the Somali population about 4,000–5,000 years ago, and that roughly 15% of Somali Y chromosomes trace to Eurasia and about 5% to sub-Saharan Africa. Haplotype diversity (0.9575) was well below European and Asian averages (0.9974 and 0.9996), a sign of strong founder effects.

Smaller samples give lower figures. In Cruciani et al. 2004 (3,401 men worldwide), 23 Somali men carried E-M78 at 52.2%, most of them in cluster γ (47.8%), while the Kenyan Borana showed 71.4% and Ethiopian Oromo 32.0%. A later paper on 6,501 Y chromosomes from 81 populations Cruciani et al. 2007 argued for a north-eastern African origin of E-M78, with migrations between north-eastern and eastern Africa in at least two episodes (about 23.9–17.3 and 18.0–5.9 thousand years ago). Hodgson et al. 2014 summarise this work: E-M78 arose in north-east Africa around 19 ka, and E-V32, characteristic of the Horn, was there by at least 6 ka. So the dominant Somali paternal lineage is an African lineage with deep roots in the Horn, not a recent arrival from Arabia.

Three names, one lineageE3b1 cluster γ (2005) = E-M78γ (2004) = E-V32 (2007 onwards). Old K2 = today's T-M70. Check the year before comparing figures across papers.
StudySampleKey Somali result

3. The maternal line: L, M1 and N

Mitochondrial DNA tells a different story. Mikkelsen et al. 2012 sequenced the full control region of 190 unrelated Somalis: 60.5% of haplotypes were of sub-Saharan origin, with L0a1d, L2a1h and L3f most common. The authors stress the contrast with the Y chromosome, where only about 5% of lineages are sub-Saharan. The rest of the maternal pool includes M1 and N-derived lineages. M1 has its highest frequency and diversity in the Horn; many Horn M1 lineages split from relatives elsewhere 20–30 thousand years ago, and N1a and N2a lineages diverged from Middle Eastern relatives 15–20 ka Hodgson et al. 2014. The paternal and maternal lines therefore have different histories, a pattern called sex-biased gene flow.

Fathers 75, mothers 60About three-quarters of Somali Y chromosomes are one Horn-rooted lineage (E-V32); about 60% of maternal lineages are sub-Saharan L types. Two lines, two histories.

4. Autosomal ancestry and the "Ethio-Somali" component

Genome-wide (autosomal) data sample the whole of ancestry. Pagani et al. 2012 genotyped 235 people from ten Ethiopian groups plus South Sudanese and 23 Somalis (expatriates in Islamabad). Cushitic and Semitic speakers carried a 40–50% "non-African" component, closer to the Levant and Egypt than to Arabia, which they dated to about 3,000 years ago. Pickrell et al. 2014 estimated 38.4% west-Eurasian-related ancestry in Somalis (37.9% in Ethiopian Somalis, 41.6% in Oromo, 46.0% in Afar) and dated the main eastern African admixture to 2,700–3,300 years ago.

Hodgson et al. 2014 partitioned genomes into African and non-African segments. Most of the non-African ancestry formed a distinct "Ethio-Somali" component, highest in Somalis (about 57% in their Somali sample) and found in all admixed Horn groups. It is differentiated from North African, Levantine and Arabian ancestry, diverged from them at least 23,000 years ago, and lacks the Arabian lactase-persistence allele (only 1.6% in Somalis). They argued that it entered the Horn in a pre-agricultural "back-to-Africa" migration, with smaller Arabian and Eurasian inputs within the last few thousand years. Their own linkage-disequilibrium dates for Somalis (about 2.6–2.9 ka) are recent, but simulations showed that later pulses can mask earlier ones.

"Non-African" is not "Arab"Hodgson's Ethio-Somali component is a back-migrated ancestry at least 23,000 years old, older than farming and far older than Islam or the Arabian genealogical traditions.

Ancient DNA sharpens the picture. The Mota genome from south-west Ethiopia, a man who lived about 4,500 years ago, shows no such Eurasian admixture Gallego Llorente et al. 2015. The paper's claim that the backflow reached West and Central Africa was withdrawn in a 2016 erratum after a bioinformatics error; the eastern African finding stood. A reassessment Molinaro et al. 2019 showed that the large autochthonous African share of Ethiopian genomes makes the exact Eurasian source hard to pin down. A sample of 95 people from north-east Somalia Ali et al. 2020 found a homogeneous population with roughly 60% East African and 40% west Eurasian-related ancestry, close to Cushitic- and Semitic-speaking Ethiopians.

5. Cushitic neighbours and the Jareer

Somalis cluster genetically with other Cushitic speakers. Sanchez et al. describe the Somali male population as closely related to the Oromo; E-M78γ peaks in the Kenyan Borana. The Afar show similar admixture proportions. Among the Beja of Sudan, the Beni Amer share an ancestry component with Somalis, and admixture with a Somali-like source was dated to about 59–75 generations ago Hollfelder et al. 2017. Genetic structure tracks language family broadly Pagani et al. 2012, but language spreads by learning as well as by descent.

Published genome-wide data on the Somali Bantu (Jareer, Gosha) are very scarce; most Somali samples come from Somali-speaking pastoral or urban populations. Historians identify two strands: long-established riverine farming communities on the Jubba and Shabelle, and descendants of people enslaved in East Africa (e.g. Zigua, Yao, Makua) and brought to the Benadir plantations in the 19th century Besteman 1999 Cassanelli 1982. Their history is one of social exclusion, and genetic labels should never be used to reinforce it (see m12).

6. Genes, genealogy and language

Somali clan genealogies trace descent through men, and some trace founders to Arabian ancestors such as Sheikh Darod or Sheikh Isaaq (see m07, m12). The Y data are consistent with patrilineal social organisation: Horn Y lineages show low diversity and strong subdivision between groups Iacovacci et al. 2017. But the dominant E-V32 lineage is rooted in the Horn thousands of years before Islam. Genetics can neither confirm nor refute a named ancestor; genealogies are political and moral charters, not lab results Lewis 1998. Language is a third, separate line of inheritance.

Trap: Do not read "west Eurasian ancestry" as proof of Arabian descent, or "sub-Saharan mtDNA" as evidence against it. Labels such as "west Eurasian", "Ethiopic" or "Ethio-Somali" are statistical components defined against reference panels, and change with the panel and the K value.

7. Limits and ethics

  • Small, unusual samples: 23 expatriates in Pakistan (Pagani); 23 men (Cruciani 2004); a north-eastern sample (Ali 2020). Southern, riverine and minority communities are under-sampled.
  • Changing nomenclature makes older and newer figures hard to compare.
  • Dating methods (ROLLOFF, ALDER) mostly capture the latest admixture pulse.
  • History of misuse: colonial "Hamitic" race theory treated Horn peoples as part-"Caucasian" outsiders Sanders 1969. Modern findings must not be recycled into such hierarchies.

Scholarly debates

When and how did the non-African ancestry in Somalis arrive?

Pagani et al. 2012 and Pickrell et al. 2014 date the main admixture to c. 3,000 years ago (2,700–3,300) from a Levantine/Egyptian-related source. Hodgson et al. 2014 argue most of it is an older Ethio-Somali component (diverged ≥23 ka) that probably arrived before farming, with LD dates reflecting only later pulses. Molinaro et al. 2019 show the source is hard to pin down. Current weight: both a deep component and a c. 3 ka pulse are plausible; the relative size of each is unresolved.

Where did E-V32 arise and when did it reach the Horn?

Cruciani et al. 2007 place E-M78 in north-east Africa with migrations along a Nile/Horn corridor; E-V32 was in the Horn by at least 6 ka (Hodgson's summary). Sanchez et al. 2005 dated the Somali cluster to 4,000–5,000 years ago using STR rates. Differences reflect mutation-rate assumptions and sampling. The consensus is an African origin, with dates uncertain by thousands of years.

What can genetics say about Somali clan genealogies and Arabian-ancestor traditions?

Historians (Lewis) treat genealogies as political charters. The dominant Y lineage is Horn-rooted and far older than Islam, which sits poorly with literal descent of whole clans from Arabian sheikhs. Some Eurasian-related Y lineages (c. 15%) exist, but none can be tied to a named ancestor. Most specialists treat genetic 'tests' of genealogy as category errors.

Module 4 · Language

Language and writing

1. A Cushitic language

Somali (Af Soomaali) belongs to the Cushitic branch of the Afroasiatic family, the family that also includes Semitic (Arabic, Amharic), Berber, Chadic, Omotic and ancient Egyptian. Within Cushitic it is East Cushitic, more precisely Lowland East Cushitic, alongside Afar and Saho and Oromo Lewis 1998 Saeed 1999. Its closest relatives are smaller languages of northern Kenya and the lower Tana, such as Rendille and Boni (Aweer). With Oromo, Somali is one of the two most widely spoken Cushitic languages, and it is the best documented, with academic study going back to the late 19th century Saeed 1999. Ethnologue's recent estimates put first-language speakers at roughly 22–24 million across Somalia, Somaliland, Djibouti, Ethiopia's Somali Region, north-eastern Kenya and the diaspora (single reference source; counts are uncertain because no full census has been held since the 1970s).

Trap: Somali is not a Semitic language and is not descended from Arabic. Arabic is a distant relative in the same Afroasiatic family and a heavy lender of vocabulary, but Somali's grammar is Cushitic.

2. Varieties: Maxaa tiri, Maay and the coast

Linguists group Somali speech into three or more clusters Saeed 1999 Lamberti 1986:

  • Northern / Common Somali, often called Maxaa tiri ("what did you say?" in its own form). It is spoken from Djibouti and Somaliland through Ethiopia's Somali Region to north-eastern Kenya, and in much of central and southern Somalia. A northern variety became the basis of the standard written language.
  • Benadir (coastal) varieties of Mogadishu and the central coast, largely intelligible with Northern Somali.
  • Maay (Af-Maay, "Maay tiri"), spoken mainly by the Digil and Mirifle (Rahanweyn) of the inter-riverine south, around Baidoa, Bay and Bakool. It differs in sound system, vocabulary and grammar and is only partly intelligible to Maxaa speakers; some classifications, including Ethnologue's, treat it as a separate language.
  • Smaller urban varieties such as Ashraaf in Mogadishu's Shingaani quarter and in Merca, studied by Lamberti.

The 2012 Provisional Constitution gives the official language as "Somali (Maay and Maxaa-tiri)", with Arabic as "the second language" (Article 5) Constitution 2012. This formula recognised Maay after decades in which state media, schools and the 1972 orthography used the northern-based standard.

Maxaa vs MaayBoth names come from the phrase "what did you say?". Maxaa is the standard; Maay is the language of the southern farming clans. The 2012 constitution names both.

3. Contact and loanwords

Centuries of Islam and Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade brought many Arabic loanwords, especially in religion, law, administration and learning. Their share of the vocabulary is sometimes put at about a fifth, but that figure could not be confirmed in a published study and should be treated as a rough estimate. Colonial rule added Italian words in the south and English in the north, mostly for modern objects and institutions. After 1972 the military government encouraged coining Somali terms in place of foreign ones.

4. Writing before 1972

For most of its history Somali was an oral language with a rich poetic tradition (see m24). Writing was done in Arabic. Religious scholars (wadaad) sometimes wrote Somali in an adapted Arabic script, known in scholarship as "wadaad's writing"; spelling was not standardised, and Arabic letters do not fit Somali's vowel length and some consonants well Lewis 1958.

In the 20th century several Somalis invented indigenous scripts:

ScriptInventorDateNotes
Osmanya (Far Soomaali)Osman Yusuf Kenadid, son of Sultan Yusuf Ali Kenadid of Hobyo (see m11)c. 1920–1922Left-to-right alphabet with letters for long vowels; later backed by many Somali Youth League nationalists
Borama (Gadabuursi) scriptSheikh Abdurahman Sheikh Nuur, later qadi of Boramac. 1933Used mainly by its inventor's circle and some merchants in Borama and Zeila; published by Lewis in 1958
KaddareHussein Sheikh Ahmed Kaddare1952Appraised by the language committee as an accurate indigenous script; no books are known in it

Sources: Lewis 1958 Laitin 1977 Tosco 2010.

5. The script debate, 1960–1972

At independence in 1960 the Somali Republic had no official written form of its national language; government worked in English, Italian and Arabic. A Somali Language Committee was set up to choose a script. Accounts of how many proposals it examined differ: a figure of 18 (11 new inventions, 4 Arabic-based, 3 Latin) derives from Laitin, while the Library of Congress country study says nine Laitin 1977 Metz 1993. Its 1962 report favoured a Latin script as best suited to Somali phonemes Metz 1993. A 1966 UNESCO mission (B. W. Andrzejewski, S. Strelcyn, J. Tubiana) was critical of the indigenous and Arabic options and had few objections to Latin, though sources differ on whether it made a formal recommendation UNESCO 1966.

The question split the country. Advocates of Arabic stressed Islam and the Arab world; opponents of Latin coined the jibe "Laatiin waa laa diin" ("Latin means no religion"). Osmanya had nationalist appeal but raised fears of clan association and printing costs. Latin supporters, such as the linguist Shire Jama Ahmed, pointed to existing typewriters and presses. Civilian governments (1960–69) postponed a decision for fear of unrest Laitin 1977.

21 October 1972The third anniversary of Siad Barre's coup: the Supreme Revolutionary Council adopted a Latin script and made Somali the official language from 1 January 1973. Arabic, Osmanya and the other scripts lost the race.

6. Adoption and the literacy campaigns

The SRC revived the committee in 1971 and on 21 October 1972 announced a Latin-based orthography, effective 1 January 1973 Metz 1993. Civil servants were required to work in written Somali, newspapers and school texts followed, and Somali became the language of primary and later secondary teaching. The government then ran mass campaigns: an urban and settled-area campaign in 1973, in three-month sessions with up to about 8,000 teachers, and a rural campaign from August 1974 in which schools closed and more than 20,000 teachers, about half of them secondary pupils, went to the nomads (other accounts give 25,000–30,000; sources differ) Metz 1993. The rural campaign overlapped with the Daba Dheer drought of 1974–75, and many teachers turned to relief work (see m18). Literacy was estimated at about 5% in 1972; government claims of rapid gains were not sustained, and the UN put adult literacy at about 24% in 1990 Metz 1993.

7. The Latin orthography

The alphabet is largely phonemic and uses ordinary Latin letters for sounds Latin lacks: c = voiced pharyngeal /ʕ/ (Arabic ʿayn), x = voiceless pharyngeal /ħ/ (Arabic ḥāʾ), q = uvular /q/, dh = retroflex /ɖ/, and kh mainly in Arabic loans. Long vowels are doubled (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu), and the apostrophe marks the glottal stop. There is no p, v or z in native words. Tone and the front/back vowel-harmony distinction are not written Saeed 1999.

C and X are throat lettersSomali C = Arabic ʿayn (Cali = ʿAlī); Somali X = Arabic ḥāʾ (Xamar = Ḥamar, Mogadishu's old quarter). Q stays q.

8. Grammar highlights

  • Word order is basically subject–object–verb, but very flexible because of focus marking.
  • Focus markers: baa and ayaa follow a focused noun phrase placed before the verb, and waxa(a) allows the focused element after the verb. Waa marks declarative sentences without a focused noun Saeed 1999.
  • Tone or pitch accent: a high pitch on a particular mora carries grammar, distinguishing for example gender (ínan "boy" vs inán "girl") and case (subject vs other forms). Andrzejewski analysed Somali as a tone language; others prefer the term pitch accent.
  • Gender polarity: many nouns switch grammatical gender between singular and plural, so a masculine singular can take a feminine plural, a feature shared with other Afroasiatic languages Tosco 2000.
  • Vowel harmony: five vowel qualities, short and long, in front and back harmonic sets Saeed 1999.
  • Definite articles are suffixes with consonant variation (-ka, -ta and their variants), e.g. nin "man" → ninka "the man".

9. Institutions and status today

Somali is official in Somalia and Somaliland, a working language of Ethiopia's Somali Region, and a national (though not official) language in Djibouti, where French and Arabic are official. In June 2013 Djibouti, Somalia and Ethiopia launched an Intergovernmental (Regional) Academy of the Somali Language in Djibouti; its Mogadishu headquarters were inaugurated on 29 December 2022 by the presidents of Somalia and Djibouti Villa Somalia 2022. A large diaspora literature, radio, satellite TV and social media now carry the language worldwide.

Scholarly debates

Is Maay a dialect of Somali or a separate language?

Lamberti and Saeed treat Maay as a major Somali dialect group; Ethnologue assigns it a separate code because of limited intelligibility. Rahanweyn activists have pressed for recognition, and the 2012 constitution names 'Maay and Maxaa-tiri' together. The answer depends on whether one weighs intelligibility, shared grammar or political identity.

Was the 1972 Latin decision technical or political?

Laitin argues it was a political act enabled by military rule after civilian governments stalled; supporters stress technical fit and printing costs, as in the 1962 committee report and the 1966 UNESCO experts. Critics, especially advocates of Arabic, saw it as a cultural break. Most scholars accept that technical arguments favoured Latin and that only the military regime could impose it.

How successful were the literacy campaigns?

The SRC claimed dramatic gains; external observers credited a real expansion of Somali-language schooling and print. But the UN estimate of 24% adult literacy in 1990 shows gains were limited or reversed by war, drought and state decline. Assessment depends on whether one measures short-term mobilisation or lasting literacy.

Module 5 · Antiquity

Punt and the ancient Red Sea

1. What Egyptians meant by Punt

Punt (Egyptian Pwenet) was the land from which Egypt obtained aromatic resins for temple ritual, above all antyw (usually translated "myrrh") and senetjer (incense), together with ebony, ivory, gold and electrum, aromatic woods, leopard skins, live animals such as baboons, and eye cosmetic Kitchen 1993 Tyldesley 1996. Egyptian texts never describe Punt as a city or a state with fixed borders; it is a region reached by long, risky voyages down the Red Sea. Trade with it is recorded for about thirteen centuries, from about 2500 to 1170 BCE Dominy et al. 2020.

Punt was also called Ta Netjer, "God's Land". The phrase marked lands to the east, towards the sunrise, that supplied sacred products. It was not unique to Punt: Breasted noted that it was also applied to eastern regions in Asia, such as Lebanon, the source of cedar Breasted 1906. Calling Punt "God's Land" therefore tells us about its religious value to Egypt, not about its location.

"Myrrh, ebony, baboons, gold"Four things Egypt wanted from Punt: resin for the gods, black wood, sacred animals of Thoth, and precious metal.

2. Thirteen centuries of voyages

PeriodRuler or sourceWhat is recorded
5th Dynasty, c. 2480 BCESahureEarliest known expedition, shown on his pyramid causeway at Abusir, with monkeys among the goods Dominy et al. 2020. The Palermo Stone annals are usually cited for about 80,000 measures of myrrh and 6,000 of electrum (figures for wood differ between editions; not checked against the original here).
5th Dynasty, 24th c. BCEDjedkare IsesiA dancing dwarf brought from Punt by the official Bawerdjed, remembered in Pepi II's letter to Harkhuf Lichtheim 1973.
11th Dynasty, c. 2000 BCEMentuhotep IIIThe official Henenu organises a Punt voyage via the Wadi Hammamat Breasted 1906.
12th Dynasty, c. 1950–1780 BCESenusret I to Amenemhat IVVoyages from the harbour of Saww (Mersa/Wadi Gawasis); cargo boxes labelled "wonderful things of Punt" Bard & Fattovich 2007.
18th Dynasty, c. 1470s BCEHatshepsut (year 9)Best-documented expedition, carved at Deir el-Bahari.
18th DynastyThutmose III, Amenhotep IIITrade continues Tyldesley 1996.
20th Dynasty, c. 1170s BCERamesses IIIPapyrus Harris I describes a fleet returning from Punt and goods carried overland via Coptos: the last well-documented pharaonic voyage Kitchen 1971.

Middle Kingdom literature also used Punt. In the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor a serpent calling himself "lord of Punt" rules a magical island and sends the sailor home with myrrh and other goods Lichtheim 1973. After the New Kingdom, Punt became more a land of legend than a trading partner.

3. Hatshepsut's expedition

The reliefs of the Punt expedition fill the southern half of the middle portico of Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari, western Thebes. They are dated to regnal year 9 (counted in the years of her co-ruler Thutmose III), in the 1470s BCE Polish–Egyptian Mission. The scenes run in sequence: an oracle of Amun ordering the voyage; the fleet of five ships arriving; the expedition leader Nehsi meeting Parahu, chief of Punt, and his wife Iti (often written Ati); Puntite goods loaded; the return; and the goods weighed and presented to Amun Polish–Egyptian Mission Tyldesley 1996.

  • Goods: living myrrh trees with their roots in baskets (a figure of 31 trees is widely repeated, but it was not confirmed in a published translation for this module), heaps of myrrh resin, ebony, ivory, electrum, leopard and cheetah skins, and live animals including baboons and a giraffe.
  • Landscape: houses raised on stilts and reached by ladders, palms and incense trees, and detailed sea fauna under the ships.
  • People: Parahu is the only named chief of Punt. Iti's body is shown very heavily built; the original block is in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

Hatshepsut presented the voyage as tribute from a distant land. Egyptologists read it as a trading mission dressed in royal ideology Tyldesley 1996.

"Sahure first, Hatshepsut famous, Ramesses last"Earliest known voyage c. 2480 BCE; best-carved 1470s BCE; last well-documented c. 1170s BCE.

4. The harbour: Mersa/Wadi Gawasis

Since the early 2000s (survey from 2001) an Italian–American team led by Kathryn Bard (Boston University) and Rodolfo Fattovich (Naples "L'Orientale") has excavated Mersa/Wadi Gawasis on Egypt's Red Sea coast, about 22 km south of Safaga. Its ancient name was Saww, and a stela of Senusret I there names Bia-Punt Bard & Fattovich 2007. Man-made caves found from December 2004 held stone anchors, cedar ship timbers, curved steering-oar blades and about 26 coils of rope. A stela records voyages to Punt and Bia-Punt under Amenemhat III, and two cargo boxes of Amenemhat IV carry the label "wonderful things of Punt". Ebony and obsidian, both Punt products, were found on site Boston University 2010. Gawasis proves that Middle Kingdom fleets sailed south from the Red Sea coast, not down the Nile, though it does not say where they landed.

5. Where was Punt? The debate

PositionMain proponentsKey arguments
Somali coastAuguste Mariette (1870s); much Somali popular historyFrankincense and myrrh trees grow in the Somali north; classical ports there exported aromatics (m06).
Eritrea, eastern Sudan, northern Ethiopia, coast and hinterlandKenneth Kitchen (1971, 1993); Rodolfo Fattovich; Kathryn BardRed Sea fish in the reliefs; African animals (giraffe, rhinoceros); Egyptian goods in the Gash Group sites of the Kassala region; "Parahu" not "Farahu" (South Arabian has no p).
Wider Horn zoneJacke Phillips (1997)Punt spread over eastern Sudan, Eritrea, northern Ethiopia and Somalia.
Western ArabiaDimitri Meeks (2003)Read all texts mentioning Punt, not just the Deir el-Bahari reliefs, and many associate it with Asiatic and eastern contexts.
Both shores of the southern Red SeaSuggested by Dominy et al. (2020)"God's Land" may have covered linked African and Arabian coasts.

Fattovich's case rests on fieldwork. The Gash Group culture (about 3000–1800 BCE) of the Gash delta near Kassala, with its main site at Mahal Teglinos, traded with Egypt, Nubia and southern Arabia, and Fattovich proposed it as Punt or part of it Fattovich 2012 Bard & Fattovich 2018. Kitchen argued that Punt lay in the Red Sea coastlands and hinterland of eastern Sudan and Eritrea, reachable both by sea and, from Nubia, by land Kitchen 1993. Meeks's Arabian thesis forces scholars to account for every text, but it struggles with the African animals in the reliefs Meeks 2003. The current weight of evidence favours an African location on or behind the southern Red Sea coast, between eastern Sudan and the northern Horn. Northern Somalia lies within that zone but is not singled out by any of the strongest arguments.

6. Science joins the debate: baboon mummies

Egyptians kept and mummified baboons, sacred to the god Thoth, but baboons are not native to Egypt. Hamadryas baboons live in the Horn and south-west Arabia, so mummified ones can act as tracers for Punt.

  • Dominy et al. 2020 (eLife) measured oxygen and strontium isotopes in mummified baboons and compared them with 155 samples of modern baboon tissue from 77 locations. Two New Kingdom hamadryas baboons in the British Museum (EA6736 and EA6738, from Thebes) were born outside Egypt; EA6736 seems to have died soon after arrival. The matching zone covers much of Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti and parts of Somalia and Yemen. Five Ptolemaic baboons from Saqqara were born in Egypt, suggesting captive breeding. The authors called their mapping of Punt provisional Dominy et al. 2020.
  • Grathwol et al. 2023 (eLife; Kopp corresponding author, Dominy co-author) tried to extract ancient DNA from ten baboon mummies; one worked. That mummy, from Gabbanat el-Qurud ("Valley of the Monkeys", Thebes), dates to about 800–540 BCE. Its mitochondrial genome groups with modern hamadryas baboons of Eritrea, Ethiopia and eastern Sudan; the authors read this as pointing to present-day Eritrea and, by extension, to the port of Adulis. The authors suggest Punt and Adulis may have been the same trading zone a thousand years apart, and stress that one sample makes the result tentative Grathwol et al. 2023.
Trap: neither study "proves Punt was in Somalia". The 2020 isotope zone is centred on Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti and only includes parts of Somalia and Yemen; the 2023 genome points to the Eritrea–Ethiopia–eastern Sudan region (and, by inference, Adulis), and it comes from a Late Period baboon, not a Punt voyage. Both authors call their results provisional.

7. Punt in Somali memory and politics

Many Somali writers and teachers have identified Punt with Somalia, pointing to the frankincense and myrrh of the north-east and to Mariette's 19th-century view. The identification gives the nation an ancient pedigree, and the north-eastern state founded at Garowe in 1998 took the name Puntland from it BBC Puntland profile. Historians treat this as modern identity-making: Puntland is a federal member state of Somalia created in 1998, not the heir of an ancient polity. No evidence links the people of Punt, linguistically or genealogically, to any present-day Somali clan, and the name "Somali" is first attested only in the early 15th century, in a victory hymn for the Ethiopian emperor Yeshaq (r. 1414–1429/30; see m08) Lewis 2002. The fairest summary is that Punt probably included parts of the southern Red Sea and the northern Horn coast, and that Somali claims, like Eritrean, Sudanese and Arabian ones, rest on geography and trade goods, not on proof of continuity.

Scholarly debates

Where was Punt?

Mariette (1870s) and much Somali popular history place it on the Somali coast. Kitchen (1971, 1993) argues for the coastlands and hinterland of eastern Sudan and Eritrea, citing Red Sea fish, African fauna and the name Parahu; Fattovich and Bard tie it to the Gash Group near Kassala; Phillips (1997) spreads it across eastern Sudan, Eritrea, northern Ethiopia and Somalia. Meeks (2003) argues for western Arabia from the whole textual record. Dominy et al. (2020) allow for both shores. The current weight favours an African location on or behind the southern Red Sea coast; northern Somalia is in the candidate zone but not singled out.

How much can baboon mummies tell us about Punt?

Dominy et al. (2020) show two New Kingdom baboons were born abroad in a zone centred on Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti; Grathwol et al. (2023) link a Late Period baboon to the Eritrea–Ethiopia–eastern Sudan region and suggest a Punt–Adulis continuity. Critics and the authors themselves note small samples (two isotope specimens, one genome), the assumption that baboon populations have not moved, and the gap between a Late Period animal and New Kingdom Punt. The studies strengthen the African case but do not fix Punt's location.

Does Punt belong to Somali history?

Somali nationalist and popular writing claims Punt as the first chapter of Somali history, and Puntland's name expresses that view. Historians accept that the Somali coast produced the same aromatics and may have been part of a Punt trade zone, but no evidence links the Puntites to Somali speakers or clans, and other countries make parallel claims. The mainstream position is that Punt belongs to the history of the region, including the Somali north, rather than to any one modern nation.

Module 6 · Antiquity

Classical trade: the Barbaroi coast

The source: a merchant's handbook

The Periplus Maris Erythraei ("Sailing around the Erythraean Sea") is an anonymous Greek handbook written by a merchant based in Roman Egypt. Lionel Casson dates it to c. 40–70 CE, chiefly because it names the Nabataean king Malichus as reigning, and the only good fit is Malichus II (c. 40–70) Casson 1989. Older proposals ranged from c. 59–62 CE (Schoff) to the early 2nd century (Huntingford); a mid-1st-century date is now the consensus. The "Erythraean Sea" meant the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the western Indian Ocean together. Chapters 7–14 describe the Somali coast, which the author calls the "far-side" ports (across the strait from Arabia), inhabited by people he calls Barbaroi Casson 1989 Schoff 1912.

The Periplus is a practical text: it lists anchorages, distances in stadia, what each market wants and what it sells. That makes it the richest single source for the Somali coast in antiquity, but also a narrow one: it records what interested a Greek trader, not how coastal society worked.

The far-side ports, west to east

Port (Periplus §)Usual identificationExports named
Avalites (§7)at or near Zeila (Saylac); a site near the Djibouti coast has also been proposedaromatics, a little ivory, tortoiseshell, a very little but excellent myrrh
Malao (§8)Berberamyrrh, a little "far-side" frankincense, hard cassia, duaka, kankamon, makeir; slaves only rarely
Mundu (§9)Heis (Xiis), with its offshore isletthe same goods plus mokrotu incense
Mosyllon (§10)the coast near Bosaso; exact site disputedcassia in such bulk that larger ships were needed; also mokrotu, frankincense, tortoiseshell, ivory, myrrh
Spice Market (§12)near Cape Guardafui (Ras Caseyr); Chittick proposed Damoseveral grades of cassia, frankincense
Opone (§13)Ras Hafunthe most cassia, "better-quality" slaves increasingly sent to Egypt, much fine tortoiseshell
"A Merchant Might Make Spices at Opone"Avalites, Malao, Mundu, Mosyllon, Spice Market, Opone: the six far-side markets in sailing order, from the strait east to Guardafui and then south to Hafun.

Between Mosyllon and the Spice Market the text lists landmarks rather than markets (a "Little Nile" river, Cape Elephant, the Akannai grove, which alone produced "far-side" frankincense in quantity and of the best grade). The Spice Market had a dangerous open anchorage; when the sea turned turbid, a sign of a coming storm, ships ran for shelter at the promontory of Tabai (§12–13). Beyond Opone the coast turns south into Azania: "bluffs" and "beaches", then seven daily "runs" (dromoi), the first called Sarapion and the next Nikon, down to the Pyralaoi islands and Rhapta, "the last market town of Azania" (§15–16). Sarapion and Nikon have never been located on the ground; commentators place them somewhere on the southern Somali coast Casson 1989.

Who traded, and what moved

Egyptian ships left for the far-side ports around July (the month Epiphi), carrying glass, grape syrup, cloth "made for the Barbaroi", wheat, wine, tin, tunics, cloaks from Arsinoe, drinking cups, copper, iron and some gold and silver coin (§7–8, 14). The coast also traded directly with Arabia: people from Avalites crossed on rafts to Ocelis and Muza, and Malao's goods were shipped to Arabia. Ships from Ariake and Barygaza in north-western India brought grain, rice, ghee, sesame oil, cotton cloth, girdles and cane sugar; some sailed to these ports on purpose, others traded along the coast in passing (§14) Schoff 1912.

Politically, the author says the region "is not subject to a king": each market town had its own chief (§14). He characterises the people of Avalites as unruly and those of Malao as more peaceable, judgements of a trader about trading partners. Note what the text does not say: it names no Somali ethnonym and no clan, so modern claims about who the Barbaroi "were" go beyond the evidence Casson 1989.

Barbaroi are not "Berbers" of North Africa. Greek barbaroi meant people who did not speak Greek. The Periplus applies it to the inhabitants of the Horn coast ("Barbaria"). The same root gave the medieval Arabic Bilad al-Barbar for the Somali coast and the name of Berbera, but Arab geographers distinguished these Barbara from the Barbar (Berbers) of the Maghrib.

Monsoons and Hippalus

The monsoon reverses twice a year: the south-west monsoon (roughly May or June to September) carries ships from Africa and Arabia towards India; the north-east monsoon (roughly November or December to March) carries them back. Periplus §57 says a pilot named Hippalus first worked out the direct open-sea route to India, and that ships now left from Kane in Arabia or from the Cape of Spices (Guardafui). Pliny the Elder (Natural History 6.100–106, published 77 CE) instead calls the wind itself hippalus Pliny NH. Hippalus probably lived in the 1st century BCE. Arabian and Indian sailors already used the monsoon; Strabo (2.3.4) tells how Eudoxus of Cyzicus, c. 118–116 BCE, sailed to India guided by a shipwrecked Indian pilot Strabo. "Discovery" therefore means discovery for Greek and Roman shipping.

Summer out, winter homeSouth-west monsoon in summer: Africa and Arabia to India. North-east monsoon in winter: India back to Africa, which is why Indian ships could call at Opone.

After Rome annexed Egypt in 30 BCE, Red Sea trade grew sharply; Strabo (2.5.12) heard that about 120 ships a year sailed from Myos Hormos to India. The Somali ports sat on the edge of this system: suppliers of aromatics and tortoiseshell, and a stop for some India-bound shipping.

Archaeology: Hafun, Heis and Damo

Neville Chittick's British-Somali Expedition of 1975 surveyed the northern coast and the Hafun peninsula, confirming that Ras Hafun was the best candidate for Opone Chittick 1976. M. C. Smith and H. T. Wright (University of Michigan) then published the pottery from two sites Smith & Wright 1988:

  • Hafun West: from the 1st century BCE to about the 3rd century CE, with Roman Mediterranean amphorae, Egyptian wares, Mesopotamian glazed ware and Indian pottery.
  • Hafun Main: c. 2nd–5th centuries CE, with Persian Gulf (Parthian-Sasanian) glazed wares and Indian pottery prominent.

The Indian sherds fit §14's Indian ships; the Gulf wares show a link the Periplus barely mentions. At Heis (Xiis) in Sanaag, Chittick found Roman glass and identified the site with Mundu, which has an islet just offshore Chittick 1979. Recent Spanish excavation of the Xiis cemeteries found Egyptian and Roman goods, South Arabian storage jars, abundant Mesopotamian glazed ware and carnelian beads, with a peak in the 1st century CE and an end around the 3rd century, but no Indian pottery Fernández et al. 2022. Chittick also reported Roman material at Damo near Guardafui and suggested it was the Spice Market (a single proposal, not tested by excavation).

Popular claims of "Mycenaean" or Bronze Age Greek pottery at Opone find no support in the published excavation reports. The published imports at Hafun begin in the 1st century BCE.

Ptolemy, Aksum and South Arabia

Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) names the Aromata promontory (Guardafui), Opone and stations south of it, and stretches "Barbaria" further south than the Periplus, which calls the land beyond Opone Azania Berggren & Jones 2000. The Periplus places Zoskales, who ruled from the Adulis region (the forerunner of Aksum's power), over the coast "as far as the other Barbaria" (§5). South Arabia mattered more for the south: Rhapta was held by the chief of Mapharitis under the Himyarite king Charibael, and Arab captains there spoke the language and married locally (§16). By the 6th century Aksum dominated the Red Sea (it invaded Himyar c. 525), and Cosmas Indicopleustes (c. 550) described Barbaria as the land that supplied frankincense and other aromatics Cosmas.

Barbaria → Bilad al-Barbar → BerberaGreek name for the coast, Arabic name for the coast and its people, modern port name: one word across fifteen centuries.

The Arabic sequel

Medieval Arabic writers kept the name. Al-Mas'udi (10th century) is said in one secondary source to have called the Gulf of Aden the Barbari gulf (al-khalij al-Barbari); this wording could not be confirmed in a second source. Yaqut (1220s) described the Barbara as a people between the Habasha (Abyssinians) and the Zanj, distinct from the North African Barbar (also given in m08, but from the same body of secondary literature) Lewis 2002. This continuity, and its link to the medieval ports, is taken up in m08; Egyptian Punt (m05) is a separate and older debate.

Scholarly debates

Who 'discovered' the monsoon route, and when did Hippalus live?

The Periplus credits Hippalus with the route, Pliny names the wind after him. Most scholars place him in the 1st century BCE. Tchernia argues the wind name came first and the link to a person arose later; others reconcile both texts by saying the route needed knowledge of the wind. All agree that Arabian and Indian sailors used the monsoon earlier (Eudoxus's Indian pilot), so 'discovery' refers only to Greco-Roman shipping.

Was the 'cinnamon' and 'cassia' of the Somali ports local or re-exported?

The Periplus presents cassia as a product of Malao, Mosyllon, the Spice Market and Opone, and Pliny placed cinnamon in 'Troglodytica'. Casson and others note that true Cinnamomum does not grow in the Horn and argue that much of it was South or South-East Asian bark shipped via these ports, with Greek traders unaware of its origin; some suggest part of the trade was a local aromatic bark. The weight of opinion favours at least partial re-export.

How secure are the identifications of the Periplus ports?

Malao (Berbera) and Opone (Hafun) are widely accepted, and Opone has archaeological support. Mundu is usually placed at Xiis because of its islet (Chittick; Fernández et al.). Avalites is usually Zeila, though Casson notes an alternative near the Djibouti coast; Mosyllon is placed near Bosaso with no excavated site; Tabai and the Spice Market are debated; Sarapion and Nikon are unlocated.

Module 7 · Islam

The coming of Islam

Two kinds of evidence

The coming of Islam to the Somali lands is told in two registers. Pious tradition (oral history, hagiography, local chronicles) places it in the Prophet's own lifetime and ties Somali lineages to Arabian saints. Documented history (dated inscriptions, excavated sites, contemporary Arabic geographers) begins later: scattered references from the late 9th century, archaeology from the 12th, and the first dated inscription in 1238. Both matter, but for different questions: tradition tells us how Somalis came to understand their Islam; documents tell us when and how it can be shown to have spread Lewis 2002 Trimingham 1952.

The first Hijra, 615 CE

According to Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet (preserved by Ibn Hisham), in Rajab of the fifth year of the mission (615 CE) a small group of persecuted Meccan Muslims, about eleven men and four women, sailed from the Arabian port of Shu'ayba to the Christian king (al-Najashi, the Negus) of Aksum. A larger party followed, with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib as its spokesman before the king when Quraysh envoys, 'Amr ibn al-'As and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a, asked for the refugees' return. The Negus refused. Many emigrants returned before or soon after the Hijra to Medina in 622; the last group reached Medina in 628 Guillaume 1955 Watt 1953.

The first Hijra went to Aksum, not to the Somali coast. The early Arabic sources name the Negus and his Aksumite (Abyssinian) kingdom in what is now Tigray and Eritrea. None mentions Zeila or any Somali port. Somali traditions that emigrants landed at or passed through Zeila are later pious traditions with no support in the early sources.

Zeila and the "mosque of the two qiblas"

Zeila (Saylac) has a ruined mosque with two mihrabs, one facing north towards Jerusalem and one towards Mecca, known as Masjid al-Qiblatayn. Tradition holds that Companions built it before the qibla (prayer direction) was changed from Jerusalem to Mecca in 2 AH (624 CE), which would make it one of the oldest mosques in Africa. The building has no foundation inscription, and no excavation has published a date for it; the 7th-century date rests on tradition, repeated in guidebooks and popular histories Lewis 2002. A second mihrab can also result from rebuilding or from correcting an inaccurate orientation, so two mihrabs do not by themselves prove a pre-624 date. Treat it as an important devotional site whose early date is unproven.

615 – 624 – 1238First Hijra (to Aksum); change of qibla (the Zeila tradition depends on it); first dated Islamic inscription in Somalia (Mogadishu). The first two are dates in Islamic history; only the third is Somali evidence.

The documented beginnings

DateEvidenceType
late 9th c.al-Ya'qubi mentions Zeila and Muslims on the northern coastArabic geography
12th c.mosque at Harlaa (near Dire Dawa) resembling mosques of the East African coastexcavation (Insoll)
c. 1200first phase of the Shangani mosque, Mogadishu, dated by potteryexcavation (Chittick)
1238 (636 AH)inscription of the Friday (Jami') mosque, Hamar Weyne, Mogadishudated inscription
1268–69 (667 AH)Arba Rukun mosque, mihrab naming Khusraw ibn Muhammad al-Shirazidated inscription
1269 (667 AH)Fakhr al-Din mosque, Hamar Weynedated inscription

Ninth-century al-Ya'qubi already knew Zeila and a Muslim presence on the northern seaboard Lewis 1955. Excavations led by Timothy Insoll at Harlaa, an inland trading town, found a 12th-century mosque comparable to those of Tanzania and the Somali coast, with imports from Egypt, Yemen and China, showing that Islam travelled up the caravan routes from Zeila towards the Harar plateau Insoll et al. 2021. On the Benadir coast, Mogadishu's inscriptions of 1238 and 1268–69 are the earliest securely dated Islamic texts in Somalia Chittick 1982 Freeman-Grenville 1962. The Arba Rukun founder's nisba "al-Shirazi" points to Persian Gulf connections, though one name is a thin basis for a "Persian colony".

How Islam spread

  • Trade first. Muslim merchants from Yemen, Hadramawt, the Gulf and Egypt settled in the ports, married locally and built mosques. Coastal towns became Muslim before most of the interior.
  • Holy men and scholars. Local tradition credits wandering shaykhs: Aw Barkhadle (identified with Shaykh Yusuf al-Kawneyn, buried near Hargeisa; his dates are uncertain and sources differ widely) is said to have given Somali names to the Arabic vowel signs, easing Qur'an teaching (tradition, reported here from one source) Lewis 1998. The religious specialist (wadaad) became a fixture of pastoral society.
  • The Shafi'i school. Somali Sunnis follow the Shafi'i madhhab, which they share with Yemen and Hadramawt, the main source of scholars and trade contacts Lewis 2002.
  • Inland routes. From Zeila, caravans carried Islam to the Harar plateau and Shewa, where Muslim sultanates emerged (m08). Organised Sufi orders came later (Qadiriyya from about the 15th century; m13).

Ibn Battuta's visit

The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta sailed from Aden to Zeila, which he called the city of the Barbara (the Somali coast-dwellers) and "the dirtiest, most abominable and most stinking town in the world" because of fish and the blood of camels slaughtered in the streets; he preferred to sleep on board Gibb 1962. He sailed on to Mogadishu, "an exceedingly large town" whose merchants slaughtered hundreds of camels a day. Young men came out in small boats (sumbuq) and each claimed a merchant as his guest; the host then bought and sold on the merchant's behalf, and a sale made without him was not valid. The ruler, Abu Bakr ibn Shaykh 'Umar, was called simply "the Shaykh"; he was "by origin of the Barbara", spoke the local language (Maqdishi) and knew Arabic. His qadi was an Egyptian. Ibn Battuta described the Friday procession under silk canopies topped with golden birds, meals of rice cooked in ghee with bananas, mangoes and green ginger, and the city's cloth, exported "as far as Egypt". He went on to Mombasa and Kilwa Gibb 1962 Hamdun & King 1994.

"Of Barbara origin" does not mean "from Berbera town". Barbara is the Arabic name for the Somali people of the coast (m06). Some popular histories also say the Ajuran ruled Mogadishu at this time; Ibn Battuta names only the city's own Shaykh.

Date. Ibn Battuta's own chronology puts the voyage in 1331, and Gibb keeps that date in his translated text; but Gibb's notes to the 1962 volume provisionally move the whole chapter to 1329. Ross Dunn, following Ivan Hrbek's reconstruction, places it in 1328–1330 Gibb 1962 Dunn 1986.

Sect. In the same passage Ibn Battuta calls the Barbara, as a people, "Shafi'ites in rite", but says that most of Zeila's own inhabitants were Rafidis (Shi'is; Gibb suggests Zaydis). Both statements are in the text, which is why modern summaries seem to disagree Gibb 1962.

The Shaykh's city: camels, cloth, hostsMogadishu in Ibn Battuta: hundreds of camels slaughtered daily, cloth sold to Egypt, every merchant assigned a host, and a ruler called "the Shaykh" with an Egyptian qadi.

Founding legends and Arabian genealogies

The 16th-century Kilwa Chronicle says settlers from al-Ahsa in eastern Arabia were at early Mogadishu, and later Benadir traditions speak of Arab and Persian (Shirazi) founding families Freeman-Grenville 1962. Archaeologists and historians (Chittick, Pouwels) read such stories as charters for immigrant merchant lineages within towns whose pottery and people were overwhelmingly local; the towns grew out of the coast's own economy Pouwels 1987.

Somali clan genealogies make the same move. The Isaaq trace descent to Shaykh Ishaq ibn Ahmad, whose hagiographies make him a descendant of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and who is buried at Maydh. The Darod trace descent to Shaykh Darod ('Abd al-Rahman ibn Isma'il al-Jabarti), whose line tradition takes back to 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and who married Dobira, daughter of a Dir chief; his tomb is at Haylaan Lewis 1998. I. M. Lewis judged literal descent from Arabian saints historically untenable: the genealogies express the prestige of Islam and of Arabian ancestry, though they may preserve memories of real Arab settlers. Mohamed Haji Mukhtar doubts that whole clans could descend from single Arab immigrants; Sada Mire calls these narratives a "Somali Islamic myth of origin" Mukhtar 2003 Mire 2020. Somali is a Cushitic language, and the genetic evidence (m03) and clan structure (m12) are treated in their own modules.

Scholarly debates

When did Islam first reach the Somali coast?

Tradition places it in the 7th century: emigrants at Zeila and a two-qibla mosque before 624. Documentary evidence starts with al-Ya'qubi in the late 9th century, archaeology with Harlaa (12th c.) and Shangani (c. 1200), and dated inscriptions with Mogadishu in 1238. Most historians (Lewis, Trimingham) accept early contacts through Red Sea trade as likely but treat a 7th-century community at Zeila as unproven; excavation at Zeila is needed to settle it.

Were the Benadir towns Arab or Persian foundations, or local towns with immigrant elites?

Older scholarship (Cerulli) and local traditions (Kilwa Chronicle, Shirazi stories) stress foreign founders. Chittick, Allen and Pouwels argue that the towns grew from local economies, with mostly local pottery and immigrant merchant lineages integrated into them; the Persian evidence is thin (one al-Shirazi inscription). The current weight of evidence favours local growth with Arab and Persian participation.

How should Arabian clan genealogies (Isaaq, Darod) be read?

Some Somali scholars, such as Sharif Aydarus, accept them as broadly historical. Lewis judges literal descent untenable but sees possible memories of real Arab settlers; Mukhtar doubts whole clans could descend from one immigrant; Mire and Ali Jimale Ahmed treat them as myths of origin that ennoble lineages through Islam. Linguistic (Cushitic) and genetic evidence (m03) do not support literal descent of whole clans from Arabian saints.

When was Ibn Battuta in East Africa?

Ibn Battuta's own dates give 1331, and Gibb keeps them in his translated text, though his notes (1962) provisionally move the chapter to 1329. Ivan Hrbek reconstructed the chronology from internal evidence and placed the voyage in 1328–1330; Ross Dunn adopts this. The disagreement is about his Arabian itinerary and pilgrimages; both dates are in current use, so give both.
