Module 8 · Medieval

Medieval city-states and the Ifat Sultanate

The sources

Between the 12th and 15th centuries the Somali coast and its hinterland entered written history through Arabic geographers, Ethiopian royal chronicles and Mamluk historians. Each sees from outside: the geographers relied on merchants' reports, and the Ethiopian and Egyptian writers wrote about wars. Local Arabic chronicles of the Walashma dynasty survive only in late copies Taddesse Tamrat 1972 Trimingham 1952.

WriterDateWhat he contributes
al-Idrisi1154Describes the coast of the Barbara south of the Gulf of Aden; Cerulli read one name in his text as the Hawiye near Merca
Yaqutc. 1224Mogadishu: foreign Muslim merchants, no king, governed by elders; the Barbara live between the Habasha and the Zanj
Ibn Sa'idd. c. 1286Merca as the chief town of a Hawiye country of some fifty villages along a river; Mogadishu well known to travellers
Ibn Battuta1331 (or 1328–30)Eyewitness of Zeila and Mogadishu (m07)
al-'Umaric. 1340sSeven Muslim states in "the land of Zayla'", with Ifat the strongest
al-Maqrizic. 1430sal-Ilmam: history of the Walashma sultans and their wars
"Zayla'" in Mamluk sources often means a region, not just the town. Al-'Umari and al-Maqrizi use bilad al-Zayla' for all the Muslim lands of the Horn, from the coast to Shewa; Muslims from the region were called Jabarti. Read "the kings of Zayla'" as "the Muslim rulers of the Horn".

Mogadishu: from elders to a sultanate

Yaqut, writing c. 1224, described Mogadishu as a town of foreign Muslim merchants with no king, run by its elders according to their customs. Inscriptions of 1238 and 1269 show a prosperous Muslim town (m07). By the time of Ibn Battuta's visit a single ruler, Abu Bakr ibn Shaykh 'Umar, called "the Shaykh" but holding court like a sultan, governed with wazirs, amirs and an Egyptian qadi Gibb 1962 Chittick 1982. Tradition names Abu Bakr ibn Fakhr al-Din as founder of the first ruling house, and the Fakhr al-Din mosque (1269) carries the name, but the dynasty's dates are uncertain.

Mogadishu struck its own copper coins, one of very few East African towns to do so. The coins carry rulers' names, mostly without dates; Freeman-Grenville's study arranged them from c. 1300 to c. 1700, and many of the rulers are known only from their coins Freeman-Grenville 1963. An issue of Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad is placed c. 1322 (one source). Around 1500 a new house, the Muzaffar dynasty, took power; its first ruler, 'Umar, is thought to have struck coins c. 1500 (one source). The Muzaffarids were allied to the Ajuran of the interior (m10) and were displaced by Abgaal (Hawiye) imams in the early 17th century Cassanelli 1982.

Trade explains the wealth. Mogadishu wove cloth sold as far as Egypt (Ibn Battuta), exported ivory, ambergris and aromatics, imported Indian textiles and Chinese wares, and, according to the Kilwa Chronicle, controlled the Sofala gold trade before Kilwa took it over Freeman-Grenville 1962.

Elders → Shaykh → Muzaffar → ImamsMogadishu's government: elders (Yaqut, 1220s), a ruler called the Shaykh (Ibn Battuta, 1331), the Muzaffar dynasty (c. 1500, allied to the Ajuran), Abgaal imams (17th c.).

Merca and Barawa

Ibn Sa'id (13th century) names Merca as the main town of a Hawiye country of about fifty villages along a river, presumably the Shabelle. With al-Idrisi, this is among the earliest written references to a named Somali clan family; but al-Idrisi's reading is disputed (see debates) Lewis 1960. Merca and Barawa were smaller ports in the Benadir network, trading with Mogadishu, Yemen and India; their later history under the Ajuran and the Portuguese is covered in m10.

Zeila: the gateway

Zeila linked the Gulf of Aden to the Ethiopian highlands. Caravans carried slaves, ivory, gold, musk and coffee-region produce to the coast, and cloth, metal and salt inland; Rasulid Yemen across the strait was its main partner. Control of this route, rather than religion alone, drove wars between the Christian kingdom and the Muslim states: whoever held the road to Zeila controlled the highland trade Taddesse Tamrat 1972.

From Shewa to Ifat

The first Muslim state in the interior was the Sultanate of Shewa, ruled by a Makhzumi dynasty. A local chronicle published by Enrico Cerulli dates its founding to 283 AH (896–97), a date Cerulli himself saw as tradition rather than fact Trimingham 1952. Weakened by succession quarrels, Shewa was annexed in 1285 by the Walashma rulers of Ifat. The pagan kingdom of Damot, whose legendary king Motalami is remembered for raids deep into the Shewan region in the 13th century, was another regional power; some writers also stress its pressure on the Muslim sultanate, a point not checked here Taddesse Tamrat 1972. The Walashma claimed Arabian descent (al-Maqrizi gives a Hashimite line through 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib); Taddesse Tamrat, following al-Maqrizi, says their ancestors first lived in Jabarta in the Zeila hinterland before moving inland Taddesse Tamrat 1972. Ifat lay on the eastern edge of the Shewan plateau, along the trade route to Zeila.

"I Do All Hard Sums Before Dawn"Al-'Umari's seven Muslim states: Ifat, Dawaro, Arababni, Hadiya, Sharkha, Bali, Dara. Ifat was the largest and nearest the coast; al-Maqrizi repeats the list.

Ifat against the Solomonic kings

The Solomonic dynasty took power in 1270 (Yekuno Amlak). Its great expansion came under Amda Seyon (r. 1314–1344). When Haqq ad-Din I of Ifat detained a royal servant, Ti'iyintay, who was probably travelling to the coast, Amda Seyon invaded and sacked Ifat. In 1332 Sabr ad-Din I, accused of seizing goods and merchants on the Zeila route, rose with support from Dawaro and Hadiya; Amda Seyon defeated him, installed his brother Jamal ad-Din as a tributary, and then crushed a rising in Adal and Mora. The Ge'ez chronicle of these "Glorious Victories" is our main source; Huntingford dated these wars to 1329, which Taddesse Tamrat judges unjustified; 1332 is generally accepted. When Jamal ad-Din proved uncooperative, Amda Seyon replaced him with another brother, Nasr ad-Din Taddesse Tamrat 1972.

Haqq ad-Din Idetains a royal servant; Ifat sackedAmda Seyon

Sa'ad ad-Din II and the dating problem

Haqq ad-Din II, who in al-Maqrizi's account began to rule c. 1363–64, moved the centre of resistance east, out of the emperor's reach, to a new town, Wahal; Taddesse Tamrat calls him the real founder of Adal as a fighting state. He was killed in action in 776 AH (Taddesse: 1373–74) under Newaya Maryam; the Walashma chronicle's dates for him run about twelve years later. His brother Sa'ad ad-Din II continued raiding, at first with success: the Egyptian encyclopedist al-Qalqashandi (d. 1418) calls him the most successful Muslim prince against the Christian kingdom Taddesse Tamrat 1972. Dawit I (r. c. 1380–1412) strengthened his frontier colonies. In al-Maqrizi's account the Christian army invaded Adal, killed Sa'ad ad-Din at Zeila and sacked the port. Tradition places his tomb on the island off Zeila that bears his name Trimingham 1952. The date of his death is genuinely disputed:

DateBasisEmperor
805 AH / 1402–03al-Maqrizi; followed by Taddesse Tamrat (1403)Dawit I
1408–09Chekroun (2020): 811 AH, from 15th-century Yemeni annals and biographiesDawit I
1410many modern summariesYeshaq or Dawit
817 AH / 1414–15the "History of the Walashma" edited by CerulliYeshaq

Fauvelle-Aymar and Hirsch, whose survey of Zeila and its island was published in 2011, recorded remains around the tomb attributed to Sa'ad ad-Din, but nothing dated that settles the question Fauvelle-Aymar et al. 2011. The scope's "c. 1403/1410" is therefore too narrow: give the full range, 1403–1415. Chekroun 2020

One sultan, four death dates1403 (Maqrizi), 1408/09 (Chekroun, Yemeni sources), 1410 (many summaries), 1415 (Walashma chronicle). Name the source with the date.

From Ifat to Adal

Sa'ad ad-Din's sons took refuge in Yemen at the court of the Rasulid sultan al-Nasir Ahmad. Most modern accounts date their return to 1415, but al-Maqrizi, as Taddesse Tamrat notes, has twenty years of Christian dominance after 805 AH and dates Sabr ad-Din's death to 825 AH (1421–22), which implies a later return; sources differ. The eldest, Sabr ad-Din (numbered II or III depending on the list), took the title "king of Adal" and set up a new base further east, later fixed at Dakkar. The new state was also called Barr Sa'd ad-Din, "the land of Sa'ad ad-Din", in his memory. A victory hymn for Emperor Yeshaq (r. 1414–1429/30) celebrating his wars against these sultans contains the first known written use of the name "Somali" Lewis 2002 Taddesse Tamrat 1972. Sabr ad-Din's brothers Mansur, Jamal ad-Din II and Badlay continued the war; Badlay was killed by Zara Ya'qob in 1445. The rest of Adal's history belongs to m09.

Ifat is not Adal. Ifat was centred on the eastern Shewan escarpment and ended with Sa'ad ad-Din's death; Adal was its successor, based further east (Dakkar, later Harar) and led by the same Walashma family. "Adal" appears earlier as a district (Amda Seyon fought there in 1332), and many accounts date the Adal sultanate from the sons' return (c. 1415); Taddesse Tamrat sees Haqq ad-Din II's move east in the later 14th century as its real start.

Who were the people of Ifat and Adal? The states were multi-ethnic: sources and modern scholars point to Argobba, Harla, Harari, Afar and Somali participants. Bahru Zewde and Pankhurst stress Argobba and Harari elements; Amélie Chekroun disputes an Argobba link for medieval Ifat; Somali histories emphasise the Somali role, especially in Adal. No single modern ethnic label fits Mukhtar 2003 Taddesse Tamrat 1972.

Scholarly debates

When did Sa'ad ad-Din II die, and under which emperor?

Al-Maqrizi gives 805 AH (1402–03) under Dawit I, and Taddesse Tamrat follows him. The History of the Walashma (ed. Cerulli) gives 817 AH (1414–15) under Yeshaq, which Cerulli defended. Many modern summaries give 1410. Chekroun (2020) uses 15th-century Yemeni annals and biographical dictionaries to argue for 811 AH (1408–09). Archaeological survey at Zeila has not settled it. No consensus; cite the source with the date.

Who were the people of Ifat and Adal?

The Walashma claimed Arabian (Hashimite) descent, which Cerulli, Laitin and Samatar treat as fictive. Bahru Zewde and Pankhurst stress Argobba and Harari elements; Chekroun rejects an Argobba identity for medieval Ifat; Somali scholarship stresses Somali roles, especially in Adal. The evidence supports multi-ethnic states; projecting modern ethnic labels back is contested.

Is al-Idrisi's 'Hawiye' the first written reference to a Somali clan?

Cerulli read a name in al-Idrisi (1154) as Hawiye, and Ibn Sa'id (13th c.) places a Hawiye country around Merca; on this reading the Hawiye are the earliest named Somali group in writing (Lewis). Others argue the al-Idrisi passage must be emended and may refer to a different name, leaving Ibn Sa'id as the first secure reference. The name 'Somali' itself first appears in Yeshaq's hymn in the 15th century.

Module 9 · Medieval

Adal and Imam Ahmad 'Gurey'

1. From Ifat to Adal

Adal was the successor of the Ifat Sultanate (see m08). After Sultan Sa'd ad-Din II was killed near Zeila (Saylac) in the early 1400s, his sons returned from Yemen and rebuilt Walashma rule in the eastern lowlands, with their base at Dakkar in the Harar region rather than in Shewa. Ethiopian chronicles called the Muslim lowlands Bar Sa'd ad-Din, "land of Sa'd ad-Din", after the dead sultan Whiteway 1902. Adal linked the port of Zeila to the highland trade in slaves, ivory, gold, musk and coffee. Its population was mixed: Harla (ancestors in part of today's Harari), Somali, Afar and Argobba, with Arab merchants and scholars Trimingham 1952.

By 1500, power was divided. The Walashma sultans held legitimacy and tended to seek truce with the Christian emperors. A war party of emirs and imams, men who led raiding armies, pressed for jihad. The best known was Emir Mahfuz of Zeila and Harar, who raided the highlands until a monk, Gabra Andreyas, killed him in single combat in 1517 during Emperor Lebna Dengel's counter-offensive Whiteway 1902. In 1520 Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad moved the capital from Dakkar to Harar; Pankhurst credits him with making the town the state's headquarters Pankhurst 1997.

2. The rise of Imam Ahmad

Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi was born c. 1506 in the Hubat lowlands near Harar. He and his father served as soldiers under Garad Abun, and Whiteway says he was only twenty-one in 1528, when his incursions began (elsewhere Whiteway gives 1527) Whiteway 1902. He married Bati del Wambara, daughter of Emir Mahfuz. In the mid-1520s he fought and killed Sultan Abu Bakr and installed Abu Bakr's brother, Umar Din, as a figurehead sultan. Ahmad ruled with the title imam, and stopped the tribute that Adal had paid to the emperor.

Gurey = Gragn = "left-handed"Somali Gurey and Amharic Gragn (Grañ) are the same nickname. Al-Ghazi is an Arabic title meaning "the raider" or "holy warrior". Different peoples gave the same man different names.

3. The conquest, 1529–1543

The imam won because he combined a religious cause with plunder and new weapons. Matchlocks had reached Arabia in the 1510s, and Turkish matchlock-men, mostly from Zabid in Yemen, fought with his armies; the Christian side had almost no firearms at first Whiteway 1902. Historians disagree about how decisive the guns were (see Debates).

DateEventMain source
7 or 9 March 1529Shimbra Kure: Lebna Dengel's much larger army defeatedFutuh; Ethiopian chronicles
17 July 1530Monastery of Debre Libanos burnedEthiopian chronicles
28 October 1531Lebna Dengel routed near Amba SelEthiopian chronicles
1539Royal prison-fortress of Amba Geshen stormed; prince Minas capturedEthiopian chronicles
2 Sept 1540Lebna Dengel dies a fugitive at Debre Damo; Galawdewos succeedsChronicles
9 July 1541400 Portuguese under Cristóvão da Gama march inland from MassawaCastanhoso
4 and 16 April 1542Portuguese defeat the imam twice in the north, near Jarte; he is wounded in the firstCastanhoso
Late August 1542Wofla: imam, reinforced by c. 900 matchlock-men from Zabid, crushes the Portuguese; Cristóvão captured and killedCastanhoso
21 February 1543Wayna Daga, near Lake Tana: Imam Ahmad shot dead; army scatteredCastanhoso; Galawdewos chronicle

The numbers in the sources are not reliable. For Shimbra Kure the Futuh gives 16,000 Christian horse and over 200,000 foot against 560 Muslim horse and 12,000 foot; the Ethiopian account gives 3,000 Christian horse against 300 Muslim horse. The two disagree on size but agree that the imam's army was far smaller Whiteway 1902. After 1531 Lebna Dengel never again fought a pitched battle. Churches were stripped of their treasure, and many Christians converted, at least for a time.

The Portuguese expedition came because Lebna Dengel had appealed to Portugal; Estêvão da Gama's fleet brought the force to Massawa, and on 9 July 1541 his brother Cristóvão marched inland. After Wofla the imam dismissed most of the Turks and kept about 200 matchlock-men. At Wayna Daga the surviving Portuguese and Galawdewos's army made for the imam himself. Castanhoso says only that a Portuguese ball struck him in the breast; Gaspar Correia names the marksman as João "the Galician" (Whiteway's "John the Gallician"), who lost his life in the charge Whiteway 1902. The imam's eldest son Muhammad was captured and later exchanged for Prince Minas.

S to W: Shimbra to WaynaThe war opens at Shimbra Kure (1529) and closes at Wayna Daga (1543): fourteen years, from the imam's greatest victory to his death.

4. Who fought: the Futuh and the Somali contingents

The chief Muslim source is the Futuh al-Habasha ("Conquest of Abyssinia") by Shihab ad-Din Ahmad ibn Abd al-Qadir, known as Arab Faqih, who wrote from the imam's side. René Basset published a French translation from 1897; Paul Lester Stenhouse's English translation, annotated by Richard Pankhurst, appeared in 2003 Stenhouse 2003. The surviving text breaks off in 1537, so the Portuguese war is known from Castanhoso, Bermudez and the Ethiopian chronicles.

The Futuh names Somali groups among the imam's forces, including the Girri, Marraihan, Harti, Yibberi, Habar Maqdi, Hawiya and Gorgora, and leaders such as Garad Matan ibn Uthman and Ahmad Girri ibn Husayn, called "the Somali" Stenhouse 2003. Lewis read names such as Geri, Marrehan and Harti as Darod lineages and Habar Magadle as an Isaaq lineage Lewis 2002. Such identifications are interpretations. The text also shows Somali groups at times quarrelling with the imam. Other core troops were Harla, the elite Malasay, Afar, Argobba and Arabs Stenhouse 2003.

Do not confuse Imam Ahmad with Ahmad Girri ibn Husayn, a separate Somali commander in the Futuh. Also: the Futuh does not describe Wayna Daga. Its text stops in 1537.

5. Who was Imam Ahmad?

The Futuh never states the imam's ethnicity. Whiteway (1902) judged him "probably a Somali" because he was closely tied to Somali leaders, but noted that "nothing even is said as to his nationality", and that his early employer, Garad Abun, was killed by Somalis whom Ahmad then fought. Whiteway also warns that he uses "Somali" loosely, for the Muslim peoples south and south-east of Abyssinia, "not in any tribal sense" Whiteway 1902. Somali nationalist historiography treats him as a Somali hero. Merid Wolde Aregay (1971) and Ewald Wagner (1991) link him to the Harla and the Walashma aristocracy. Mohammed Hassen Hinika (2017) argues for a Balaw (Beja-descended) father and an Afar mother, and treats the other claims as unproven Hinika 2017. The debate shows how a shared past is claimed by several modern nations.

6. After 1543: Nur, the wall and the Oromo

Bati del Wambara agreed to marry the imam's nephew Nur ibn Mujahid on condition that he avenge her husband. Nur killed Emperor Galawdewos in Fatagar in March 1559 Hassen 1990. The Ottomans, meanwhile, took Massawa under Özdemir Pasha in 1557 and set up the province of Habesh. Harar's people credit Nur with the city wall (jugol); tradition links it to the Oromo threat and to Nur's rule (c. 1551–1567/68), though some accounts date the walls earlier and the exact date is uncertain. Nur died in 1567 or 1568.

The decisive change was the Oromo expansion. The monk Bahrey, writing in 1593, placed the first Oromo advance into Bale in the reign of Lebna Dengel, in the Melbah gada period, which historians date to 1522–1530. Mohammed Hassen argues that the war of 1529–1543 emptied the frontier lands between Christian and Muslim states and so opened the way. An Oromo victory at Hazalo in 1559 ended Harar's military power Hassen 1990. In 1577 Imam Muhammad Jasa moved the capital to the Aussa oasis in Afar country. The Aussa imamate lasted until the later 17th century, and Harar became an independent emirate under the Ali ibn Daud dynasty from 1647 Pankhurst 1997.

1520 Harar → 1577 AussaAdal's capital moved twice: west to Harar (1520) as the war party rose, then east to Aussa (1577) as the Oromo advanced.

Scholarly debates

What was Imam Ahmad's ethnic origin?

The Futuh is silent. Whiteway (1902) inferred a Somali origin from his close ties to Somali leaders, while using 'Somali' loosely for the Muslim peoples of the lowlands and noting the sources' silence; and Somali nationalist historiography claims him as a national hero. Merid Wolde Aregay (1971) and Ewald Wagner (1991) connect him to the Harla aristocracy linked to the Walashma, which Harari writers stress. Mohammed Hassen Hinika (2017) argues for a Balaw (Beja-descended) father and an Afar mother and calls the other claims unproven. No single view is accepted; the evidence is thin and the question is bound up with modern national identities.

How decisive were firearms in Adal's victories?

Whiteway (1902) and older works stress Adal's early access to matchlocks and Turkish gunners from Zabid. Merid Wolde Aregay (1980) argued that early firearms were few and slow, and that leadership, mobility, cavalry and morale counted for more; the Futuh's battle narratives are mostly about cavalry and spearmen. Most historians now see guns as one factor among several, decisive mainly in 1541–43 when both sides had them.

Did the 1529–43 war cause the Oromo expansion?

Bahrey (1593) dates Oromo advances from 1522, before the war began, so the war did not start the movement. Mohammed Hassen (1990) argues that the mutual destruction of Christian and Muslim frontier settlements created a vacuum that the Oromo filled with great speed. In his later work (2015) he argues that Oromo groups already lived inside the Christian kingdom before the 16th century, which challenges the older picture of a sudden invasion. The current weight of evidence favours internal gada dynamics plus wartime opportunity.

Module 10 · Medieval

The Ajuran Empire and the Benadir coast

1. How we know about the Ajuran

The Ajuran (Ajuuraan) are the first Somali power of the southern interior that historians can describe in any detail, but almost everything known about them comes from oral tradition. No Ajuran documents, chronicles or securely attributed inscriptions survive. Portuguese and Arabic writers of the 15th–17th centuries describe the Benadir towns (Mogadishu, Merca, Barawa) but do not name an inland Ajuran state. The main reconstructions rest on traditions collected by Enrico Cerulli in the 1920s–50s and by Lee Cassanelli in field interviews in the 1970s, published in The Shaping of Somali Society (1982) Cassanelli 1982. Mohamed Haji Mukhtar summarises the same material Mukhtar 2003.

The common date range, c. 13th to late 17th century, is therefore a reconstruction, not a recorded chronology. Cassanelli's traditions mostly concern the period just before the Ajuran collapse, which he places in the later 17th century. Many popular claims (an Ajuran navy, an "only hydraulic empire" in Africa, an Ajuran–Ottoman alliance, Ajuran coins) go far beyond the evidence. Treat any precise date or battle attributed to the Ajuran as doubtful unless a contemporary source supports it.

"Ajuran" in modern summaries often stands for everything that happened in southern Somalia between 1300 and 1700. Contemporary sources name towns (Mogadishu, Barawa), not the Ajuran. Coastal battles with the Portuguese were fought by the towns themselves.

2. Who the Ajuran were

Today the Ajuran are a clan living mainly in north-eastern Kenya (around Wajir) and in Ethiopia's Somali Region. Their place in Somali genealogy is disputed: some genealogies link them to the Hawiye, others treat them as a separate lineage Lewis 2002. Tradition remembers a ruling lineage, the Gareen (Garen), whose heads used the title imam. Cassanelli argues that their authority rested on three supports: genealogical prestige, religious charisma (baraka inherited, in tradition, from a holy ancestor) and control of water Cassanelli 1982. Traditions place Ajuran centres in the Shabelle valley, from Qallaafo in the upper valley to the Mareeg area and the hinterland of Merca and Mogadishu.

Cassanelli calls the system a pastoral hegemony: a dominant lineage that drew tribute from allied and subject groups, not a bureaucratic empire with fixed frontiers. Officials are remembered with Islamic titles (governors, tax collectors, judges), but their exact functions cannot be checked.

3. Water, wells and tribute

In the semi-arid inter-riverine region, whoever controlled dry-season water controlled the herds. Traditions credit the Ajuran with digging many deep, stone-lined wells in the interior, and local people still call some old wells "Ajuran wells". By taxing access to wells, the Ajuran could draw tribute from nomads; along the Shabelle, farming communities paid in grain (sorghum) and herders in livestock and butter Cassanelli 1982. Some traditions also credit them with channels and dykes for flood-recession and canal farming on the Shabelle. None of these works has been archaeologically dated.

Traditions also remember Ajuran oppression: heavy levies, and stories that rulers demanded a share of bride-wealth or even the "first night" with brides. Cassanelli reads these stories as a memory of resented rule. They were told by the groups who later overthrew the Ajuran, and they should not be taken literally Cassanelli 1982.

Ajuran = water + baraka + lineageCassanelli's three pillars: control of wells and river water, religious charisma, and genealogical prestige. When the water monopoly and religious legitimacy failed, the hegemony failed.

4. The Benadir coast and the Indian Ocean

Benadir comes from Persian bandar, "port" (Arabic plural banadir), and names the southern coast from Warsheikh to Barawa. Mogadishu (Muqdisho), Merca (Marka) and Barawa (Baraawe) were self-governing Muslim towns. They exported ivory, hides, ambergris, gum and slaves, and woven Mogadishu cloth. They imported Indian cotton cloth (above all from Gujarat), beads, metal goods and Chinese porcelain Freeman-Grenville 1962. Mogadishu issued its own copper coins naming its sultans; no coin can securely be attributed to an Ajuran ruler. Tradition links the 16th-century Muzaffar rulers of Mogadishu to the Ajuran by alliance, and both lost power in the 17th century Cassanelli 1982.

Ming China. Envoys from Mogadishu, Barawa and Malindi reached the Ming court in 1416. Zheng He's fifth voyage (1417–19) took them home and visited Mogadishu (Mugudushu) and Barawa (Bulawa). Squadrons of the sixth voyage (1421–22) went there again, and the seventh (1431–33) listed both towns Dreyer 2007. The fleet's officer Fei Xin (1436) described Mogadishu's stone houses of four or five storeys and its dry, barren land (in Duyvendak's rendering). The famous giraffes were not Somali: one came in 1414 as a gift from Bengal, and Malindi sent another in 1415. The court read them as the auspicious qilin Duyvendak 1949.

Giraffe ≠ MogadishuThe giraffes that astonished Ming China came via Bengal (1414) and Malindi (1415). Mogadishu's link is the envoys of 1416 and the fleet visits of 1417–19 and 1421–22.

5. Portuguese and Ottomans

DateEventNote
Feb 1499Vasco da Gama, sailing home from India, bombards MogadishuFirst Portuguese hostility on the Somali coast
1507Tristão da Cunha and Afonso de Albuquerque sack BarawaOften misdated 1506, the year the fleet left Lisbon; Mogadishu was not taken

March 1589Mir Ali's second expedition destroyed at Mombasa by the Portuguese under Tomé de Sousa Coutinho and by the ZimbaMir Ali captured and taken to Lisbon

The Portuguese never controlled Mogadishu; they demanded passes (cartazes) at sea and raided towns that resisted Strandes 1961. Mir Ali's voyages show that the Benadir towns were seeking Ottoman support against Portugal Casale 2010. Claims that the Ajuran state organised these alliances or fought named "Ajuran–Portuguese" battles do not appear in the contemporary sources.

6. Decline and successors

Traditions give several causes for the end of Ajuran hegemony in the later 17th century: revolts against tribute and abuses; the loss of religious legitimacy; and new pastoral groups moving into the inter-riverine lands, which upset the old water monopoly Cassanelli 1982. Two successors stand out. North of the Shabelle, the Hiraab (Abgaal and related Hawiye lineages) formed an imamate whose leaders took over Mogadishu's hinterland and parts of the town Lewis 2002. Near Afgooye, the Silcis, remembered as the Ajuran section that governed the district, were driven out by the Geledi under Ibrahim Adeer, in alliance with the Wacdaan. This founded the Gobroon dynasty of the Geledi (see m11) Luling 2002. Ajuran lineages moved to the margins of their former domain, which helps explain their present location in Kenya and Ethiopia.

7. Method: reading Ajuran traditions

Cassanelli's work shows how a historian can use oral evidence. The standard checks are to compare versions told by different lineages, to look for details that serve no living group's interest, to match remembered places (wells, river crossings, old town sites) with the landscape, and to compare genealogies in order to estimate generations. The result is a picture of patterns (tribute, water control, migration, revolt) rather than a list of reigns and battles. The Ajuran also matter in modern Somali memory: they offer a southern, inter-riverine precedent for large-scale Somali political organisation before colonial rule, which is one reason the evidence is sometimes stretched Cassanelli 1982.

Ajuran → Hiraab + GelediNorth of the Shabelle the Hiraab imams; at Afgooye the Geledi after defeating the Silcis. Both inherited the river, the wells and the coastal trade.

Scholarly debates

Was the Ajuran polity an 'empire' or a looser hegemony?

Popular and some nationalist writing calls the Ajuran a centralised empire with a navy, officials, coinage and great hydraulic works. Cassanelli (1982), the main scholarly reconstruction, describes a pastoral hegemony: a prestigious lineage using religious authority, alliances and control of water to draw tribute, with no fixed bureaucracy. Because the evidence is almost entirely oral, Cassanelli's cautious model carries most scholarly weight; claims of an Ajuran navy or Ottoman alliance have no contemporary support.

How reliable are the traditions of Ajuran tyranny?

Traditions describe heavy tribute, levies on wells and outrages such as demands for the 'first night' with brides. Cassanelli treats them as political memory, told by the groups who overthrew the Ajuran and used to justify the new order; they confirm resentment of tribute but not specific practices. No independent source checks them.

When did the Ajuran rise and fall?

Modern summaries give c. 13th to late 17th century. The start date rests on genealogies and is very uncertain; the traditions Cassanelli collected relate mainly to the late phase and the collapse, which he places in the later 17th century. Contemporary Portuguese, Arabic and Chinese sources do not name the Ajuran, so no date can be checked independently.

Module 11 · Early modern

Later sultanates and kingdoms (17th–19th c.)

1. A landscape of lineage polities

Between the end of Ajuran hegemony (late 17th century) and colonial partition (1884–1889), no single power ruled the Somali lands. Instead there were lineage-based polities headed by men with titles such as suldaan (sultan), boqor (king), garaad, ugaas and imam. They differed greatly. Some, like the Geledi of Afgooye and the Majeerteen sultanate, collected tribute, fielded armies and dealt with foreign powers. Others, especially among northern pastoralists, were titled clan heads whose authority rested on consent, mediation and religious prestige. Lewis stressed that a northern sultan was at most first among equals, with little coercive power; real decisions were made by assemblies of men (shir) and by diya-paying groups Lewis 1961. Calling all of them "sultanates" can hide these differences.

2. The Geledi Sultanate

The Geledi, a Digil-Mirifle (Rahanweyn) community on the lower Shabelle, rose when Ibrahim Adeer, with Wacdaan allies, drove the Silcis (remembered as an Ajuran section) out of Afgooye (see m10). His descendants, the Gobroon dynasty, ruled from Afgooye Luling 2002. The state was at its height under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim (r. c. 1828–1848). He drew tribute from farming villages, built alliances among the Shabelle and inter-riverine clans, and controlled the caravan trade from the interior to Mogadishu, Merca and Barawa Cassanelli 1982.

The Bardera jihad. In about 1819 reformist scholars founded a religious community (jama'a) at Bardera on the Jubba. They demanded strict observance: they banned tobacco, dancing and saint-veneration practices they saw as un-Islamic, and they enforced stricter dress for women. In the 1830s they spread their rule by force, and in 1840 they attacked Barawa. Yusuf Mahamud led a large coalition of southern clans against them and destroyed Bardera in 1843 Mukhtar 2003. Cassanelli reads the conflict as both religious and commercial: Bardera threatened the ivory trade of the Jubba and the coastal towns allied to the Geledi Cassanelli 1982.

Yusuf was killed in 1848 fighting the Biimaal of the Merca hinterland at Adaddey Suleyman. His son Ahmed Yusuf (r. 1848–1878) restored Gobroon power, and Osman Ahmed came to terms with Italy early in the 20th century Luling 2002. The French naval officer Charles Guillain, who toured the Benadir in 1846–48, left the main European description of the Geledi at their height Guillain 1856.

19 – 40 – 43 – 48Bardera founded c. 1819; attacks Barawa 1840; destroyed by Yusuf Mahamud 1843; Yusuf killed by the Biimaal 1848.

3. The Benadir ports and Zanzibar

Oman's ruler Sayyid Said (r. 1806–1856), who moved his court to Zanzibar, claimed sovereignty over the Benadir towns from the 1820s–40s. He placed governors and small garrisons in Mogadishu, Merca and Barawa and taxed their customs. In practice Zanzibar's authority was weak: the towns' hinterlands belonged to the Geledi, the Biimaal and the Abgaal, and caravans moved on Somali terms Cassanelli 1982. Zanzibar's paper claims mattered later, when it leased the ports to Italy in 1892 (see m14).

Zanzibar's "sovereignty" over the Benadir was largely a claim on the customs house. Do not picture Omani rule over the interior: the Geledi and other clans controlled the land and the trade routes.

4. The north-east: Majeerteen, Hobyo and Warsangali

The Majeerteen Sultanate (Darod/Harti) controlled the Bari coast and its frankincense trees, with its main base at Aluula and a seasonal seat at Bargal. Boqor Osman Mahamuud ruled from about the 1860s until Italy deposed him in 1927. Revenue came from frankincense, the salvage of ships wrecked off Cape Guardafui, and trade with Aden and Arabia Lewis 2002. His cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid lost a succession struggle, went into exile in Arabia, returned with Hadrami musketeers and took Hobyo (Obbia) from the Habar Gidir. He founded the Sultanate of Hobyo c. 1878; sources give dates from the 1870s to 1884 Cassanelli 1982. Both rulers accepted Italian protection in 1889, Hobyo on 8 February (9 February in some lists; the sultan had asked for protection in late 1888) and the Majeerteen on 7 April, each hoping to use Italy against the other Hess 1966. Yusuf Ali's son Osman Yusuf Kenadid later devised the Osmanya script (see m04).

On the Gulf of Aden coast, the Warsangali (Darod/Harti) were led by a garaad, later styled sultan, based at Las Qoray. On 27 January 1886, at Bunder Gori (Las Qoray), their garaad Muhammad Mahmud Ali signed an agreement with Britain. Their sultan Mohamoud Ali Shire was later exiled by the British for supporting the Dervishes (see m15) Lewis 2002.

5. The north-west: Isaaq sultans and the Berbera fair

Isaaq tradition holds that Guled Abdi of the Eidagale was installed as the first Isaaq sultan in about 1749/50, after an Isaaq victory over the Absame at Lafaruug, with his seat at Toon. The Habar Yunis later chose their own sultan, and the Habar Awal followed. These dates come from oral tradition and recent Somali writing; the earliest outside observers are mid-19th-century British writers such as Cruttenden (1848) and Burton, who calls the Ismail Arrah "the royal clan" of the Habar Gerhajis Burton 1856. Lewis's fieldwork shows that their power depended on the consent of lineage assemblies.

The economic heart of the north was the Berbera fair. Burton, quoting Lieutenant Cruttenden (1848), describes a town that was empty from April to October. When the north-east monsoon turned, it filled with up to 20,000 people and with ships from Yemen, Muscat, Sur, Ras al-Khaimah, Bahrain and Basra, and with Banian traders from Porbandar, Mandvi and Bombay. By the end of March the fair broke up Burton 1856. Caravans brought livestock, ghee, gums, ostrich feathers, coffee and ivory from Harar and the Ogaden, and enslaved people from the highlands. The Habar Awal held the port and quarrelled with the Habar Gerhajis over its profits. At Zeila, Hajj Sharmarke Ali Salih ruled as governor under the Ottoman authorities in Yemen Burton 1856.

Burton entered Harar in January 1855 disguised as an Arab merchant and stayed ten days. In April 1855 his camp at Berbera was attacked: Lieutenant Stroyan was killed, and Burton and Speke were wounded. Britain answered with a blockade and an 1856 treaty with the Habar Awal Lewis 2002.

Berbera: October in, April outThe fair followed the monsoon: ships and caravans gathered from October, and by the first week of April the town stood empty again.

6. Egypt in the Horn, 1870s–1885

Khedive Ismail of Egypt sought an African empire. Egypt took over Zeila from the Ottoman administration and occupied Berbera in 1874–75. Muhammad Ra'uf Pasha marched from Zeila and occupied Harar on 11 October 1875; Emir Muhammad ibn Ali Abd al-Shakur was killed soon after Bahru Zewde 2002. An Egyptian force under McKillop Pasha landed at Barawa and Kismayo in 1875 but withdrew under British pressure on behalf of Zanzibar. Egypt's defeats by Ethiopia at Gundet (1875) and Gura (1876), and then the Mahdist revolt in the Sudan, ended the project. Egypt withdrew in 1884–85: Britain took over Zeila and Berbera, and Harar passed to Emir Abdullahi until Menelik took it in 1887 (see m14) Lewis 2002.

By the 1880s, then, the Somali lands were divided among local polities, Zanzibari claims, Ethiopian expansion and European agents. Religious networks were also spreading: Sufi orders (Qadiriyya, Ahmadiyya and from the 1880s the Salihiyya) built settlements and loyalties across clan lines. The militant reform of Bardera and the spread of these orders prepared the ground for the Dervish movement (see m13, m15).

Scholarly debates

Were the Isaaq and Habar Yunis 'sultanates' states?

Recent Somaliland-based writing presents an Isaaq sultanate founded c. 1749/50 with dynasties, capitals and a sultan list, and a Habar Yunis sultanate that broke away from it. Lewis's fieldwork (1961) described northern sultans as lineage figureheads and mediators with little coercive power, with decisions made by assemblies and diya-paying groups. Mid-19th-century British writers (Cruttenden 1848, Burton 1856) confirm that sultans existed but show limited authority. The evidence supports titled offices with real prestige rather than states with bureaucracies or armies; the founding dates rest on tradition.

Was the Bardera jihad religious or economic?

Older accounts treat Bardera as a religious revival crushed by traditionalists. Cassanelli (1982) argues that religious reform and commercial rivalry were intertwined: Bardera's control of the Jubba and its ivory trade, and its attack on Barawa, threatened the Geledi and their coastal partners. Most historians now accept a mixed explanation.

How real was Zanzibar's sovereignty over the Benadir?

Zanzibar and later Italy treated the Benadir ports as Zanzibari possessions, which made the 1892 lease possible. Cassanelli and Reese stress that Zanzibar's governors controlled little beyond the customs house, while the Geledi, Biimaal and Abgaal held the hinterland and the trade routes. The evidence favours a nominal sovereignty that mattered more in European diplomacy than on the ground.

Module 12 · Society

Clans, kinship and customary law

1. The classic model: a segmentary lineage system

Most English-language analysis of Somali kinship starts from I. M. Lewis's fieldwork among northern pastoralists in the 1950s, published as A Pastoral Democracy (1961) Lewis 1961. Lewis described a segmentary lineage system. Each person traces descent through the father, and reciting that chain of names is called abtirsiinyo ("counting of fathers"). Groups nest inside one another: clan-family, clan, sub-clan, primary lineage and diya-paying group. Two lineages that feud at one level combine against a more distant group at the next level up. Genealogy therefore works as a map of potential alliances, not just a family record Lewis 1994.

Lewis usually distinguished six clan-families. Four (Dir, Isaaq, Hawiye and Darod) he grouped as Samaale: they are mainly pastoral and speak Maxaa-tiri (Northern-Standard) Somali. Two (Digil and Mirifle, together called Rahanweyn) he grouped as Sab: they are agro-pastoralists between the Jubba and Shabelle rivers and mostly speak Maay. In tradition, Samaale and Sab are brothers. Lewis presented these genealogies as political charters whose literal historical truth cannot be checked. The table lists the families alphabetically; the order implies no rank.

Clan-familyMain areas (today)Examples of major clans
DarodNortheast Somalia, Ethiopia's Somali Region, NE Kenya, Jubba valleyHarti (Majeerteen, Dhulbahante, Warsangali), Ogaden, Marehan
Digil and Mirifle (Rahanweyn)Bay, Bakool, parts of Gedo and Lower ShabelleDigil: Geledi, Tunni, Jiido; Mirifle: many lineages in two confederations
DirDjibouti, western Somaliland, Ethiopia's Somali Region, pockets in the southIssa, Gadabuursi, Biimaal, Surre
HawiyeCentral Somalia, Mogadishu, Hiiraan, NE KenyaAbgaal, Habar Gidir, Hawadle, Murusade, Degodia
IsaaqCentral and eastern SomalilandHabar Awal, Garhajis (Habar Yoonis, Ciidagale), Habar Jeclo
Four Samaale, two SabDir, Isaaq, Hawiye and Darod are the Samaale; Digil and Mirifle (Rahanweyn) are the Sab. Read "Rahanweyn" as the umbrella name for the two Sab families.
Two meanings of "Sab". In Lewis's classification, Sab means the Digil and Mirifle. In northern speech, sab is also a demeaning label for occupational minorities such as the Madhiban, Tumal and Yibir. Check which meaning a source uses.

Is Isaaq part of Dir? Lewis lists Isaaq as a clan-family of its own, beside Darod and Hawiye. Isaaq and Darod genealogies both trace patrilineal descent to Arabian holy men (Sheikh Ishaaq and Sheikh Darod), and tradition says each married a Dir woman, which links them to the Samaale stem through their mothers. The 4.5 power-sharing formula, by contrast, counts Isaaq within the Dir share RVI 2023. So "Dir" means different things in different contexts. Historians treat the Arabian-ancestor claims as Islamic charters rather than as biological history (see m07 and m03).

2. Contract beside kinship: xeer and mag

In "Clanship and Contract in Northern Somaliland" (1959), Lewis argued that descent alone does not create political units. Lineages bind themselves by xeer, an agreed body of customary rules. Its core unit is the diya-paying group: a few hundred to a few thousand men who pay and receive blood-compensation (mag, Arabic diya) together. Lewis counted more than 360 such groups in British Somaliland in 1958 Lewis 1959. The tariff most often current in the north was 100 camels for a man and 50 for a woman, modelled on the shari'a tariff and now usually paid in cash. Lewis noted that these groups were larger and more stable among the inter-riverine agro-pastoralists than among the nomads ICRC 1997. In the south, the equivalent unit is often called a jilib.

Xeer treats homicide and injury as wrongs between groups, settled by compensation, rather than as crimes punished by a state. Elders (odayaal) argue cases in an assembly (shir), and xeer specialists hear disputes. A Somali-led oral-history study for the ICRC recorded the wartime code of birmageydo ("spared from the spear"). It protected women, children, the aged, the sick, guests, religious men and traditional leaders. Camels and horses were the only property custom allowed raiders to loot ICRC 1997. Lewis contrasted two ideal male roles: the warrior (waranle, "spear-bearer") and the man of religion (wadaad), who mediated for peace. Married women, linked to both their father's and their husband's lineage (xidid, in-laws), often acted as go-betweens.

After 1991, xeer became the main working justice system across much of Somalia. Reviews of it note real strengths, such as speed, legitimacy and restitution, and also weaknesses: liability falls on the group rather than the individual, and women and members of weak lineages, who cannot rely on a strong mag-paying group, are poorly protected Le Sage 2005.

Kinship + contract = politicsThe clan-family shows who could ally. The diya-paying group, bound by xeer, shows who actually pays and fights. Lewis called it "the basic political unit".

3. Elders and titles

Lewis called northern pastoral politics a "democracy" because any adult man could speak in the shir and there were no hereditary chiefs with coercive power. Titled leaders such as the suldaan, ugaas, garaad, islaan, boqor (the Majeerteen rulers), imaam and malaaq (an inter-riverine title) worked mainly as arbitrators and symbols of unity. Which title a group uses varies by clan; the titles form no single hierarchy. The British paid lineage headmen called akils. The Barre regime publicly condemned "tribalism" (qabyaalad) yet relied on state-recognised elders, renamed nabadoon ("peace-seekers"; the LoC study renders it "peacekeepers") Lewis 2002. Somaliland gave a council of elders, the Guurti, a constitutional place after the 1993 Borama conference (see m21).

4. Minorities

The clan-family scheme leaves out many Somalis. No reliable census exists, and estimates of the minority share of the population vary widely EUAA 2025.

GroupWhereNotes
Somali Bantu / Jareer (Gosha, Mushunguli and others)Jubba and Shabelle valleys, Bay; now also citiesRiverine farmers. Partly descended from people enslaved in East Africa and brought in during the 19th century, and partly from older riverine populations. Jareer ("hard hair") is a racialised label.
Benadiri (Reer Xamar, Reer Marka, Bravanese)Mogadishu, Merca, BarawaLong-settled urban merchant communities. The Bravanese speak Chimiini, a Swahili variety.
BajuniCoast and islands near KismayoFishing communities speaking Kibajuni, close to Swahili. Estimated at 10,000–15,000 people.
Occupational groups ("Gabooye": Madhiban, Tumal, Yibir and others)Throughout, especially the northLeather-workers and barbers, blacksmiths, ritual specialists. Majority clans usually do not intermarry with them. "Midgan" is now considered derogatory.
AshraafBenadir coast, BayLineages claiming descent from the Prophet. They have religious prestige but little armed strength.

Martin Hill's report for Minority Rights Group, No Redress (2010), documented killings, rape, land seizure and exclusion suffered by minorities who had neither armed militias nor strong mag-paying alliances to protect them Hill 2010. Besteman showed that southern society used the paired terms jareer and jileec (hard and soft hair) to mark a racialised status line that the northern clan model did not see Besteman 1999.

5. Genealogy as a political tool

Genealogies can be changed. Weak groups attach themselves to stronger ones as protected clients (magan) or by adopting the stronger group's genealogy (sheegad). Over generations, the adopted ancestry can become the accepted one, especially among the mixed inter-riverine Rahanweyn Cassanelli 1982. Politicians mobilise abtirsiinyo for votes, militias and jobs. That is why the 4.5 formula became central after state collapse.

The 4.5 formula. The Sodere conference in Ethiopia (1996–97) set up a National Salvation Council with nine seats for each of four clan-families and five for the remaining groups. At Arta, Djibouti, in 2000 the principle was formalised. Darod, Hawiye, Dir and Digil-Mirifle each received 44 seats, the "0.5" communities 24 seats, and women 25 more, in an assembly of 225 seats (some contemporary reports give 245, including later additions) RVI 2023 IRIN 2000. In 2004 the transitional parliament had 275 seats: 61 for each of the four clan-families and 31 for the 0.5. By convention, the presidency and premiership alternate between Darod and Hawiye and the Speaker usually comes from the Rahanweyn. The 2012 Provisional Constitution never mentions 4.5, yet seats are still allocated by it (see m19, m20).

9 → 44 → 61These are the per-family seat counts in the three bodies. Sodere 1997: 9 each and 5 for the rest. Arta 2000: 44 each and 24. Mbagathi 2004: 61 each and 31, making 275 seats.

6. Critiques of the "clan paradigm"

  • Catherine Besteman, in "Representing Violence and 'Othering' Somalia" (1996) and Unraveling Somalia (1999), argued that explaining the war as clan feuding hides class, race, slavery's legacy and the scramble for southern farmland. Lewis replied in "Doing Violence to Ethnography" (1998), and Besteman answered with "Primordialist Blinders" (1998) Besteman 1996.
  • Ali Jimale Ahmed (ed.), The Invention of Somalia (1995), and Abdi Kusow challenged the picture of a homogeneous, pastoral, Arabian-descended nation. They argued that the paradigm generalised northern nomadic experience to inter-riverine, urban and minority Somalis Ahmed 1995 Kusow 2004.
  • Abdi Ismail Samatar (1992) called for analysis "beyond the tribal convention", focused on the post-colonial state, class formation and the competition to accumulate wealth through state office Samatar 1992.
  • Lidwien Kapteijns, in Clan Cleansing in Somalia (2013), treats the 1991–92 violence as a new, deliberate use of clan labels by political and military entrepreneurs. She holds them, not "clan" as such, responsible. Critics such as Mohamed Haji Ingiriis question her method and sources Kapteijns 2013.

Lewis's defenders reply that kinship really does organise mutual aid, compensation and mobilisation. The current consensus treats clan as a powerful but changeable resource that interacts with the state, markets and violence, not as a fixed essence.

Clan is a resource, not a scriptLewis described how kinship works. His critics ask who mobilises it, against whom, and whom the model leaves out (minorities, women, southern farmers).

Scholarly debates

Is the segmentary 'clan paradigm' an adequate explanation of Somali politics and conflict?

Lewis (1961, 1994, 1998) held that agnatic kinship and contract really organise Somali society and war. Besteman (1996, 1999) argued that this hides race, class, slavery's legacy and land struggles in the south. Ahmed (1995) and Kusow argued that it generalises northern nomadic experience. Abdi I. Samatar (1992) stressed the predatory post-colonial state. Kapteijns (2013) blames political entrepreneurs who mobilised clan, while her critics (e.g. Ingiriis) dispute her sources. Current weight: kinship matters, but as a changeable resource used by state and market actors, not as a fixed cause.

Should the Isaaq be counted as part of the Dir?

Lewis treats Isaaq as a separate clan-family. Isaaq genealogies trace paternal descent to Sheikh Ishaaq, with a maternal link to Dir. The 4.5 formula and some TFG-era usage count Isaaq inside the Dir share, but many Isaaq reject this and it carries political weight in Somaliland. There is no scholarly consensus; the answer depends on whether one follows paternal genealogy or political convention.

Has the 4.5 formula stabilised Somalia or entrenched clan politics?

Supporters see it as a Somali-owned compromise that made the inclusive transitional bodies of 2000, 2004 and 2012 possible. Critics, including the Somali Dialogue Platform (2023) and minority advocates (Hill 2010), say a temporary fix has become permanent. In their view it blocks one-person-one-vote, rewards armed strength and fixes minorities at a 'half'. Most analysts now treat it as a transitional tool that has outlived its purpose, though there is no agreement on a replacement.

Are the Arabian-ancestor genealogies of the Darod and Isaaq historical?

Tradition traces both to Arabian holy men who married Dir women. Lewis treated such claims as Islamic charters that confer prestige. Kusow and contributors to The Invention of Somalia see them as myths that reinforce a hierarchy of 'noble' descent. Genetic studies (see m03) find mostly local Horn ancestry, so the claims are best read as statements of religious and political identity, not literal biology.

Module 13 · Islam

Religion and Sufi orders

1. Foundations: Sunni, Shafi'i and saint-centred

Somalis are almost entirely Sunni Muslims who follow the Shafi'i school of law, as do most Muslims along the Red Sea and Indian Ocean coasts. Islam reached the coast through trade and settlement and spread inland over centuries (see m07). By the 19th century, Islam and lineage were closely intertwined: the founders of whole clan-families were remembered as Arabian holy men, and lineage elders worked alongside religious specialists Lewis 1998. Lewis described two ideal male roles: the warrior (waranle) and the man of religion (wadaad, plural wadaaddo). The wadaad taught, wrote amulets, led prayers, officiated at marriages and mediated between feuding groups.

Basic religious learning took place in the dugsi (Qur'anic school). A teacher (macallin) taught children to recite and write the Qur'an on a wooden board (loox), often moving with the nomads' camps. Advanced students, the xer, travelled between teachers to study law, grammar and Sufi texts, often to Harar, Zeila, the Benadir towns, Yemen or Mecca. Scholars also wrote Somali in Arabic letters ("wadaad's writing"), especially for devotional poetry (see m04) Reese 2008.

2. The Sufi orders (dariiqo)

From the late 18th century, the Sufi brotherhoods (Arabic tariqa, Somali dariiqo) became the main framework of organised religious life. Three orders dominated, with a small Rifa'iyya presence among Arabs in Mogadishu LoC 1993.

OrderOriginKey Somali figuresBase
Qadiriyya (the oldest and largest)Named after Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani of Baghdad (d. 1166). Present in Harar by the 15th century.Abd al-Rahman al-Zayla'i (d. 1882; the Library of Congress study gives 1883): the Zayla'iyya branch. Uways al-Barawi (1847–1909): the Uwaysiyya. Sheikh Sufi (Abd al-Rahman Abdallah) of Mogadishu.Qulunqul in the western Somali lands (Zayla'i); Barawa and Biyooley (Uways); the Benadir towns
Ahmadiyya (Idrisiyya)Ahmad ibn Idris al-Fasi (1760–1837), MeccaSheikh Ali Maye Durogba of Merca (d. 1917)Merca and the lower Shabelle
SalihiyyaFounded in Mecca in 1887 by Muhammad ibn Salih, after a split in the Idrisi successionMuhammad Guled al-Rashidi (d. 1918) and Sayyid Mohamed Abdullah HassanShidle settlements on the middle Shabelle; the north and the Ogaden
Q-A-S, oldest to newestQadiriyya: Baghdad, 12th century. Ahmadiyya: Ahmad ibn Idris, d. 1837. Salihiyya: 1887, an offshoot of the Idrisi line. The Sayyid belonged to the youngest, S.

The Qadiriyya was more tolerant of local custom, such as saint veneration and intercession at tombs. The Salihiyya, which Martin calls the most puritanical, condemned practices such as chewing qat and smoking tobacco, and was suspicious of tomb cults Martin 1976. Tradition says that Uways, returning from Baghdad, met al-Zayla'i at Qulunqul shortly before al-Zayla'i's death and received his authority. Said Samatar's study (1992) is reported to argue instead that Uways only visited the tomb and claimed a symbolic licence (ijaaza); that reading could not be checked against a second source, so treat both versions with caution Samatar 1992. Uways had studied in Baghdad from about 1870 under Sayyid Mustafa b. Salman al-Jilani. He wrote devotional poetry in Maay Somali in Arabic script, and his network reached Zanzibar, Tanganyika and the eastern Congo. Reese shows that men like Uways and Sheikh Sufi were themselves "renewers" (mujaddids), presenting reform through Sufi idioms and poetry Reese 2008.

3. The jama'a: farming communities of the faithful

Religious leaders founded agricultural settlements called jama'a (Somali jamaaco) on land that clan heads granted "as a gift to God". There they farmed, taught and gave refuge to people who had left their lineages, such as runaways, clients and freed slaves. The first, at Bardera on the Jubba, was founded in 1819 by Sheikh Ibrahim Hassan Jebro. By the 1830s it had become militant and tried to impose its reformist rules on its neighbours, until a coalition led by Sultan Yusuf Mahamud of the Geledi sacked it in 1843 Cassanelli 1982 (see m11). Most later jama'a were peaceful. In the 1950s there were more than ninety in the south, with about 35,000 members LoC 1993.

4. Saints, baraka and siyaaro

A saint (Arabic wali) possesses baraka, a blessing-power that can perform miracles (karaamaat) and stays at his tomb after death. Followers make an annual pilgrimage (siyaaro, from Arabic ziyara) on the anniversary of the saint's birth or death. There they recite praise poems and the dhikr (sikri), slaughter animals and ask for cures, rain or children. Lewis contrasted two kinds of saint. Northern pastoralists honour lineage founders, such as Sheikh Ishaaq at Maydh or the shrine of Aw Barkhadle near Hargeisa. Southern farmers and townspeople honour scholar-saints for their learning and miracles, such as Sheikh Sufi in Mogadishu, Ali Maye at Merca and Uways at Biyooley Lewis 1998 LoC 1993. Lewis argued that the northern cult of ancestors projects the lineage system into the religious sphere.

Ancestors in the north, scholars in the southNomads venerate the founders of their genealogies. Farmers and townspeople venerate learned holy men of any origin.

5. Rival orders and the Dervish war

Sayyid Mohamed Abdullah Hassan joined the Salihiyya in Mecca and returned to Berbera in 1895. He denounced the Qadiriyya's tolerance of tomb rites and qat, and the two sides exchanged poems accusing each other of unbelief. When his movement became an armed jihad (1899–1920, see m15), Qadiri leaders condemned it. In 1909 Dervish partisans killed Sheikh Uways at Biyooley, and the Qadiriyya remembers him as a martyr Samatar 1992 Martin 1976. Samatar's study of the Sayyid's poetry shows how he used verse as a religious and political weapon Samatar 1982.

Common confusion: the Sayyid was Salihi, not Qadiri, and Uways was not killed by colonial troops. He died at the hands of fellow Somali Muslims during a conflict between rival orders.

6. The state, reform and political Islam

The 1960 constitution (approved by referendum in 1961) declared Islam the religion of the state while guaranteeing freedom of religion. After the 1969 coup, Siad Barre's regime said that "Scientific Socialism" did not conflict with Islam, but it treated religion as a private matter. On 11 January 1975 it announced a Family Law that gave women equal inheritance rights. Scholars who preached against it in Mogadishu mosques were arrested, and ten were executed on 23 January 1975 LoC 1993 Abdullahi 2015. Sources disagree on the numbers: the Library of Congress study says twenty-three leaders protested in their mosques and were arrested; other accounts say about 35 were detained.

From the 1970s, migrant labour in the Gulf, scholarships to Saudi and Egyptian universities and imported literature spread both Salafi (Wahhabi-influenced) and Muslim Brotherhood ideas. Both currents attacked Sufi saint veneration. Harakat al-Islah (1978) followed the Brotherhood's gradualist line and later concentrated on education and civil society. al-Itihaad al-Islaami (AIAI) formed in 1983 from a merger of the southern al-Jama'a al-Islamiyya and the northern Wahdat al-Shabab al-Islami ICG 2005. After 1991 AIAI took up arms. It briefly held the port of Bosaso until Puntland's SSDF drove it out in 1992, then dominated Luuq in Gedo until Ethiopian strikes in 1996–97 (dates differ in sources). Its veterans went on to al-I'tisaam, the Islamic Courts and, in some cases, al-Shabaab (see m20). Sufi leaders formed Ahlu Sunna wal Jama'a in 1991. It took up arms in 2008 after al-Shabaab began destroying Sufi tombs MMP.

The 2012 Provisional Constitution makes Islam the state religion, bars the propagation of any other religion and requires that no law contradict the shari'a Constitution 2012. Today's religious field is plural. Sufi orders, Salafi networks, Brotherhood-derived movements, the apolitical Tabligh and the armed jihadists of al-Shabaab and Islamic State-Somalia all compete for authority.

1975 → 1978 → 1983 → 19911975: Family Law executions. 1978: Islah founded. 1983: AIAI formed. 1991: state collapse, the Islamists arm, and Sufis organise as Ahlu Sunna wal Jama'a.

Scholarly debates

Did Uways receive the Qadiriyya succession from al-Zayla'i in person?

Qadiri tradition says the two met at Qulunqul shortly before al-Zayla'i's death and that al-Zayla'i handed over authority. Said Samatar (1992) is reported to argue that Uways only visited the tomb and claimed a symbolic ijaaza, his real authority coming from his Baghdad training; this summary could not be checked against a second source. Hagiography supports the first view; source criticism counsels caution about both.

Is Somali reformism an import or an indigenous tradition?

One view, common in journalism and some security studies, treats Salafism and political Islam as Gulf imports of the 1970s–80s. Reese (2008), Martin (1976) and Cassanelli point to older internal reform: the Bardera jama'a (1819), Salihi puritanism and Sufi 'renewers' in Benadir. The weight of evidence suggests that external funding and ideas built on a long internal history of reform debate.

Does the Somali cult of saints mirror the lineage system?

Lewis (1998) argued that northern pastoralists sanctify the founders of their genealogies, so religion reinforces segmentary identity. Reese and others emphasise trans-regional scholarly networks, urban piety and Sufi poetry that cut across clan. Both patterns exist; the disagreement is about which explains more.

Was the Sayyid's movement primarily religious reform or proto-nationalism?

Samatar (1982) reads the Sayyid's poetry as nationalist mobilisation within an Islamic idiom. Lewis and Martin emphasise Salihi reform and the rivalry between orders, and note his violence against Somali Qadiris, including Uways. Most now treat it as a religious jihad whose memory was later nationalised (see m15).

Module 14 · Colonial

The scramble for the Horn

Why the Horn was partitioned

Between 1884 and 1925 the Somali-speaking lands were divided among five administrations: British, French, Italian, Ethiopian and, after 1895, the British East Africa Protectorate (Kenya). The motives differed. Britain had held Aden since 1839, and after the Suez Canal opened in 1869 the port became a coaling station on the route to India that depended on livestock from the opposite Somali coast. France wanted its own coaling station on the Red Sea. Italy, unified only in 1861, sought prestige and an outlet for emigration, and took territory where no stronger power objected Hess 1966. Ethiopia under Menelik II expanded eastward for land, tribute and security Lewis 2002.

The catalyst was Egypt. Khedive Ismail occupied the northern ports in the 1870s and took Harar on 11 October 1875. The Mahdist revolt in the Sudan cut Egypt's lines, and in 1884–85 its garrisons were evacuated with British help. Britain filled the vacuum on the coast; at Harar a local emir, Abdullahi, was left in power LoC 1993. (For the earlier Egyptian occupation, see m11.)

Britain: treaties of protection, ruled from Aden

Major F. M. Hunter arrived at Berbera in February 1884 to negotiate treaties of friendship and protection. Between 1884 and 1886 agreements were signed with the elders of the Habr Awal, Habr Garhajis, Habr Toljaala, Gadabursi and Esa (Issa), and in 1886 with the Warsangali. The clans promised not to cede or sell territory to any other power except Britain; they did not cede their own land. British vice-consuls were posted at Zeila (Saylac), Berbera and Bulhar, and the protectorate was notified to the other powers in July 1887 Lewis 2002 EB 1911.

The protectorate was run as a dependency of Aden under the Government of India until 1898, then by the Foreign Office, and from 1905 by the Colonial Office. Its northern edges were fixed by an Anglo-French agreement of February 1888 (Zeila–Djibouti) and an Anglo-Italian protocol of 5 May 1894. The legal character of the 1884–86 treaties mattered later: in 1955 MPs argued that Britain could not hand the Haud to Ethiopia because it had promised protection to the clans that grazed there Hansard 1955.

Meat, coal, prestige, landBritain wanted meat for Aden; France wanted coal on the Red Sea; Italy wanted prestige; Menelik wanted land and tribute. The four motives match the four outside powers.

France: from Obock to Djibouti

France bought Obock from Afar chiefs by a treaty of 11 March 1862 for 10,000 thalers but did not occupy it until 1884. Léonce Lagarde, commandant from 1884 and later governor, extended protectorates over Tadjoura and the Issa coast. Djibouti, which had a better harbour, was developed from 1888 and became the seat of government in the mid-1890s; dates of 1894, 1895 and 1896 appear in different sources. The colony was named Côte française des Somalis in 1896. Building began in 1897 on the railway to Ethiopia, which reached Dire Dawa in 1902 and Addis Ababa in 1917. The territory's population was Issa Somali and Afar, a division that shaped later politics (see m22).

Italy: protectorates in the north-east, leases on the Benadir

Italy's agent was Vincenzo Filonardi, consul at Zanzibar. Two rival Majeerteen rulers each accepted Italian protection to strengthen himself against the other. Yusuf Ali Kenadid of Hobyo (Obbia) signed on 8 February 1889 (9 February in some lists; the LoC study dates Hobyo's first acceptance of protection to 1888, and some sources to December 1888), and his kinsman Boqor Osman Mahamud of the Majeerteen Sultanate signed on 7 April 1889. The treaties left internal administration to the sultans LoC 1993. Italy notified the powers of the Berlin Conference.

The Benadir ports (Brava, Merca, Mogadishu and Warsheikh) belonged to the Sultan of Zanzibar. In August 1892 he leased them to Italy. Most modern accounts give a 25-year term and an annual rent of 160,000 rupees; the 1911 Britannica says fifty years. Rome had no wish to pay for direct rule. It handed the ports first to Filonardi's company (1893–96), then, after Somali resistance, to the Benadir Company (Società Anonima Commerciale Italiana del Benadir, from 1898–99) Hess 1966 EB 1911.

Resistance was strongest in the hinterland. On 26 November 1896, at Lafolé near Afgoye, fighters of the Wacdaan and Biimaal (as most accounts name them) killed the consul Antonio Cecchi and about thirteen companions. Both companies failed. Reports that the Benadir Company tolerated slavery caused a scandal in Italy. By an agreement of 13 January 1905 the Sultan of Zanzibar ceded his sovereign rights for a lump sum of £144,000, and the Italian state took direct control. A 1908 law united the territories as Somalia Italiana Hess 1966. The northern sultanates kept indirect rule until the Fascist conquest of 1925–27 (see m16).

Protectorate, lease and purchase are different instruments. Hobyo and the Majeerteen Sultanate were protectorates (1889) that kept their own rulers. The Benadir ports were leased from Zanzibar (1892) and then bought (1905). Jubaland was ceded by Britain (1925). Confusing them distorts both chronology and law.

Ethiopia: a colonial competitor

Menelik, king of Shoa and emperor from 1889, defeated Emir Abdullahi at Chelenqo in January 1887 (6 or 9 January; sources differ) and annexed Harar, which he gave to his cousin Ras Makonnen. From Harar, Ethiopian columns raided the Ogaden through the 1890s and set up posts such as Jigjiga. Because the army lived off the country, these expeditions seized much livestock LoC 1993. Ethiopia's victory over Italy at Adwa on 1 March 1896 made Menelik a power the Europeans had to treat with.

Three agreements followed. A Franco-Ethiopian treaty (March 1897) fixed the Djibouti border. On 14 May 1897 James Rennell Rodd signed the Anglo-Ethiopian treaty at Addis Ababa. Britain gave up much of the Haud that its 1884–86 treaties had covered. In letters of 4 June 1897 Rodd and Ras Makonnen agreed that clans from either side could cross the line to graze, but would be under the authority of the territory they were in. The line was demarcated only in 1932–35 Treaty 1897 Touval 1963. With Italy, an understanding reached by Nerazzini in 1897 was followed by the Italo-Ethiopian convention of 16 May 1908. Its line ran from Dolo, where the Dawa and Ganale rivers meet, towards the Webi Shabelle, and beyond that partly along clan grazing areas. The two sides were to mark it on the ground but never did UN 1957. This vagueness left Walwal open to dispute in 1934 (m16).

'97 sets the Haud; '54 hands it overEthiopian title to the Haud comes from the 14 May 1897 treaty. The 1954 agreement only ended British administration. The grazing rights in Rodd's 1897 letters link the two.

Kenya: Jubaland and the Northern Frontier District

Britain inherited Zanzibar's mainland coast, including Kismayo, through the East Africa Protectorate (1895). An Anglo-Italian protocol of 24 March 1891 took the Juba river as the boundary between the two spheres. British posts in the north, such as Moyale and Archer's Post, date from about 1909. Under Article 13 of the secret Treaty of London (26 April 1915) Britain promised Italy colonial compensation for joining the war. The Anglo-Italian treaty of 15 July 1924 ceded the land west of the Juba. On 29 June 1925 it was handed over at Kismayo, governed briefly as Oltre Giuba, and merged into Italian Somalia in mid-1926. The Somali-inhabited land left west of the new line formed Kenya's Northern Frontier District, which became a closed district in 1926 Touval 1963 Lewis 2002. Its fate in 1962–67 is covered in m17 and m22.

TerritoryPowerKey instrumentsSeat
Somaliland ProtectorateBritainClan treaties 1884–86; protectorate notified 1887Berbera (Hargeisa from 1941)
Côte française des SomalisFranceObock treaty 1862; Lagarde's protectorates 1884–85; Anglo-French agreement 1888Obock, then Djibouti
Somalia ItalianaItalyHobyo and Majeerteen 1889; Benadir lease 1892, purchase 1905; Jubaland 1925Mogadishu
Ogaden and HaudEthiopiaChelenqo 1887; treaties of 1897; Italo-Ethiopian convention 1908Harar, Jigjiga

Five territories, five pointsBritish, French, Italian, Ethiopian and Kenyan Somali lands. They became the five points of the star on the 1960 flag (m17), the symbol of the pan-Somali claim.

Historiography

Touval (1963) and Lewis (1965; 4th ed. 2002) set the standard account. They stress that partition cut across clan grazing systems and created the "Somali question". Hess (1966) traces Italian policy through Italian archives and shows how small Italy's investment was and how far it relied on chartered companies. Somali nationalist writing treats Ethiopia's expansion as colonial conquest, equal to the European one. Ethiopian historiography usually describes it as the reunification or expansion of the empire. That disagreement still shapes the border dispute. The treaties themselves are an issue. Lewis and Touval note that the British agreements were treaties of protection, not cession, and Somali leaders later used them to argue that Britain had no right to hand grazing lands to Ethiopia.

Scholarly debates

Was Ethiopia's expansion into the Ogaden colonial conquest?

Somali nationalist writers, and in comparative terms Lewis and Touval, place Menelik among the partitioning powers: he conquered Harar and the Ogaden by force in the same years as the Europeans and negotiated borders with them. Ethiopian historiography has usually framed the same events as the expansion or reunification of the empire into areas it claimed historically, and Haile Selassie used that argument in the 1950s. Scholars agree on the facts of conquest and on treaties with European powers; they differ on whether 'colonial' is the right category for an African empire. The question still affects the legitimacy of the Ethiopia–Somalia border.

Did the Somali signatories of the 1884–86 treaties intend to give up sovereignty?

The texts promise protection and forbid alienating land to other powers; they do not transfer land, and Lewis and Touval stress this. Britain nonetheless treated the protectorate as its own to define, and in 1897 accepted a border that placed much of the clans' grazing in Ethiopia. In the 1955 Commons debate, critics argued that Britain had no right to hand over land whose people it had promised to protect, and the government replied that Ethiopian title rested on the 1897 treaty. Historians accept the protective form of the treaties; whether that limited Britain's freedom to make the 1897 treaty is a legal and political judgement, not a settled fact.

Why did Italy hold on to an unprofitable Somali colony?

Hess shows that the Benadir produced little revenue, and that Rome relied on chartered companies to keep costs down. He and the LoC study point to prestige and the wish to stake out territory without confronting a stronger power. Others stress settlement and plantation hopes for the Shabelle and Juba valleys, realised only partly after 1920. The weight of evidence favours prestige and strategic positioning before 1905, and economic projects only after it.
