Module 15 · Colonial

The Dervish State

The man and his sources

Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan (Maxamed Cabdulle Xasan) led an armed movement in the northern Somali interior from 1899 until his death in late 1920. The British called him the 'Mad Mullah', a label that says more about colonial attitudes than about him. His followers called him the Sayyid, and their movement the Dervishes (daraawiish). Much of the narrative evidence comes from British officials. Douglas Jardine's The Mad Mullah of Somaliland (1923), written by the Secretary to the Somaliland administration with a foreword by Viscount Milner, Colonial Secretary when the 1920 expedition was sent, is a detailed but openly hostile British colonial source. Somali evidence comes mainly from the Sayyid's poetry and from oral testimony, analysed by Said S. Samatar (1982) and Abdi Sheik-Abdi (1993). Robert Hess (1964) first framed him for academic readers as a precursor of Somali nationalism Hess 1964.

Even his birth is disputed. Sheik-Abdi's biography and Samatar give 1856. The Encyclopedia of World Biography and Britannica give 1864, and Jardine says only 'the early seventies'. His father, Abdille Hassan, was of the Ogaden (Bah Geri section, according to Jardine). His mother was Dhulbahante, and he grew up in Dhulbahante country near Kirrit Jardine 1923. Both clans later formed the core of his support LoC 1993.

The Salihiyya and the road to war, 1895–1899

On pilgrimage and study in Arabia, Hassan joined the Salihiyya, a reformist order founded by the Sudanese teacher Muhammad Salih in Mecca; it was a branch of the Ahmadiyya tradition of Ahmad ibn Idris. He returned to Berbera in 1895 as Salih's deputy Jardine 1923. He preached strict observance and attacked qat, tobacco and lavish living. He clashed with the dominant Qadiriyya, and denounced a French Catholic mission that took in Somali orphans (see m13 for the orders). Berbera's merchants and clerics resented him, and he moved inland to his mother's people.

In March 1899 a small dispute became open defiance: a rifle said to have been stolen was taken to the Sayyid's camp, and he answered the vice-consul's request for it with an insulting reply. In August 1899 he occupied Burao with several thousand men. Jardine says he proclaimed himself the expected Mahdi; that claim rests on British reports and should be treated as a colonial account. The British consul-general proclaimed him a rebel Jardine 1923 EB 1911. The Dervishes called Somalis who refused to join them infidels and raided them. This internal war is central to how the movement is remembered.

"1899 to 1920: twenty-one years"The war ran from the occupation of Burao (August 1899) to the fall of Taleh and the Sayyid's death (1920). Jardine's own phrase is "one-and-twenty years".

Four expeditions, 1901–1904

ExpeditionCommanderKey actionResult
1st, 1901Lt-Col E. J. E. Swayne (Somali levies, with an Ethiopian force in the Ogaden)Ferdiddin, SamalaDervishes driven south; not destroyed
2nd, 1902SwayneErigo, 6 Oct 1902Indecisive; the British turn to regular troops
3rd, 1903Brig.-Gen. W. H. Manning, via ObbiaGumburu, 17 Apr 1903; Daratoleh, 22 Apr 1903Plunkett's column destroyed: 9 British officers and 187 men killed
4th, 1903–04Maj.-Gen. Sir Charles EgertonJidballi, 10 Jan 1904Dervish defeat: 668 dead counted, more in the pursuit

Gumburu was the worst colonial defeat in Somaliland. Among the Sayyid's leading allies was Sultan Nur of the Habr Yunis, an Isaaq leader whom Jardine places at the Sayyid's side in 1901; some later accounts also credit him with the cavalry charge at Gumburu, which Jardine does not record. His role shows the movement did not draw on Darod clans alone Jardine 1923. Ethiopian forces cooperated from the west in 1901 and 1903. At Jidballi a square of British, Indian, African and Somali troops broke the Dervish attack in about twenty-five minutes. The 1911 Britannica confirms the date and the rout EB 1911.

Illig and the Nugaal, 1905–1910

Defeated, the Sayyid withdrew into Majeerteen territory under Italian protection. Italy's envoy Pestalozza negotiated the Illig (Eyl) agreement, signed at Illig on 5 March 1905. The Dervishes were allowed to settle in the Nugaal, between the British and Italian zones, as Italian protégés, and promised peace Jardine 1923 Hess 1964. Hess notes that Italy in effect granted the movement the Nogal territory as a way of managing it.

The truce did not last. Around 1909 Muhammad Salih wrote from Mecca condemning the Sayyid's conduct. Prominent followers, including Abdullah Shahari, publicised the letter and left him, and the Sayyid answered in verse. The rivalry with the Qadiriyya had already turned deadly: in 1909 Dervish partisans killed the Qadiri leader Sheikh Uways al-Barawi (m13). Raiding resumed. In 1910 Britain chose 'coastal concentration'. It withdrew to Berbera, Bulhar and Zeila and armed friendly clans. The interior collapsed into war and famine, and Jardine estimates that 'not less than one-third of the male population' died Jardine 1923.

The 'one-third' mortality figure comes from a British colonial source. Jardine wrote of one-third of the male population, and the LoC study repeats a broader one-third of northern Somalia's population. No census existed, so treat it as an estimate that combines Dervish raids, inter-clan war after the 1910 withdrawal, and famine, not as a count of Dervish killings alone.

Taleh and Dul Madoba, 1913–1919

In 1913 the Sayyid made Taleh (Taleex) his headquarters. Yemeni masons built stone forts there and at Jidali, Medishe and Shimber Berris, an unusual permanent base for a pastoral movement Jardine 1923. On 9 August 1913 at Dul Madoba, near Burao, the Dervishes attacked the new Somaliland Camel Constabulary. Its commander, Richard Corfield, and some 35 of his men were killed. The Sayyid's poem on Corfield's death, translated by Andrzejewski and Lewis, is among the best-known Somali poems Andrzejewski & Lewis 1964. Britain rebuilt its force as the Somaliland Camel Corps and took Shimber Berris in 1914–15.

During the First World War the Dervishes looked for allies abroad. They had contacts with Ethiopia's Muslim-leaning ruler Lij Iyasu, deposed in September 1916, and with Ottoman and German agents. A German mechanic, Emil Kirsch, was sent to Taleh to repair rifles. A Dervish letter of March 1917 ridicules British suggestions that it depended on these friends Jardine 1923.

The 1920 campaign and the end

The Colonial Office under Lord Milner approved a combined operation. "Z" Force of the Royal Air Force, under Group Captain Robert Gordon, landed at Berbera in December 1919. Its de Havilland DH.9 bombers, about a dozen in most accounts (Jardine records six in the first raid), struck the Dervish camp at Medishe on 21 January 1920, while the Camel Corps, King's African Rifles, Indian troops and clan levies advanced. Taleh fell in February 1920. Milner's foreword claims the expedition lasted three weeks and cost less than £100,000 Jardine 1923. It is often cited as an early case of colonial 'air control', though ground forces did most of the pursuit LoC 1993.

The Sayyid escaped to the upper Shabelle at Imi, in the Ogaden, and refused Governor Archer's offer of terms. He died there of an illness, probably influenza. Most sources, including the Encyclopedia of World Biography, give 21 December 1920; Jardine gives 23 November 1920; a few give 1921. The movement broke up with his death.

G-D-I-T: Gumburu, Dul Madoba, Illig, TalehTwo Dervish victories (Gumburu 1903, Dul Madoba 1913), one peace (Illig 1905) and one fortress (Taleh, bombed 1920).

Poetry, memory and judgement

Samatar shows that the Sayyid's gabay were weapons of politics. They recruited allies, insulted enemies and answered the Salihiyya's condemnation, and many of his most serious poems date from 1905–09 Samatar 1982. From the 1940s the Somali Youth League and later governments made him the father of Somali nationalism. Siad Barre's regime gave him a statue in Mogadishu and a national cult. Sheik-Abdi presents him as a religious reformer whose anti-colonial war was also a struggle for power among Somalis Sheik-Abdi 1993. Many Isaaq, Majeerteen and other communities remember Dervish raids on them, and some writers in Somaliland question the national cult built around him. A balanced view treats him as anti-colonial leader, poet and religious reformer, and also as the head of a movement whose violence fell heavily on Somalis.

Scholarly debates

Was the Dervish movement a nationalist struggle?

Hess (1964) called the Sayyid a precursor of Somali nationalism, and the Somali Youth League and later governments made him its founding hero. Samatar (1982) shows that his poetry addressed a wide Somali audience against foreign rule, which supports a proto-nationalist reading. Lewis and Sheik-Abdi stress that his support was concentrated in particular clans and that his war was fought largely against other Somalis, and that his aims were framed religiously, not in terms of a nation-state. The prevailing view is that he was a religious and anti-colonial leader whose legacy was later nationalised, not a nationalist in the modern sense.

How many died, and who was responsible?

Jardine (British colonial source) estimated that at least one-third of the male population of the protectorate died, and the LoC study repeats a one-third estimate for northern Somalia. No census existed. Deaths came from Dervish raids, British and Ethiopian operations, inter-clan war after the 1910 withdrawal, and famine. Somali critics of the Sayyid cite the figure against him, while defenders note that British policy, especially arming clans and then withdrawing, created the anarchy. The figure is best treated as an impressionistic order of magnitude.

When was the Sayyid born, and when did he die?

Birth: 1856 (Samatar; Sheik-Abdi), 7 April 1864 (Encyclopedia of World Biography; Britannica gives 1864), or the early 1870s (Jardine). Death: 21 December 1920 in most accounts, 23 November 1920 in Jardine, and 1921 in a few. Oral sources and colonial intelligence both fed into these dates, and none is from a written record made at the time. Learners should give the range and the source.

Module 16 · Colonial

Fascism, war and trusteeship

Fascist Somalia, 1923–1935

Mussolini's first governor, the Fascist quadrumvir Cesare Maria De Vecchi (8 December 1923 – 1 June 1928), ended the indirect rule left over from the 1889 protectorates (m14). In 1925–27 Italian forces disarmed the clans of the north-east and destroyed the sultanates of Hobyo and the Majeerteen. Boqor Osman defied an ultimatum in October 1925, and his son Hersi Boqor led resistance that briefly drove the Italians from Hurdiya and Hafun. By 1927 both sultanates had been annexed directly, and Oltre Giuba (Jubaland) had been merged into the colony in 1926 Hess 1966. De Vecchi and his successors pushed plantation agriculture: sugar at the Villaggio Duca degli Abruzzi (Jowhar) and bananas around Genale on the Shabelle. Somali labour was recruited, often under compulsion LoC 1993.

Walwal and the conquest of Ethiopia

Because the 1908 Italo-Ethiopian line was never demarcated (m14), Italy could build a fort in 1930 at the Walwal wells in the Ogaden, inside territory Ethiopia claimed. It was held by dubat, Somali irregulars under Italian officers. An Anglo-Ethiopian boundary commission reached the area in November 1934. On 5 December 1934 fighting broke out between Ethiopian troops and the dubat. Accounts give roughly 100 or more Ethiopian dead and about 30 Somali soldiers in Italian service killed; the figures differ by source. In September 1935 a League of Nations arbitration found neither side responsible, since each believed Walwal lay in its own territory. Mussolini used the incident as a pretext. Italy invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935, with Rodolfo Graziani, governor of Somalia, leading the southern front from Mogadishu with many Somali troops. Addis Ababa fell on 5 May 1936, and Italian East Africa (Africa Orientale Italiana, AOI) was organised by a law of 1 June 1936. The Somalia governorate was enlarged to include the Ogaden Hess 1966 Lewis 2002.

Walwal is in the Ogaden, not on the British Somaliland border. The 1934 clash concerned the Italo-Ethiopian line of 1908. The Anglo-Ethiopian boundary commission was nearby only because it was surveying the British line of 1897.

War in the Horn, 1940–1941

Italy entered the Second World War on 10 June 1940. On 3 August 1940 Lt-Gen. Guglielmo Nasi's columns crossed into British Somaliland. The small British force, including the Somaliland Camel Corps, held the Tug Argan gap from 11 to 15 August under Maj.-Gen. A. R. Godwin-Austen. When Observation Hill fell, it was evacuated from Berbera, embarking by 18 August. The Italians entered Berbera on 19 August. The British official history gives about 260 British and 2,052 Italian casualties Playfair 1954. It was the only British colony Italy captured. For a few months the Italians governed the Ogaden, Italian Somalia and British Somaliland as one territory; the LoC study notes that this was the first time in forty years most Somali clans had lived under one administration LoC 1993.

The reconquest was fast. Lt-Gen. Alan Cunningham's forces from Kenya took Kismayo on 14 February 1941, crossed the Juba from 17 February, and reached Mogadishu unopposed on 25 February. On 16 March two battalions from Aden landed at Berbera (Operation Appearance), and Jigjiga (17 March) and Harar (26 March) followed Playfair 1954.

The British Military Administration, 1941–1950

Britain now held almost every Somali territory except Djibouti, with the NFD still under Kenya. Military administrations ran ex-Italian Somalia until 1 April 1950, British Somaliland until civil rule returned in 1948, and the Ogaden. Under Anglo-Ethiopian agreements of 1942 and 1944, Britain kept the Ogaden, the Haud and a 'Reserved Area' along the railway and the French Somaliland border under its control. The 1944 agreement could be ended on three months' notice Hansard 1955. In the south the BMA raised the Somalia Gendarmerie, doubled elementary schooling, and replaced Italian-appointed chiefs with clan-elected councils. In the north the capital moved from Berbera to Hargeisa LoC 1993.

Under BMA protection the Somali Youth Club was founded in Mogadishu on 15 May 1943 by thirteen young men; Britannica gives 13 May Trunji 2017. Opposition to clannishness was among its declared aims. Its leaders included Abdulkadir Sakhawuddin and Yasin Haji Osman Sharmarke. By 1946 it claimed 25,000 members, and in 1947 it became the Somali Youth League (SYL). The SYL aimed to unite all Somali territories, spread modern education, adopt a standard script for Somali and oppose the return of Italy. A rival, the Hizbia Digil Mirifle (HDM), spoke for the inter-riverine clans and at times took Italian support LoC 1993.

13 men, 1943; League in '47The Somali Youth Club had 13 founders in 1943, became the Somali Youth League in 1947, and had five ministers by 1956.

Bevin, the Four Powers and the return of the Ogaden

In 1946 the Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, proposed that British Somaliland, ex-Italian Somalia and the Ogaden be united under British trusteeship. Ethiopia would be compensated elsewhere. The United States and the Soviet Union saw imperial ambition in the plan and Ethiopia rejected it, so it was dropped Touval 1963. Under the Paris peace treaty of 10 February 1947 Italy renounced its colonies. If the Four Powers (Britain, France, the USSR and the USA) failed to agree within a year, the question would go to the UN General Assembly.

The Four Power Commission of Investigation reached Mogadishu in January 1948. On 11 January an SYL demonstration and a pro-Italian counter-demonstration led to rioting. The LoC study gives 51 Italians and 24 Somalis killed. A British Army statement at the time gave 42 Italians and 11 Somalis, so the figures differ. The commission favoured something close to the SYL's request for a ten-year international trusteeship leading to independence, but the powers could not agree. In 1948 Britain handed the Ogaden back to Ethiopia under US and Soviet pressure, against strong Somali protest LoC 1993.

The Italian trusteeship (AFIS), 1950–1960

General Assembly resolution 289 (IV) of 21 November 1949 decided that Italian Somaliland should become independent ten years after the approval of a trusteeship agreement. Italy was named Administering Authority. An Advisory Council of Colombia, Egypt and the Philippines, based in Mogadishu, would advise it, and a declaration of constitutional principles drafted from an Indian text would be annexed UNGA 1949. The Amministrazione Fiduciaria Italiana della Somalia (AFIS) took over from the BMA on 1 April 1950 under Giovanni Fornari. The Trusteeship Agreement was approved by resolution 442 (V) on 2 December 1950 UNGA 1950. Before that vote the Fourth Committee let the SYL address it, by 20 votes to 11 with 13 abstentions UN A/1550.

C-E-P watched AFISColombia, Egypt and the Philippines formed the Advisory Council in Mogadishu. The clock ran ten years from approval of the agreement on 2 December 1950, but independence came early, on 1 July 1960.

Relations were tense in 1950–53, when AFIS jailed or dismissed SYL activists. They improved with development plans from 1954 and with Somali staff replacing Italians in the administration. A 35-member Territorial Council sat from 1950. The first territory-wide elections, in 1956, chose a 70-seat Legislative Assembly, 60 of whose seats were for Somalis: the SYL won 43 and the HDM 13. Abdullahi Issa became the first prime minister, with five Somali ministers. Women voted from 1958, and the SYL dominated the 1959 elections LoC 1993. Tripodi, using the AFIS archives, argues that Rome acted mainly from economic self-interest and a wish to end a costly commitment, not from any civilising mission Tripodi 1999.

The north: the Haud and the parties

By an agreement signed in London on 29 November 1954, Britain recognised Ethiopian sovereignty over the Haud and Reserved Area under the 1897 treaty. Ethiopia agreed to respect grazing rights 'as far as possible'. The agreement took effect on 28 February 1955. MPs estimated the area at about 25,000 square miles with some 300,000 people, and said the clans had been told only on 5 January Hansard 1955. Protest gave northern politics its mass base. The National United Front (NUF), led by Michael Mariano, sent delegations to London and the UN. Britain even tried to buy the Haud back LoC 1993. The main parties were the Somali National League (SNL), mainly Isaaq, and the United Somali Party (USP), backed by Gadabursi, Issa, Dhulbahante and Warsangali voters. In the February 1960 elections to the 33-seat Legislative Council the SNL won 20 seats, the USP 12 and the NUF 1, which set up the union of 1960 (m17).

Scholarly debates

Was the trusteeship a success in preparing Somalia for independence?

The LoC study and Lewis credit AFIS and the UN Advisory Council with giving the south real experience of elections, a Somali administration and a stable SYL government by 1956–60, an advantage the north lacked. Tripodi, using AFIS archives, argues that Italy acted mainly from economic self-interest and wished to leave quickly, and that development was shallow: exports trebled from 1954 but the budget depended on subsidies, and education was hampered by the lack of a written Somali standard. The current view is that political preparation was relatively good by African standards, but economic and administrative foundations were weak, and north–south disparities were built into the 1960 union.

Was Britain's handling of the Ogaden and Haud a betrayal of Somali interests?

Somali nationalists, and critics in the 1955 Commons debate, argued that Britain broke the 1884–86 protection treaties by returning the Ogaden (1948) and recognising Ethiopian sovereignty over the Haud (1954–55). The British government replied that Ethiopian title rested on the 1897 treaty, and that the 1942–44 arrangements were temporary wartime administration. The LoC study stresses US pressure in 1948. Historians largely agree that the 1897 treaty gave Ethiopia legal title and that Bevin's alternative failed for great-power reasons. Whether Britain's obligations to the clans should have outweighed that title remains a political judgement.

How should the Mogadishu riots of January 1948 be interpreted?

Somali nationalist accounts treat the riots as the result of pro-Italian provocation against an SYL rally. Italian accounts stress the killing of Italian civilians, and some blame British laxity or connivance. Recent work on the 'pro-Italia' movement shows that substantial Somali groups backed Italy's return for economic and clan reasons. Casualty figures vary from 42 Italians and 11 Somalis in a contemporary British statement to 51 and 24 in the LoC study, and higher in Italian sources.

Module 17 · Modern

Independence and the civilian republic (1960–1969)

Two independences, one republic (June–July 1960)

The Somali Republic was born from two separate decolonisations. The British Protectorate of Somaliland became the independent State of Somaliland on 26 June 1960, with Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal of the Somali National League (SNL) as head of government. Five days later, on 1 July 1960, the Italian-administered UN Trust Territory (AFIS, see m16) became independent and the two merged as the Somali Republic. Aden Abdullah Osman (Aadan Cabdulle Cismaan) of the Somali Youth League (SYL) became provisional president, confirmed in office in 1961, and Abdirashid Ali Shermarke became prime minister Lewis 2002 LoC 1993. The 123-seat National Assembly joined 90 southern deputies to 33 northern ones LoC 1993.

The legal basis of the merger was untidy. The northern legislature passed a Union of Somaliland and Somalia Law on 27 June 1960, the southern assembly approved a different text only in principle on 30 June, and the National Assembly passed a fresh Act of Union in January 1961 with retroactive effect. Legal scholars arguing Somaliland's case stress this gap Carroll & Rajagopal 1993. Somali historians who defend the union describe much the same sequence of texts but hold that the 1961 Act settled the matter; the dispute is over the legal effect, not the dates (see the debate below).

"Five days of Somaliland"26 June 1960 (north independent) + 1 July 1960 (south independent and union). Somaliland's later claim (m19, m21) rests on those five days of separate statehood.

The problems of integration

Britain and Italy left two administrations with different laws, courts, taxes, police, currencies and official languages (English in the north, Italian in the south, Arabic in religious and some official use). In 1960 the UN set up a Consultative Commission for Integration under the Italian jurist Paolo Contini to harmonise legal systems LoC 1993. Northerners quickly felt subordinated: the capital, the presidency, the premiership and most senior posts went south, and northern civil servants were transferred to Mogadishu.

The constitutional referendum of June 1961 exposed the divide. The draft was approved overwhelmingly in the south but was supported by less than 50 percent of the northern electorate LoC 1993. The SNL urged a boycott; some accounts put the northern 'no' at about 60% of roughly 100,000 votes cast, and critics suspected that southern totals were inflated.

On 10 December 1961 a group of British-trained junior officers in Hargeisa and Burao, angered at being placed under Italian-trained southern officers, attempted a coup aimed at restoring northern independence. Northern non-commissioned officers suppressed it within hours LoC 1993. Accounts of the trial differ: one tradition holds that the British judge acquitted the officers because no valid Act of Union bound the north; another attributes the acquittal to a procedural technicality. In May 1962 Egal and another northern minister left the cabinet and formed the Somali National Congress (SNC) LoC 1993.

Trap: the December 1961 revolt was not a separatist uprising by northern clans or parties. It was a small conspiracy of junior officers (about two dozen), defeated by fellow northern soldiers. Northern discontent was real, but the SNL and SNC pursued it inside parliament.

Pan-Somalism: the five-pointed star

The flag, designed by Mohammed Awale Liban and adopted by the trust territory's council on 12 October 1954, carries a white five-pointed star for the five areas of Somali settlement: the former Italian and British territories, French Somaliland (Djibouti), the Ogaden and Kenya's Northern Frontier District (NFD). The 1961 constitution committed the republic to promote "by legal and peaceful means" the union of these territories and treated Somalis everywhere as citizens LoC 1993. Touval 1963, writing at the height of the campaign, saw Somali nationalism as rooted in shared language, religion and pastoral culture, and predicted that its irredentist claims would collide with the African consensus on colonial borders.

That collision came quickly. A British commission in 1962 found overwhelming Somali (and Oromo) support in the NFD for leaving Kenya, but Britain left the district in Kenya. Somalia broke off relations with Britain (March 1963 in most accounts; the LoC study dates it to 1962). After Kenyan independence on 12 December 1963, NFD insurgents, called shifta ("bandits") by Nairobi, fought Kenyan forces until 1967; estimated deaths run from about 4,200 to claims of over 10,000 Whittaker 2014. The full story of the NFD belongs to m22.

In the Ogaden a 1963 revolt (the Nasrallah movement) escalated into open war between Ethiopia and Somalia from February 1964, with heavy fighting at Tog Wajaale and Feerfeer. A ceasefire mediated by Sudan under OAU auspices took hold in April 1964, creating a joint commission and demilitarised zone LoC 1993; one war dataset puts deaths at 1,000–2,000 Dixon & Sarkees 2015. Ethiopia and Kenya signed a mutual defence pact in 1964, and in July 1964 the OAU's Cairo resolution bound members to respect colonial borders. Somalia refused to accept it. Western reluctance to arm Somalia pushed Mogadishu to Soviet credits from 1962; by the late 1960s some 300 Soviet advisers served in Somalia LoC 1993.

"Two points won, three lost"Of the star's five points, only two (British and Italian Somalilands) united in 1960. The 1960s were spent fighting for the other three: NFD (shifta war), Ogaden (1964 war), Djibouti (diplomacy).

Parliamentary politics, 1964–1969

In the March 1964 elections the SYL won 69 of 123 seats. President Osman passed over Shermarke and nominated Abdirizak Haji Hussein, who favoured domestic development over militant pan-Somalism; his first cabinet lost a confidence vote before a reshuffled one passed LoC 1993. In June 1967 the Assembly elected Shermarke president over Osman by secret ballot. Osman accepted the result and left office, a transfer often cited as one of independent Africa's first peaceful handovers after an electoral defeat. Shermarke named Egal prime minister, confirmed in August 1967.

Egal pursued détente without renouncing the territorial claims. At the OAU summit in Kinshasa (September 1967) Somalia and Kenya agreed to seek a settlement, and the Arusha Memorandum of Understanding, mediated by Kenneth Kaunda in October 1967, ended the states of emergency and restored relations. In September 1968 Ethiopia and Somalia agreed on air and telecommunication links, and Ethiopia lifted its border emergency LoC 1993. Critics in the army and among pan-Somali nationalists saw détente as surrender.

"Osman–Hussein = inward; Shermarke–Egal = outward, then softer"The 1967 vote was fought on pan-Somali militancy versus development, yet the winners then made peace with Kenya and Ethiopia.

The 1969 election and the end of the civilian republic

The elections of 26 March 1969 drew 64 parties, many of them single-lineage vehicles. The SYL won 73 of 123 seats; within weeks most other winners crossed the floor, raising the SYL bloc to 109, and 77 incumbents lost their seats. Losing candidates alleged fraud, the Supreme Court declined to hear petitions, and the police commander, General Mohamed Abshir, had resigned on the eve of the poll after refusing to lend police vehicles to the SYL LoC 1993. Laitin & Samatar 1987 describe this as a politics of clan patronage in which the state became a prize; Lewis 2002 applies his model of "pastoral democracy", in which lineage segments compete as equals, to explain both the open competition and the fragmentation.

On 15 October 1969, while Egal was abroad, President Shermarke was shot dead in Las Anod by a member of his police guard; the government study describes the killer as coming from a lineage the president was said to have wronged LoC 1993. On 21 October 1969, as parliament prepared to choose a successor, the army under Major General Mohamed Siad Barre seized power without serious resistance, detained Egal and other leaders, suspended the constitution and renamed the state the Somali Democratic Republic (continued in m18).

Trap: do not confuse Abdirashid Ali Shermarke (PM 1960–64, president 1967–69, assassinated) with Abdirizak Haji Hussein (PM 1964–67). And Egal is the same man who led Somaliland in 1960, was prime minister of Somalia in 1967–69, and became Somaliland's president in 1993 (m19).

Scholarly debates

Was the 1960 union legally valid?

Advocates of Somaliland's independence (e.g. Carroll and Rajagopal 1993) argue that the two legislatures passed non-identical instruments and that the January 1961 Act of Union was applied retroactively without northern ratification, a defect echoed in the 1961 coup trial and the northern 'no' in the referendum. Defenders of the union stress that both legislatures voted to unite, that northern leaders served in national government for three decades, and that state practice since 1960 created a single state. Most international actors have treated the union as valid; the legal argument matters mainly to the Somaliland recognition debate (m21).

Was the civilian republic a functioning democracy or a failed clientelist state?

One view, common in Somali memory and in comparative surveys, praises competitive elections, a free press and the peaceful 1967 handover. Laitin and Samatar (1987) and Lewis (2002) stress lineage-based parties, vote-buying and the 1969 floor-crossing that left almost no opposition, which made the coup popular. Most scholars combine the two: real pluralism, undermined by patronage and the fiscal pressures of pan-Somali militarism.

Were Shermarke's assassination and the coup linked?

The government study describes the assassin as a guard with a lineage grievance, and notes that Siad Barre was not seen as the coup's author. Ingiriis (2017) reopens the question, weighing Cold War, clan and coup-planning explanations. No archival evidence has settled whether officers planned to exploit, or had foreknowledge of, the killing; the speed of the coup after the funeral keeps the question open.

Module 18 · Modern

Siad Barre and the Supreme Revolutionary Council (1969–1991)

The coup and the Supreme Revolutionary Council

On 21 October 1969, six days after President Shermarke's assassination (m17), the army seized Mogadishu. A 25-member Supreme Revolutionary Council (SRC) of officers, chaired by Major General Mohamed Siad Barre, took the powers of president, assembly and cabinet under Law No. 1, abolished parties and suspended the constitution; the state became the Somali Democratic Republic LoC 1993. Rivals were removed early: First Vice President Jama Ali Qoorsheel was arrested in April 1970, and in May 1971 Second Vice President Mohamed Ainanshe and Lt Col Salaad Gabeyre Kediye were arrested for an alleged plot and later executed LoC 1993.

On the coup's first anniversary (21 October 1970) Siad Barre proclaimed Scientific Socialism, which he presented as combining self-reliant community development, Marxist socialism and Islam LoC 1993. The regime attacked "tribalism": paid clan headmen were replaced by state "peacekeepers", marriages were celebrated at orientation centres, collective diya payment was abolished, and a uniform civil code (1973) replaced the Italian and British codes. A cult of the Guulwaade ("Victorious Leader") grew around Siad. Laitin & Samatar 1987 read the ideology as a pragmatic nationalist programme in Marxist dress rather than a doctrinaire Marxism.

"Three pillars, one leader"Scientific Socialism = self-help (iskaa wax u qabso) + Marx + Islam, all channelled through the Guulwaade.

The developmental years, 1972–1976

On 21 October 1972 the SRC adopted a Latin script for Somali, effective 1 January 1973. Urban literacy classes followed, and in August 1974 a rural campaign sent more than 20,000 teachers, many of them secondary students, to the nomads; literacy had been estimated at about 5% in 1972 LoC 1993 (details in m04). Somalia joined the Arab League in February 1974 and signed a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with the USSR in 1974, which gave Soviet forces access to facilities at Berbera LoC Ethiopia 1991.

The Daba Dheer ("long-tailed") drought of 1974–75 devastated the northern and central rangelands. The regime airlifted nomads, with Soviet help, into agricultural settlements in the riverine south and fishing cooperatives on the coast; about 140,000 pastoralists were resettled LoC 1993. In January 1975 a new family law gave women equal inheritance rights, and ten religious scholars who preached against it were executed. In July 1976 the SRC dissolved itself into the Somali Revolutionary Socialist Party (SRSP), but a five-man politburo of former SRC officers kept real power LoC 1993. By 1975, ten of the twenty SRC members were Darod, and the Digil and Rahanweyn had none.

The Ogaden War, 1977–1978

Mogadishu exploited Ethiopia's revolutionary turmoil. The Western Somali Liberation Front (WSLF), rebuilt with Somali officers, attacked across the Ogaden from early 1977, and the Somali National Army (SNA) invaded in July 1977 (13 and 23 July are both given). Tareke 2000, using Ethiopian military archives, shows that Ethiopia had more men (about 47,000 to 35,000) but Somalia had nearly three times as many tanks. Somali forces were repulsed at Dire Dawa in August, but took Jijiga on 12 September 1977 after a mutiny in its garrison, and then the Marda (Karamara) Pass. The offensive stalled before Harar, besieged from October 1977 to January 1978.

The Soviet Union, now courting Mengistu's Derg, withdrew its advisers from Somalia. On 13 November 1977 Somalia annulled the 1974 treaty, expelled the remaining Soviet personnel and broke with Cuba. From late November a Soviet air and sea lift poured arms into Ethiopia, followed by Cuban combat troops and some 1,000–1,500 Soviet advisers. Counts of the Cubans differ: about 15,000 in the LoC Somalia study, about 17,000 in the LoC Ethiopia study and about 18,000 at the peak in Tareke LoC 1993 LoC Ethiopia 1991 Tareke 2000. The counteroffensive of February–March 1978 outflanked the Marda Pass; Ethiopian and Cuban forces retook Jijiga on 5 March 1978, Siad Barre announced withdrawal on 9 March, and Addis Ababa declared the war over on 23 March. Ethiopian records give 6,133 Ethiopian and 6,453 Somali dead Tareke 2000. Tareke argues that Ethiopian tenacity created the stalemate but Cuban–Soviet intervention decided it.

Trap: the formal rupture was Mogadishu's act: on 13 November 1977 Somalia annulled the treaty and expelled Soviet personnel, after Moscow had begun to back Ethiopia. And the WSLF was a front organised by Mogadishu, not an independent Ethiopian Somali party (compare the later ONLF in m22).

Aftermath: refugees, coup and realignment

Nearly half a million people fled the Ogaden Tareke 2000, and refugee aid became a pillar of the economy; by 1989 the government claimed 837,000 refugees in camps, about double outside estimates US State Dept 1989. In April 1978 officers led by Colonel Mohamed Sheikh Osman, a Majeerteen, attempted a coup. The plotters executed afterwards number 17 in one account and about a dozen in another; Lt Col Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed escaped to Ethiopia and founded what became the Somali Salvation Democratic Front (SSDF) in October 1981 LoC 1993. Collective punishment followed in Mudug: the Red Berets destroyed water reservoirs around Galkayo, and the government study reports over 2,000 deaths from thirst in May–June 1979 (a single source).

The West filled the gap. A 1980 access agreement gave the United States use of Somali ports and airfields in a crisis, in return for arms and training; the US replaced the USSR as the main user of Berbera, though Congress cut aid deeply by 1987 over human rights LoC 1993. A 1979 constitution created a People's Assembly, but in October 1980 a state of emergency revived the SRC. Power narrowed to the "MOD" coalition (Siad's Marehan, his mother's Ogaden and his son-in-law's Dhulbahante) and to the Red Berets (Duub Cas) and the National Security Service Laitin & Samatar 1987.

"MOD"Marehan (Siad's lineage), Ogaden (his mother's), Dhulbahante (his son-in-law Abdullahi's): the narrowing base that critics said had replaced the nation.

War against the north (1981–1989)

The Somali National Movement (SNM) was founded in London on 6 April 1981 by Isaaq exiles and from 1982 operated from Ethiopia LoC 1993. After Siad Barre's car crash of 23 May 1986, succession rivalries sharpened. On 3 April 1988 Somalia and Ethiopia agreed to stop backing each other's rebels. Facing loss of its bases, the SNM struck first: it captured Burao on 27 May and much of Hargeisa on 31 May 1988. The army answered with artillery and aerial bombardment of both cities, then with killings of civilians, destruction of wells and the mining of farmland. Some 90% of Isaaq property in Hargeisa was destroyed or badly damaged, and over 300,000 people fled to Ethiopia US State Dept 1989 LoC 1993.

Death estimates differ in method and period. The US State Department's Gersony report (August 1989), based on about 300 refugee interviews, concluded that the army killed at least 5,000 unarmed civilians between May 1988 and March 1989, and that the SNM also killed hundreds of civilians and refugees Gersony 1989. Africa Watch's January 1990 report, A Government at War with Its Own People, documented systematic killing, and the estimate attributed to it is 50,000–60,000 deaths from May 1988 to early 1990 Africa Watch 1990. Somaliland sources and some genocide scholars give figures up to 100,000–200,000.

The "genocide" label is contested. It is used by the Somaliland government, by historian Mohamed Haji Ingiriis, who calls it a "forgotten genocide" Ingiriis 2016, and by a preliminary study commissioned by the UN in 2001, whose author, Chris Mburu, concluded that genocide was "conceived, planned and perpetrated" against the Isaaq Mburu 2002. The Library of Congress study calls the policies "genocidal". No international court has ruled on the question, the UN has not formally adopted the Mburu finding, and Africa Watch and Gersony documented the killings without making a legal genocide determination. Many general histories use "massacres" or "state terror".

Trap: "5,000" and "50,000–60,000" are not contradictory counts of the same thing. Gersony counted documented army killings of unarmed civilians over ten months; the Africa Watch figure is a total estimate over about twenty months.

The regime unravels, 1989–1991

The Hawiye-based United Somali Congress (USC) was founded in Rome in January 1989; Ogaden officers formed the Somali Patriotic Movement (SPM) in 1989 (the LoC study traces it to 1985). In Mogadishu, Bishop Salvatore Colombo was shot dead on 9 July 1989. After the arrest of leading sheikhs, Friday-prayer protests on 14 July were met with gunfire: Africa Watch estimated about 400–450 dead, the government admitted 23. Days later 46 or 47 men, mostly Isaaq, were executed at Jasiira beach US State Dept 1989 LoC 1993. The US ended military aid in 1989. In May 1990, 114 notables signed the Manifesto demanding reform; on 6 July 1990 the presidential guard killed at least 65 people at the stadium. The USC entered Mogadishu at the end of December 1990, and Siad Barre fled the capital on 26 January 1991 (m19).

"Majeerteen 1978, Isaaq 1988, Hawiye 1989"The order in which the regime turned on clan-based opposition, and the order of the SSDF, SNM and USC.

Scholarly debates

Should the 1988–89 killings of Isaaq civilians be called genocide?

Ingiriis (2016), the UN-commissioned Mburu study (2001) and the Somaliland government call it genocide, citing intent to destroy the Isaaq as a group: bombardment of cities, killings of civilians identified by clan and destruction of water and farmland. The LoC country study calls the policies 'genocidal'. Africa Watch (1990) and Gersony (1989) documented systematic, clan-targeted killing but made no legal finding, and no court has tested the specific intent required by the 1948 Convention. Other writers prefer 'massacre' or 'counter-insurgency atrocity'. The evidence for mass, clan-targeted state violence is strong; the legal classification remains unadjudicated.

Was Scientific Socialism genuine Marxism or pragmatic nationalism?

The regime's rhetoric, Soviet alliance and nationalisations suggest Marxist commitment. Laitin and Samatar (1987) and Lewis (2002) see a pragmatic, nationalist and personalist project: the Islamic pillar, the 1977 break with Moscow and the swift turn to the US suggest ideology served state-building and regime survival. Most scholars now favour the pragmatic reading.

How decisive was the Ogaden defeat in the collapse of the Somali state?

Tareke (2000) calls the defeat possibly the catalyst of the state's decomposition: it produced the 1978 coup attempt, clan-based rebellions and refugee dependence. Others place more weight on Siad Barre's clan-based rule and the drying-up of Cold War aid after 1987–89. The positions are compatible: most accounts treat 1978 as the turning point and the late-1980s loss of external patronage as the final blow.

Module 19 · Modern

Collapse and civil war (1991–2000)

The victors divide (1991)

When Siad Barre fled Mogadishu on 26 January 1991 (m18), he left for his home region of Gedo; the state did not survive him. Within days the Manifesto group and its USC allies named Ali Mahdi Mohamed, an Abgaal businessman, interim president, without consulting the SNM, SPM or SSDF LoC 1993. The USC's military chairman, General Mohamed Farrah Aidid of the Habar Gidir, rejected the appointment. Two conferences in Djibouti in June and July 1991 endorsed Ali Mahdi, but the endorsement had no force on the ground Lewis 2002. In the first months after the fall, USC fighters and armed civilians killed and expelled many Darod civilians from Mogadishu; Kapteijns 2013 calls this "clan cleansing" and argues it was organised political violence, not spontaneous revenge.

On 17 November 1991 Aidid's forces (about 10,000 fighters) attacked Ali Mahdi's (about 5,000) and split the city along a "green line": Aidid held the south, the port and the airport; Ali Mahdi held the north LoC 1993. Africa Watch and Physicians for Human Rights estimated 14,000 killed and 27,000 wounded in Mogadishu between 17 November 1991 and 29 February 1992 Africa Watch & PHR 1992. After UN-convened talks in New York (12–14 February), the two leaders signed a ceasefire in Mogadishu on 3 March 1992 UN UNOSOM I. Barre's Somali National Front advanced on Mogadishu in April 1992, was beaten back, and Barre went into exile; he died in Lagos on 2 January 1995.

The 1992 famine

The famine struck hardest in the inter-riverine farming zone (Bay, Bakool, Gedo, Lower Shabelle), home to Rahanweyn and Somali Bantu farmers who had few militias of their own and whose land was crossed repeatedly by Aidid's and Barre's forces. Baidoa, where thousands of displaced people died, was called the "city of death" in press reports. By late 1992 the UN reckoned that 4.5 million people were threatened, 1.5 million were at immediate risk, almost a million had fled abroad and "perhaps 300,000" had died since November 1991 UN UNOSOM I. Scholarly estimates of famine deaths range from about 200,000 to 300,000. The figures were themselves political: MSF objected that its survey of displaced people in Merca was extrapolated by UN officials to the whole country, and that exaggerated claims of aid looting helped justify military intervention MSF Speaking Out.

Trap: the famine was not caused by drought alone. Drought mattered, but war, looting of grain and livestock, and the targeting of unarmed farming communities turned scarcity into mass death.

From UNOSOM I to UNITAF

Security Council resolution 733 (23 January 1992) imposed an arms embargo. Resolution 751 (24 April 1992) created the UN Operation in Somalia (UNOSOM, later "UNOSOM I") with 50 ceasefire observers and an agreed 500-strong security unit; the Pakistani battalion arrived only on 14 September. Resolution 775 (28 August) raised the authorised strength to 3,500 plus logistics units. The Algerian diplomat Mohamed Sahnoun, appointed Special Representative in April, favoured patient work with elders and clan leaders; he resigned in October 1992 after publicly criticising UN agencies and was replaced by Ismat Kittani UN UNOSOM I.

After US Acting Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger offered to lead a force, resolution 794 (3 December 1992) authorised, under Chapter VII, "all necessary means" to secure relief. The US-led Unified Task Force (UNITAF), Operation Restore Hope, landed on 9 December 1992. It grew to about 37,000 troops (UN figure; US Army historians give 38,000 from 23 nations), covering about 40% of the country in the south and centre, and avoided forcible disarmament UN UNOSOM I CMH 2002. In Addis Ababa, 15 Somali movements signed an agreement on 27 March 1993 for disarmament and a Transitional National Council.

UNOSOM II and the Battle of Mogadishu

Resolution 814 (26 March 1993) gave UNOSOM II, under Turkish General Çevik Bir and Special Representative Admiral Jonathan Howe, an unprecedented Chapter VII mandate covering disarmament and rebuilding the state; it took over on 4 May 1993 UN UNOSOM II. On 5 June 1993, after an inspection of weapons sites near Aidid's Radio Mogadishu, militia attacks killed Pakistani peacekeepers: 24 according to US Army historians, 25 in the UN account CMH 2002 UN UNOSOM II. Resolution 837 (6 June) authorised the arrest of those responsible. Howe issued a warrant for Aidid with a $25,000 reward on 17 June. On 12 July a US helicopter attack on a meeting at a house of Aidid's supporters killed many Somalis (figures are disputed), and a crowd then killed four foreign journalists.

On 3–4 October 1993 US Task Force Ranger, which was not under UN command, raided a building in central Mogadishu and captured 24 suspects, but militia shot down two Black Hawk helicopters. In the night-long battle and rescue, 18 American soldiers were killed (UN: 75 wounded); Malaysian and Pakistani armour reached the trapped troops, and one or two Malaysians were killed (sources differ) UN UNOSOM II CMH 2002. Somali casualties are uncertain: the SNA figure reported at the time was 312 killed and 814 wounded; US Army historians cite estimates of 500 to 1,500 casualties; Bowden 1999, a journalist's reconstruction, puts Somali dead at about 500 and wounded at over 1,000. President Clinton announced withdrawal by 31 March 1994; US forces left by 25 March. Resolution 897 (4 February 1994) dropped coercive disarmament, and the last UNOSOM II troops left under the cover of Operation United Shield on 2–3 March 1995.

"18 and 24"18 US dead on 3–4 Oct 1993 changed Washington's policy; the 24 (or 25) Pakistani dead of 5 June 1993 had already turned the UN against Aidid.
Trap: Task Force Ranger and the US Quick Reaction Force operated under US, not UN, command. The UN noted this itself, though the raids served UNOSOM II's resolution 837 mandate.

Somaliland: peace from below

In the north the SNM took Hargeisa, Burao and Berbera by the end of January 1991. After a clan-reconciliation meeting in Berbera in February, the Grand Conference of the Northern Clans at Burao (April–May 1991) resolved to revoke the 1960 union; Somaliland's independence was proclaimed on 18 May 1991 (the LoC study gives 17 May for the SNM announcement), with SNM chairman Abdirahman Ahmed Ali "Tuur" as president LoC 1993 Bradbury 2008. The Borama conference (January–May 1993), a meeting of elders from all northern clans, adopted a National Charter, created a bicameral legislature including an upper house of elders (Guurti) and elected Egal president. Bradbury 2008 argues that this sequence of locally financed, elder-led conferences, rather than external state-building, produced Somaliland's relative peace, despite renewed fighting in 1994–96 and Egal's re-election at the 1996–97 Hargeisa conference. No state recognised Somaliland (m21).

"Burao declares, Borama builds"Burao (1991) proclaimed independence under Tuur; Borama (1993) built the institutions and chose Egal.

The south, Puntland and Arta (1995–2000)

Aidid declared himself president in June 1995 (unrecognised) and took Baidoa in September 1995, provoking the Rahanweyn Resistance Army. He was wounded in July 1996 and died on 1 August 1996 (his militia announced the death the next day); his son Hussein Aidid succeeded him. Mediation multiplied: Ethiopia's conference at Sodere (1996–97) created a National Salvation Council, boycotted by Hussein Aidid, and Egypt's Cairo talks (1997) produced a declaration with Ali Mahdi and Hussein Aidid that was never implemented Menkhaus 2004. In the northeast, a conference at Garowe established Puntland on 1 August 1998 as an autonomous state of the Harti clans, under former SSDF leader Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed; unlike Somaliland it did not seek independence. Menkhaus 2007 describes this landscape as "governance without government": municipal administrations, business-funded security, sharia courts in Mogadishu from 1994 and customary law filled the vacuum.

Djibouti's President Ismail Omar Guelleh then convened the Arta conference (2000), which seated clan elders and civil society delegates rather than faction leaders and selected a Transitional National Assembly by the "4.5" clan formula (m12); sources differ on its size, giving 225 or 245 seats. On 26 August 2000 the assembly elected Abdiqasim Salad Hassan president of the Transitional National Government. Somaliland, Puntland and most faction leaders rejected it, and it never controlled more than parts of Mogadishu (continued in m20).

Scholarly debates

Did the 1992–95 intervention succeed?

The UN credits the effort with saving at least a quarter of a million lives and some institution-building (district councils, police). Critics from MSF and African Rights argue the worst famine mortality had passed by December 1992, that mortality and looting data were inflated to justify intervention, and that UNOSOM II's coercive turn against Aidid made it a party to the war. US accounts (CMH) blame mission expansion under UN direction; UN accounts note that Task Force Ranger was under US command. Most scholars judge UNITAF's humanitarian phase a qualified success and UNOSOM II's state-building a failure.

Why did the Somali state collapse rather than pass to a successor regime?

Lewis (2002) emphasises segmentary clan dynamics resurfacing once the centre fell. Kapteijns (2013) rejects a natural 'clan' explanation and points to political leaders who mobilised clan identity and organised 'clan cleansing' in 1991. Menkhaus (2004, 2007) stresses a war economy and the interests of actors who gained from statelessness, so that each state-building attempt threatened them. These views overlap; current scholarship treats clan as mobilised by elites and economies rather than as an automatic cause.

Was Somaliland's 1991 declaration a secession or the dissolution of a voluntary union?

Somaliland argues it resumed the sovereignty it held on 26 June 1960 and that the union was never legally completed (m17). Somalia's governments and the AU's general practice treat it as secession from a recognised state. Bradbury (2008) documents broad but not universal northern support: many Dhulbahante and Warsangali in Sool and Sanaag looked to Puntland, a fault line that persists (m21).

Module 20 · Contemporary

Transition, Islamists and the federal state (2000–present)

From Arta to Mbagathi (2000–2004)

The Transitional National Government created at Arta in 2000 (see m19) never controlled Mogadishu. A second IGAD-sponsored conference opened at Eldoret, Kenya, in October 2002 and moved to Mbagathi outside Nairobi. It produced the Transitional Federal Charter (2004), a 275-seat Transitional Federal Parliament allocated by the clan-based 4.5 formula (see m12), and on 10 October 2004 the election of the Puntland founder Colonel Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed as president of the Transitional Federal Government (TFG), with 189 votes. The TFG first sat in Nairobi, then Jowhar and Baidoa, because Mogadishu's factions rejected it. Ken Menkhaus called the Somalia of these years a case of governance without government: local orders built by business people, clan elders and sharia courts, with external state-building often producing "spoilers" who profited from continued collapse Menkhaus 2007.

The Islamic Courts Union and the Ethiopian intervention (2006–2009)

Clan-based sharia courts had appeared in Mogadishu from the 1990s to restore order and protect commerce. In 2006 they united as the Islamic Courts Union (ICU), with Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed heading its executive and Hassan Dahir Aweys its consultative council. A coalition of warlords calling itself the Alliance for the Restoration of Peace and Counter-Terrorism, widely reported to be US-funded, was defeated, and in early June 2006 the ICU took Mogadishu. For six months the capital was more secure than at any time since 1991, but hard-liners in the ICU's youth militia, al-Shabaab ("the youth"), talked of jihad against Ethiopia. On 24 December 2006 Ethiopia openly entered the war; Ethiopian and TFG forces took Mogadishu on 28 December Menkhaus 2007.

The occupation turned al-Shabaab from a minor wing into the core of a nationalist-religious insurgency Hansen 2013. The AU Peace and Security Council authorised the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) on 19 January 2007, endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 1744 (20 February 2007); Ugandan troops arrived in March 2007, later joined by Burundi, Kenya, Ethiopia, Djibouti and Sierra Leone. The Djibouti process (2008) split the Islamist opposition: Sheikh Sharif's wing joined an enlarged 550-seat parliament, which elected him TFG president on 31 January 2009 as Ethiopian troops withdrew.

Al-Shabaab is not "the ICU under a new name". The ICU was a coalition of courts, businessmen and clerics; al-Shabaab was one militant wing. Sheikh Sharif, the ICU's best-known leader, became the TFG president who fought al-Shabaab after 2009.

Al-Shabaab: leaders, ideology, methods

Harakat al-Shabaab al-Mujahideen drew on veterans of al-Itihaad al-Islaami and of Afghanistan (see m13). Its first military leader, Aden Hashi Ayro, was killed by a US strike in Dhusamareb on 1 May 2008. The US designated the group a foreign terrorist organisation in March 2008. Under the emir Ahmed Abdi Godane ("Abu Zubayr"), al-Shabaab announced its merger with al-Qaeda in February 2012 and in 2013 purged rivals: Ibrahim al-Afghani was killed and the American recruit Omar Hammami was hunted down. Godane was killed by a US airstrike on 1 September 2014; on 6 September the group named Ahmad Umar "Abu Ubaidah", also known as Ahmed Diriye, as emir, and he was still described as leader as of November 2026.

Stig Jarle Hansen argues the movement is a hybrid: a transnational jihadist ideology fitted to local clan politics, with a disciplined bureaucracy that offers courts, taxation and predictable punishment where the state offers little Hansen 2013. Its intelligence wing, the Amniyat, runs assassinations and infiltration. The UN Panel of Experts reported that its income in 2023 exceeded US$150 million, mostly from coercive taxation of goods, livestock, farms and road traffic at checkpoints PoE 2024. Major attacks include the Kampala bombings (July 2010), Westgate Mall in Nairobi (September 2013, 67 killed), Garissa University College (April 2015, 148 killed) and the twin truck bombs at Zoobe junction, Mogadishu, on 14 October 2017. A government committee raised the Zoobe death toll to 587 in March 2018, making it the deadliest attack in Somali history. Al-Shabaab did not claim it, although investigators and the government blamed it.

AMISOM → ATMIS → AUSSOM2007 Mission, 2022 Transition (1 April 2022, Res. 2628), 2025 Support and Stabilisation (1 January 2025, Res. 2767). Each renaming promised a smaller, more Somali-led role.

Famine, withdrawal from Mogadishu, piracy (2008–2012)

On 20 July 2011 the UN declared famine in Bakool and Lower Shabelle, later in other southern areas. Drought, high food prices and al-Shabaab's ban on most aid agencies combined. A study commissioned by FSNAU and FEWS NET estimated about 258,000 excess deaths between October 2010 and April 2012, including about 133,000 children under five, roughly 4.6% of the south-central population Checchi & Robinson 2013. On 6 August 2011 al-Shabaab withdrew most of its forces from Mogadishu under AMISOM pressure. Kenya invaded in October 2011 (Operation Linda Nchi), and Kenyan troops with the Ras Kamboni militia took Kismayo in late September 2012.

Piracy grew from about 2005 out of Puntland and central-coast fishing towns (Eyl, Hobyo, Harardhere). Pirates claimed to be defending fisheries against illegal foreign trawling and dumping; investigators found investor-financed criminal syndicates. The tanker Sirius Star was seized in November 2008, and the EU's Operation Atalanta began in December 2008. The International Maritime Bureau counted 237 Somali-attributed attacks in 2011 but only 28 hijackings, down from 49 in 2010, a fall it credited to naval pre-emption and armed guards on ships IMB 2012. Successful hijackings largely ended after 2012; brief resurgences came in 2017 and in 2023–24.

The Federal Government of Somalia (2012–2022)

The transition ended in 2012. A National Constituent Assembly adopted the Provisional Constitution on 1 August 2012, a federal text still labelled provisional in 2026. Elders chose a new 275-member House of the People, which on 10 September 2012 elected the academic and civil-society figure Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. Elections remained indirect: in 2016–17, 14,025 clan delegates (51 per seat) elected MPs, who chose Mohamed Abdullahi "Farmaajo" on 8 February 2017; in 2021–22 there were 101 delegates per seat. Farmaajo's mandate expired on 8 February 2021; a two-year extension voted in April 2021 triggered armed clashes in Mogadishu on 25 April and was reversed. On 15 May 2022 MPs re-elected Hassan Sheikh by 214 votes to Farmaajo's 110.

Hassan Sheikh's second term: war, debt relief, integration (2022–2025)

After the Hayat Hotel siege (August 2022) Hassan Sheikh declared "total war". Clan militias (ma'awisley) rose in Hiiraan and Middle Shabelle, and the army retook towns such as Adan Yabaal (December 2022). Crisis Group warned that holding territory and delivering governance would decide whether the gains lasted Crisis Group 2023. They did not all last: from February 2025 al-Shabaab retook areas, including Adan Yabaal on 16 April 2025 and Moqokori in Hiiraan on 7 July 2025. Diplomatic gains were firmer. The IMF and World Bank declared Somalia's HIPC completion point on 13 December 2023, worth about US$4.5 billion; external debt fell from 64% of GDP in 2018 to under 6% by the end of 2023 IMF 2023. Resolution 2714 (1 December 2023) lifted the arms embargo on the federal government. Somalia was admitted to the East African Community on 24 November 2023 and became its eighth member on 4 March 2024. AUSSOM replaced ATMIS on 1 January 2025 under Resolution 2767, adopted on 27 December 2024 with the United States abstaining over funding UNSC 2024.

"Four-Five-Three" of March 2024The 2024 amendments to chapters 1–4: terms of five years instead of four, a cap of three national parties, and a planned move to one-person-one-vote elections.

The constitutional crisis (2024–2026)

On 30 March 2024 parliament amended the first four chapters of the constitution. The amendments strengthened the presidency against the prime minister, introduced direct elections and capped national parties at three. Puntland withdrew recognition of the federal government the next day. Jubaland broke with Mogadishu after Ahmed Madobe's re-election in November 2024 (see m21). In May 2025 Hassan Sheikh launched the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP). Mogadishu held its first one-person-one-vote local election since 1969 on 25 December 2025: JSP won 177 of 390 council seats, and the opposition boycotted. On 4 March 2026, 222 of 329 MPs and senators approved further amendments by acclamation, extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years Reuters 2026. The opposition, including former presidents, said parliament's mandate ended on 14 April 2026 and the president's on 15 May 2026. Federal troops took Baidoa on 30 March 2026, forcing South West's president to resign. Fighting in Mogadishu on 3–4 June 2026 killed at least 13 people, according to a UN protection-cluster count (no official toll was issued). The electoral commission set parliamentary polls for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote for 15 May 2027. On 5 November 2026 the Supreme Court's Constitutional Division, ruling on a petition by Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, held that the extension could not apply to sitting office-holders. It ordered agreement on an electoral framework within 30 days and elections within 90 days. The Attorney General rejected the ruling, and the president's attempt to replace the chief justice was disputed Geeska 2026. The UN political mission (UNTMIS) closed on 31 October 2026, and Uganda began withdrawing troops on 2 November 2026. The outcome was unresolved as of November 2026.

Three Mogadishu dates to keep apart1 Aug 2012: Provisional Constitution adopted (still provisional). 25 Dec 2025: first direct local vote in the capital since 1969. 5 Nov 2026: Supreme Court rules the term extension cannot apply to sitting office-holders.
Two different "extensions". April 2021 (Farmaajo, two years, reversed after clashes) is not March 2026 (Hassan Sheikh, four to five years by constitutional amendment, ruled inapplicable to his term on 5 November 2026).

Scholarly debates

Did the 2006 Ethiopian intervention create al-Shabaab's insurgency, or only accelerate it?

Menkhaus and Hansen both stress that the occupation transformed al-Shabaab from a small ICU wing into a mass insurgency, drawing on nationalist resentment. Others, including US officials at the time, argued that the ICU's hard-liners were already planning jihad against Ethiopia and that intervention pre-empted a regional war. The evidence of rapid recruitment in 2007–08 supports the view that intervention accelerated the movement, though its jihadist core predated 2006.

Should the Somali government negotiate with al-Shabaab?

Crisis Group (2022) argued that a purely military strategy had failed for fifteen years and that the government should test political engagement, while noting that al-Shabaab draws confidence from the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan. The Hassan Sheikh government chose 'total war' from 2022 and treats al-Shabaab as non-negotiable, while accepting individual defectors such as Mukhtar Robow. Critics of talks note the group's rejection of the state and its al-Qaeda allegiance. The 2025 reversals revived the debate; as of November 2026 no talks were public.

Was the 2024–26 move to direct elections a democratic reform or a means of extending power?

Supporters, including the president, present the end of the clan-based indirect system as long overdue and cite the 25 December 2025 Mogadishu vote. Opponents, including former presidents, Puntland and Jubaland, argue that changing the constitution without consensus and extending terms by a year concentrated power. The Supreme Court ruling of 5 November 2026 sided with critics on the term extension, but the reform debate was unresolved as of November 2026.

Module 21 · Contemporary

Somaliland, Puntland and the federal member states

Somaliland: building a state from clan conferences (1991–1997)

The Somali National Movement and northern clan elders declared the restoration of Somaliland's independence at the Grand Conference of Burao on 18 May 1991, inside the borders of the British protectorate that became independent on 26 June 1960 (see m17, m19). The first president, Abdirahman Ahmed Ali "Tuur", governed weakly amid fighting between SNM factions. Mark Bradbury describes the decisive step as peace-building from below: a series of inter-clan conferences, culminating at Borama in 1993, where some 150 voting delegates elected Mohamed Haji Ibrahim Egal president. Borama adopted a National Charter and a beel (clan-based) system of government, with a House of Elders, the Guurti, alongside an appointed House of Representatives Bradbury 2008. Renewed fighting around Hargeisa and Burao in 1994–96 ended with the Hargeisa conference of 1996–97, which re-elected Egal.

Michael Walls argues that Somaliland's distinctive achievement was a hybrid political order: customary clan authority was folded into, rather than replaced by, constitutional institutions, so that elders could underwrite the risks of multiparty competition Walls 2014.

Constitution and elections (2001–2024)

A constitution approved by a referendum on 31 May 2001 (about 97% "yes", with low participation in the eastern Sool and Sanaag regions) confirmed independence and introduced multiparty politics. To avoid clan parties, Article 9 limits national parties to three, chosen in periodic open "association" contests (2002, 2012, 2024). Egal died on 3 May 2002 and was succeeded by his vice-president, Dahir Riyale Kahin. Riyale won the April 2003 presidential vote by just 80 votes (205,595 to 205,515 for Ahmed Silanyo), and the loser accepted a court ruling Bradbury 2008. Elections were repeatedly delayed, but power changed hands peacefully three times: Silanyo (Kulmiye) won in June 2010; Muse Bihi Abdi (Kulmiye) won in November 2017 with about 55%; and on 13 November 2024 the opposition leader Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi "Irro" (Waddani) won 63.92% to Bihi's 34.81%. Irro was inaugurated on 12 December 2024 VOA 2024. The parliamentary and local elections of 31 May 2021, the first parliamentary vote since 2005, gave Waddani 31 seats, Kulmiye 30 and UCID 21 of 82 Crisis Group 2021. Weaknesses remain: the Guurti has never been elected, and on 1 October 2022 it extended Bihi's term by two years after the election commission had proposed a nine-month delay.

The recognition question

Hargeisa's position: Somaliland was a separate British protectorate, independent for five days in 1960 and recognised then by about 35 states; the 1960 Act of Union was never properly ratified in both territories; the union was voluntary and was broken by the Barre regime's violence against the north (see m18); Somaliland's borders are the colonial borders the AU principle protects; and three decades of relative peace and elections justify recognition. Supporters cite an AU fact-finding mission (30 April–4 May 2005, led by Patrick Mazimhaka), which called the case "unique and self-justified" and urged a special approach. The AU never acted on that report Walls 2014.

Mogadishu's position: the Federal Government regards Somaliland as an integral part of Somalia under the Provisional Constitution. It cites the 1960 union as a sovereign act of Somali unification, the AU and UN commitment to Somalia's territorial integrity, and the absence of consent from communities in Sool, Sanaag and Awdal. It also warns that unilateral secession would encourage fragmentation across Africa. The AU, the Arab League and most states share that position. Talks between the two governments, including rounds in Turkey (2013–15) and in Djibouti (2020), produced no settlement.

The question became sharper after 2016. DP World won a 30-year concession for Berbera port in 2016, with a pledged US$442 million investment. Ethiopia agreed to take a 19% stake in 2018, but Somaliland announced in 2022 that Ethiopia had failed to complete it. On 1 January 2024 Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed and Muse Bihi signed a memorandum of understanding. Its text was not published, but it reportedly gave Ethiopia 20 km of coast for a naval base and port on a 50-year lease in return for an "in-depth assessment" of recognition African Business 2024. Somalia expelled Ethiopia's ambassador in April 2024 and drew closer to Egypt and Turkey. The Turkish-mediated Ankara Declaration of 11 December 2024 committed Ethiopia and Somalia to commercial sea access "under the sovereign authority" of Somalia. It did not mention the MoU, which Hargeisa said remained valid. On 26 December 2025 Israel became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Somalia called it a deliberate attack on its sovereignty, the AU Commission rejected it, and the US president said the US would not follow. Israel's first ambassador presented credentials in Hargeisa around 1 November 2026 Al Jazeera 2026.

"Recognised" vs "engaged". Ethiopia, the UAE, Taiwan (offices exchanged in 2020) and the UK deal with Hargeisa directly, but as of November 2026 Israel is the only UN member to recognise Somaliland.

Las Anod and the eastern borderlands

Sool, Sanaag and Cayn (SSC) are mainly inhabited by the Dhulbahante and Warsangali, Harti Darod lineages linked by kinship to Puntland. Somaliland claims them by the colonial boundary; Puntland claimed them by kinship. Markus Hoehne shows how these borderlands became militarised, with rival administrations from the Khatumo movement (2012) onward Hoehne 2015. After the killing of a local politician in Las Anod on 26 December 2022 and protests, Dhulbahante elders on 6 February 2023 declared the area part of Somalia, not Somaliland. Fighting followed; estimates of the dead run to several hundred, and roughly 150,000–200,000 people were displaced. On 25 August 2023 SSC-Khatumo forces overran Somaliland's Goojacade base, and Somaliland withdrew from Las Anod. Mogadishu recognised SSC-Khatumo as an interim administration in October 2023 and as the federal member state North Eastern State in July 2025. Its parliament elected Abdikadir Ahmed Aw-Ali "Firdhiye" president on 30 August 2025, and Hassan Sheikh attended his inauguration in Las Anod in January 2026. Somaliland rejects the new state. Contests continue around Erigavo in Sanaag, where Somaliland said it had repelled an SSC-Khatumo attack and kept control of the town in December 2024.

Puntland

Puntland was declared at a Garowe conference on 1 August 1998 by Harti clans, with Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed as president. Unlike Somaliland it does not seek independence; it presents itself as a building block of a federal Somalia Crisis Group 2009. Its history includes the 2001–03 dispute between Abdullahi Yusuf and Jama Ali Jama and the piracy economy of its coast (see m20). Presidents since 2005 are Mohamud Muse Hersi "Adde", Abdirahman Farole, Abdiweli Gaas and Said Abdullahi Deni. On 8 January 2024 Deni became the first Puntland president to be re-elected, winning 45 of 66 votes in parliament. Puntland withdrew recognition of the federal government on 31 March 2024 over the constitutional amendments. From late 2024 it fought Islamic State fighters in the Cal Miskaad mountains of Bari, largely without federal help, and Deni claimed in April 2026 that IS-Somalia's capabilities had been destroyed. On 26 October 2026 Puntland rejected the federal plan for 2027 elections Dawan 2026.

Puntland = "Somali, not separate"Somaliland claims statehood on the colonial border; Puntland claims autonomy within Somalia on kinship lines. The two collide in Sool and Sanaag.

Jubaland's president Ahmed Mohamed Islaam "Madobe", a former Ras Kamboni commander, has led the state since May 2013, elected by about 500 delegates at Kismayo on 15 May 2013 and accepted by Mogadishu in an Addis Ababa agreement on 28 August 2013 Reuters 2013. After he amended the state constitution and won a third term on 25 November 2024, a Mogadishu court issued a warrant for his arrest. A failed federal operation near Ras Kamboni followed in December 2024. In December 2025 Jubaland dropped "Federal Member State" from its constitution's name for itself Geeska 2025. In South West, federal forces took Baidoa on 30 March 2026 after President Abdiaziz Laftagareen was re-elected against Mogadishu's wishes; he resigned and named Ahmed Mohamed Hussein acting president. The capital region, Banadir (Mogadishu), has an unresolved status: Article 9 of the Provisional Constitution leaves it to future negotiation, so it has no seats in the Upper House, and its governor doubles as the appointed mayor.

Order of birth: P-J-S-G-H-NPuntland 1998, Jubaland 2013, South West 2014, Galmudug 2015, Hirshabelle 2016, North Eastern 2025.
Somaliland is not a federal member state. Mogadishu counts it as part of Somalia, but it has never joined the federal system; its seats in the federal parliament are filled by northern politicians living in Mogadishu.

Scholarly debates

Is Somaliland's claim to independence a case of decolonisation or secession?

Hargeisa and scholars sympathetic to its case (e.g. Bradbury, Walls) note it was a separate colony, briefly independent in 1960, so its claim fits the AU principle of colonial borders and is not secession. Mogadishu, the AU and most states treat the 1960 union as creating a single state and regard the claim as secession. The 2005 AU mission called the case 'unique', but the AU's position has not changed. Israel's 2025 recognition did not shift the wider consensus as of November 2026.

Did Somaliland's stability come from clan institutions or from the absence of foreign intervention?

Bradbury and Walls stress local ownership: clan conferences financed by Somalis, and elders institutionalised in the Guurti. Others add that limited international involvement in the 1990s let local deals mature without spoilers funded from outside. Critics note that the model rests on Isaaq predominance and has struggled to include the Dhulbahante and Warsangali, as the 2023 Las Anod war showed.

Has federalism strengthened or fragmented Somalia?

Supporters see the federal member states as a way to share power among clans and regions after 1991. Critics, including Crisis Group, point to states created along clan lines with uncertain borders, disputes over revenue and security, and repeated breaks with Mogadishu (Puntland 2024, Jubaland 2024, South West 2026). The disputed 2024–26 constitutional amendments sharpened the question, which remained open as of November 2026.
